sections.overview: Polystyrene (PS, PSt) is the styrene homopolymer, which can be produced by aqueous suspension or living anionic polymerization. Its molecular weight, tacticity, and any additive package distinguish a commercial resin or molded article from the base polymer.
sections.nomenclature: PS and PSt identify polystyrene itself, not rubber-modified high-impact polystyrene, styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer, or an expanded-foam article. Those related materials contain additional phases, comonomers, or processing-defined structures and require their own names.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polystyrene is produced by addition polymerization of styrene. The dominant family chemistry is free-radical polymerization, which can be run in bulk, solution, aqueous suspension, or emulsion. Peroxide or azo initiators generate radicals; heat can also initiate styrene in bulk. In suspension polymerization, styrene droplets are dispersed in water with a protective colloid or suspending agent and polymerize into beads, while staged initiator addition helps manage conversion and heat generation. One cited patent documents aqueous suspension polymerization with peroxides dosed during reaction. A distinct patent demonstrates living anionic polymerization of styrene with sec-butyllithium in a hydrocarbon medium; exclusion of water and other protic impurities preserves active chain ends. Initiator concentration and monomer/initiator ratio control molar mass in the anionic route, and sequential monomer addition can form blocks, although ordinary polystyrene requires only styrene. Chain-transfer agents, regulator feeds, or reactor staging are route controls rather than changes to the repeat unit. Rubber modification and styrenic copolymers are separate compositions or families.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polystyrene (PS) is an amorphous, glassy thermoplastic under ordinary room-temperature service, so its tensile and fracture response is sensitive to molecular mass, thermal and physical-aging history, temperature and strain rate, molding-induced orientation and residual stress, specimen geometry, and crazing. Rubber modification (HIPS), plasticization, recycled content, and mineral or nanoscale fillers create materially different products and must not be collapsed into a single PS value. In one study of unfilled PS film specimens, tensile testing gave strength at break 56 ± 1 MPa, Young's modulus 1.6 ± 0.1 GPa, and strain at break 5.6 ± 0.2%; the same study found that filler identity and loading changed the response. Independently, injection-molded recycled HIPS from electronics waste had room-temperature ISO 527 tensile strength 40.1 ± 0.87 MPa, modulus 3460 ± 49 MPa, and break strain 1.5 ± 0.06% at 5 mm min−1; the study also tested its temperature and tuff-filler dependence. The numerical values are therefore for the named unfilled research material and recycled-HIPS comparator, not universal values for GPPS, HIPS, expanded PS, or filled/recycled grades.
sections.processing:
General-purpose polystyrene (GPPS), high-impact polystyrene (HIPS), and filled PS compounds are melt converted by injection molding and extrusion into profiles, film, and sheet; suitable grades are also blow molded or injection-blow molded and extruded sheet is thermoformed. Grade selection matters because molecular mass, rubber modification, filler, melt flow, heat resistance, and melt strength change filling, drawdown, sag, and cooling. PS absorbs little bulk water, so routine drying is usually unnecessary, but pellets carrying condensation or stored outdoors should be dried; color concentrates and clean regrind should be mixed consistently and contamination from incompatible polymers purged. In injection molding, cylinder/nozzle temperature, screw speed and back pressure, shot size and residence time, injection and hold profile, gate and vent design, and uniform mold cooling govern fill, weld lines, sink, shrinkage, frozen orientation, residual stress, and warpage. Extrusion requires stable melt temperature and pressure, controlled shear, clean streamlined dies, limited drawdown, uniform roll or air cooling, and matched take-up; sheet gauge and orientation then carry into thermoforming. Uniform sheet heating, sag and stretch control, tool temperature, cooling, and demolding govern wall distribution and distortion, while blow-molding grades require sufficient parison melt strength. Excess temperature or residence time can cause yellowing, volatiles, odor, and degradation. Styrene polymerization and rubber-phase formation belong in Synthesis; this section covers compounding and shaping existing resin.

Numerical guidance is bounded to its source. The BASF Polystyrene/Styrolux guide recommends drying outdoor-stored material at 60–80 °C for 2–3 h or using vacuum-vented extrusion, and its route guidance applies to the named BASF GPPS and HIPS grade portfolio rather than every PS. In a distinct open experiment, Moskalyuk and co-workers compounded PS 585 with the study's fillers in a 5 mL twin-screw microcompounder at 220 °C for 10 min and 50 rpm, injected the melt into an 80 °C die, and allowed the removed die to cool in room-temperature air. Their selected 200–220 °C melt-processing range and below-100 °C mold constraint, as well as the strong filler-dependent viscosity and agglomeration behavior, apply only to PS 585 and those nanocomposite formulations and laboratory equipment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polystyrene is the styrene homopolymer; molecular weight and chain architecture depend on the suspension or anionic polymerization route.
sections.properties: Unfilled PS tensile behavior differs from filler-containing materials, and rubber-modified HIPS is a separate multiphase polystyrene material.
sections.applications: The cited sources directly use PS as unfilled tensile-control specimens and as suspension-polymerized resin.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Pure-PS controls, recycled HIPS, and filler composites are not interchangeable; grade, additive, thermal history, specimen geometry, temperature, and test rate determine the reported result.

sections.overview: High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is a rubber-modified polystyrene material produced by polymerizing styrene in the presence of dissolved rubber. Grafting and phase inversion generate the characteristic rubber-modified morphology.
sections.nomenclature: HIPS names the rubber-modified polystyrene material, not general-purpose polystyrene or the rubber feedstock alone. The rubber type, grafting conditions, and resulting morphology are formulation and grade variables; they should be retained when identifying a particular HIPS product.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is a rubber-modified polystyrene made by polymerizing styrene in the presence of a dissolved elastomeric rubber, commonly polybutadiene or a styrene–butadiene rubber. The resulting material contains a polystyrene matrix and a dispersed rubber-rich phase with polystyrene grafting; it is not simply a dry blend of the two polymers. During solution or bulk polymerization, homopolymerization of styrene and grafting onto unsaturation in the rubber occur together, and phase inversion changes the morphology from a rubber-continuous to a polystyrene-continuous system. Documented processes control initiators, conversion, temperature, shear, and phase inversion to set rubber-particle morphology. These conditions are process examples rather than a universal HIPS recipe; extrusion and molding occur after the material has been made.
sections.mechanicalProperties: High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is polystyrene modified with a rubber impact modifier; the commercial record for RP-HIPS specifically identifies a butadiene-rubber modifier.  Accordingly, the stiffness--impact balance is formulation- and grade-specific, and the two commercial records below differ in recycled content and melt-flow range.  As a bounded fresh-grade example, ASCHEM HIPS 825E, identified for extrusion and thermoforming with melt-flow rate 4.0 g/10 min (200 °C/5 kg), reports typical ASTM D638 tensile strength 20 MPa, elongation at break 44%, and tensile modulus 2,090 MPa; its notched Izod impact is 135 J/m at 23 °C by ASTM D256.  The supplier marks these as typical rather than specification values.  Separately, The Plastics Group lists a reprocessed RP-HIPS grade (melt-flow range 3--8) at 73 °F with 3,600 psi tensile strength, 20% elongation at break, 260 kpsi tensile modulus, and 2.0 ft-lb/in notched Izod impact; that product-specific record should not be used to infer values for virgin HIPS grades.
sections.processing:
High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) is converted by injection molding and by extrusion into sheet or profile followed by thermoforming. The rubber-modified amorphous melt is generally easy to process, but feed moisture/volatiles, colorant dispersion, gate size, mold temperature, cooling, and residence time affect molded stress, weld lines, shrinkage, and surface quality. Regrind and additive packages should therefore be kept within the grade supplier's limits.

Americas Styrenics' EB6400 sheet gives a bounded grade example: injection molding uses approximately 199–249 °C barrel zones, 213–243 °C nozzle, 2–12 bar back pressure, and 60–150 °F (16–66 °C) mold-surface temperature; its extrusion guidance gives approximately 193–232 °C melt, 199–232 °C die, 66–104 °C polish rolls, and 10–21 MPa head pressure. The same guide recommends a mixing head or static mixer for colorants/additives and warns that sheet orientation above 30% sharply reduces brittleness/tear performance. Independently, an open thermoforming study used HIPS sheet temperatures of 130–170 °C and mold temperatures of 30, 60, or 80 °C; a plug mold and suitable mold temperature improved wall-thickness uniformity. These are EB6400- and experiment-specific settings, not universal HIPS windows; styrene/rubber polymerization is upstream Synthesis rather than Processing.
sections.structureAndMorphology: HIPS is a polystyrene matrix modified with a dispersed rubber phase, typically polybutadiene, formed by grafting and/or physical phase separation during polymerization or compounding. The rubber particles absorb impact energy while the glassy polystyrene matrix provides shape and surface finish.
sections.properties: Compared with general-purpose polystyrene, HIPS has improved impact toughness and resistance to crack propagation while retaining low density, rigidity, and easy melt processing. The tradeoff is reduced transparency and often lower heat resistance or stiffness than unmodified polystyrene, with properties set by rubber content and morphology.
sections.applications: HIPS is used for appliance liners, refrigerator interiors, packaging, disposable products, toys, housings, and thermoformed sheets. It is also used where a printable, opaque, impact-modified styrenic sheet or injection-molding grade is more useful than transparent GPPS.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Impact performance depends on rubber particle size, grafting, rubber type, matrix molecular weight, orientation, thickness, and temperature. HIPS is combustible and can degrade under excessive heat or weathering; a flame-retarded, colored, foamed, or recycled grade should not be assumed to match a base resin.

sections.overview: Styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer is a thermoplastic copolymer containing styrene and acrylonitrile units. Its acrylonitrile content differentiates it from polystyrene and contributes to the material family’s performance balance.
sections.nomenclature: SAN abbreviates styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer. The name denotes a styrene/acrylonitrile copolymer, not ABS, which additionally contains a butadiene-rubber phase.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–acrylonitrile (SAN) is formed by free-radical copolymerization of styrene and acrylonitrile. Industrial routes include continuous bulk or solution polymerization and aqueous suspension or emulsion polymerization. In continuous bulk manufacture, a styrene/acrylonitrile feed can include a small amount of solvent, a peroxide or azo initiator, and a mercaptan chain-transfer agent; the viscous polymer solution is then devolatilized to recover unreacted monomers and solvent. One cited patent example continuously polymerizes styrene and acrylonitrile in ethylbenzene with a peroxide initiator and n-dodecyl mercaptan before vacuum devolatilization. A distinct historical patent uses aqueous suspension polymerization and adjusts styrene feed during conversion to compensate for monomer reactivity and acrylonitrile partitioning, then strips residual acrylonitrile with inert gas. Monomer ratio and feed profile control incorporated acrylonitrile and compositional drift; initiator level, temperature, residence time, and chain-transfer agent regulate conversion and molar mass. SAN is the ungrafted binary copolymer. ABS, ASA, or other rubber-modified materials add a dispersed elastomeric phase or grafting step and are not synonyms for SAN.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SAN is an amorphous random styrene/acrylonitrile copolymer that is typically stiff but has limited unmodified elongation and notch impact. Acrylonitrile fraction, molar mass, residual stress and moisture, injection or extrusion history, temperature and rate, and rubber, fiber, or alloy modifiers determine the strength–toughness tradeoff. NETZSCH describes unfilled SAN as having an elastic modulus near 4 GPa. For Taitalac 1200 SAN, the producer reports at 23 °C ASTM D638/5 mm min⁻¹ yield and break stresses of 700 and 690 kg/cm² (about 68.6 and 67.7 MPa), 5% break elongation, and ASTM D790/2.8 mm min⁻¹ flexural modulus 34,000 kg/cm² (about 3.33 GPa). These are average values for that named resin and test configuration, not a SAN-family range.
sections.processing:
Styrene–acrylonitrile copolymer (SAN) is an amorphous thermoplastic converted primarily by injection molding; suitable grades are also extruded or compounded as blends, alloys, and glass-fiber-reinforced materials. Pellets should be protected from moisture and dried when storage or handling has allowed uptake. Melt and mold temperature, screw speed and back pressure, injection speed and pressure, gate design, reinforcement, wall thickness, residence time, and cooling determine fill, transparency, surface quality, shrinkage, residual stress, and warpage. High speed can help fill because SAN solidifies quickly, but the machine window must be adjusted for the selected acrylonitrile content, molar mass, reinforcement, pigment, and part geometry. Copolymerization belongs in Synthesis; pellet preparation, compounding, molding, and cooling belong here.

Taita Chemical's injection guide gives a bounded supplier window for its general-purpose TAITALAC 1200(Z) and 1400(N/Z) SAN grades: dry at 80–85 °C for 2–4 h, use a 205–235 °C nozzle, a 40–70 °C mold, 50–70 psi back pressure, and 30–100 rpm screw speed, with moderate-to-moderately-high injection pressure and moderate-to-fast injection. The sheet explicitly calls these reference conditions that require equipment and molding adjustment. Autodesk's independent Moldflow material reference gives broader SAN starting guidance of 80 °C drying for 2–4 h, 200–270 °C melt temperature (230–260 °C for most applications), 40–80 °C mold temperature, 35–130 MPa injection pressure, and high injection speed; it also recommends at least 60 °C molds for reinforced grades. These are separate technical starting windows, not a family specification or a reason to combine their endpoints into one universal range.
sections.structureAndMorphology: SAN is a styrene/acrylonitrile thermoplastic copolymer.
sections.properties: Acrylonitrile content and molecular weight affect heat, stiffness, and chemical behavior.
sections.applications: SAN is used in transparent and engineering molded articles.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Supplier data apply to named SAN grades.

sections.overview: Acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene copolymer (ABS) is a multiphase thermoplastic made from acrylonitrile, styrene, and butadiene-derived rubber. Its impact-modified morphology is established during manufacture and varies with composition and production route.
sections.nomenclature: ABS names the acrylonitrile, butadiene, and styrene material class; it is not a synonym for the styrene–acrylonitrile matrix phase or for a particular molding grade. The abbreviation therefore covers commercially variable ABS resins while retaining the butadiene-rubber component in the record boundary.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: ABS combines acrylonitrile, styrene, and butadiene in a SAN-rich continuous phase with a dispersed rubber phase. Two important manufacturing routes are mass polymerization, in which styrene and acrylonitrile polymerize in the presence of a rubber substrate, and emulsion production, in which a polybutadiene latex is made and then grafted with styrene and acrylonitrile. The selected route and component proportions control particle morphology and are therefore material-definition variables, not minor processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Impact resistance and toughness are characteristic design targets for ABS, but grades vary with rubber content, SAN composition, additives, and morphology. Increasing polybutadiene can raise impact resistance while changing other responses. Injection-molding literature also reports that mold temperature and injection pressure affect molded-part properties; measured modulus, tensile, flexural, or impact values must therefore remain attached to the grade and molding conditions.
sections.processing: ABS grades are commonly designated for extrusion or injection molding. The polymerization route produces a resin that is compounded and pelletized before melt conversion, while injection-molding studies show that mold temperature and injection pressure can change mechanical outcomes. Reprocessing behavior can also differ between low- and high-viscosity ABS grades, so a generic setting should not be represented as an all-grade processing window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ABS is a multiphase material in which a rubbery butadiene-rich phase is dispersed within a styrene–acrylonitrile matrix. Particle morphology and the relative component proportions influence its fracture behavior and processing response.
sections.properties: ABS combines the stiffness and processability of the styrene–acrylonitrile matrix with impact modification from the rubber phase. Mechanical and thermal response vary with ABS grade, rubber morphology, additives, and processing route.
sections.applications: ABS is used for injection-molded and additively manufactured plastic parts, including applications where material traceability is relevant.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The traceability review addresses ABS plastics as a varied commercial-material class, while the injection-molding review concerns particular process methods; neither supports a universal property value or processing condition for all ABS grades.

sections.overview: Acrylonitrile–styrene–acrylate copolymer (ASA) is an impact-modified thermoplastic that combines a styrene–acrylonitrile phase with acrylic-rubber particles. In a documented core–shell route, the acrylic phase is grafted and then melt blended with SAN, illustrating the material's multiphase character.
sections.nomenclature: ASA identifies the acrylonitrile, styrene, and acrylate-rubber material class. It is distinct from ABS at the impact-modifier level: the documented ASA system uses an acrylic-rubber core rather than a butadiene-rubber phase; a particular core–shell composition or SAN blend is a formulation within, not the definition of, ASA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: ASA is generally built as an acrylic-rubber impact modifier, commonly a poly(butyl acrylate) core, combined with a styrene-acrylonitrile (SAN) phase. A reported emulsion-graft route slightly crosslinked the butyl-acrylate core and grafted styrene and acrylonitrile onto it; the resulting graft copolymer was melt blended with SAN. This is a documented route and composition, not a universal specification for ASA resins.
sections.mechanicalProperties: ASA mechanics reflect the balance between a glassy SAN phase and dispersed acrylic-rubber particles. In the reported core-shell study, changes in acrylonitrile content and particle-size distribution changed interfacial adhesion and impact response; the highest notched impact result belongs to that 4/6 graft-copolymer/SAN blend. For material-extrusion specimens, tensile, flexural, and impact results varied with the printer settings, so values from printed filament are process-specific.
sections.processing: ASA can be converted by material-extrusion printing as well as conventional melt processing. One FDM study used 1.75 mm filament and varied layer height, infill, raster angle, nozzle temperature, bed temperature, and print speed; these variables affected the measured response. In the laboratory synthesis, emulsion-grafted core-shell particles were melt blended with SAN, illustrating that latex-polymer production and later melt compounding are distinct stages.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ASA is an impact-modified styrenic material with an acrylate-rubber phase associated with a styrene–acrylonitrile matrix. Core–shell particle design and acrylonitrile content alter the morphology relevant to toughening.
sections.properties: ASA provides a balance of rigid-matrix behavior and impact modification. Its response depends on the matrix composition, rubber-particle architecture, additives, and the fabrication route.
sections.applications: The cited study evaluates ASA for fused-filament 3D printing, an application that uses its thermoplastic processability.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The core–shell report concerns particles of specified acrylonitrile content, and the printing study tests particular printing parameters; those results do not define all ASA compositions or manufactured parts.

sections.overview: Methacrylate–butadiene–styrene copolymer is a multiphase impact-modifier copolymer family incorporating methacrylate, butadiene-rubber, and styrene components. It is used as an impact modifier in PVC formulations.
sections.nomenclature: MBS abbreviates methacrylate–butadiene–styrene copolymer. The name describes the component chemistry of the impact-modifier family and should not be conflated with ABS or with generic styrene–butadiene rubber.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Methacrylate–butadiene–styrene copolymer (MBS) generally denotes a staged core–shell graft particle rather than a single random terpolymer. The elastomeric core is commonly polybutadiene or styrene–butadiene rubber, sometimes lightly crosslinked; a harder shell containing methyl methacrylate, optionally with styrene, is grafted onto that rubber latex. A detailed process patent performs the first butadiene-rich emulsion-polymerization stage under free-radical initiation, then feeds a methacrylate and/or vinyl-aromatic monomer mixture to build the outer stage. An independent patent likewise identifies MBS as a core–shell resin produced by grafting methacrylate and optional styrene shell components onto crosslinked butadiene or styrene–butadiene rubber. Core composition, graft level, shell sequence, and particle-size management are route-specific controls, not universal composition limits.
sections.mechanicalProperties: MBS is principally a core–shell rubber impact modifier, so its mechanical significance is usually the response of the host polymer rather than a standalone family tensile value. A butadiene-rich rubber core dissipates impact energy, while the methyl-methacrylate/styrene graft shell promotes adhesion and refractive-index matching with PVC. Modifier loading, core crosslinking, shell composition, particle size and dispersion, matrix compatibility, test temperature, and moulding morphology govern toughening. For a bounded PVC/wood-composite example, an open Thai research report found that 16.7 wt% MBS increased Izod impact strength from 2 to about 7 kJ/m². This is a composite-and-loading result, not MBS itself or a neat-PVC constant. Independent Kaneka documentation identifies the rubber-core/graft-shell architecture and PVC applications; it supports the mechanism but supplies no standalone MBS endpoint.
sections.processing: MBS is generally supplied as a core–shell impact-modifier powder or dispersion and is compounded into a host resin rather than shaped as an isolated neat polymer. Commercial guidance places MBS-modified PVC in extrusion, calendering, film, pipe, blow-molding, and injection-molding operations; engineering-resin MBS grades likewise require selection of a compatible matrix and conversion method. A bounded PVC/MBS formulation patent illustrates the resulting grade dependence: high-speed mixing for 12 min to about 95 ± 2 °C, cooling below 45 °C, twin-screw compounding with zones of about 150/165/175/175 °C and a 170 °C die at 200 rpm, pellet drying at 80 ± 2 °C for 4 h, and injection at 165–175 °C into a mold cooled near 40 °C. Those settings belong to the disclosed PVC formulation, screw, and specimen conditioning, not to all MBS products.
sections.structureAndMorphology: MBS impact modifiers use a rubbery butadiene-containing core with methacrylate/styrene-associated outer phases.
sections.properties: Impact modification depends on particle architecture, PVC matrix compatibility, and formulation.
sections.applications: MBS is used to improve impact performance of PVC materials.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Supplier claims and PVC studies concern named MBS grades and PVC compounds, not all MBS compositions.

sections.overview: Styrene–maleic anhydride copolymer contains styrene and reactive maleic-anhydride units. Its anhydride functionality distinguishes it from polystyrene and enables compatibility or reaction with suitably functionalized formulations.
sections.nomenclature: SMA abbreviates styrene–maleic anhydride copolymer. The term names a composition-variable copolymer family, not a blend of separate polystyrene and maleic anhydride materials.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–maleic anhydride copolymer (SMA) is formed by free-radical copolymerization of styrene with maleic anhydride. The strong tendency of the two monomers to cross-propagate permits nearly alternating, approximately equimolar SMA when the feed is near 1:1, whereas styrene-rich feeds and controlled maleic-anhydride addition give lower-anhydride random copolymers or, in some processes, blends containing polystyrene. Routes include solution or precipitation polymerization, bulk polymerization, and combined mass–suspension manufacture. In one industrially scoped process, maleic anhydride or its styrene solution is fed gradually into polymerizing excess styrene during a mass stage, with an optional radical initiator and chain-transfer agent; the partially converted mass is then dispersed in pH-controlled water and polymerization is completed with a free-radical initiator to form beads. Maleic-anhydride hydrolysis during the aqueous stage can be reversed by later dehydration. A distinct historical route dissolves approximately equimolar styrene and maleic anhydride with a radical generator in a medium that dissolves the monomers but precipitates and chain-terminates the copolymer, providing a low-molar-mass route variant. Monomer ratio and feed profile control composition and sequence distribution, while initiator, chain transfer, temperature, solvent, and conversion regulate molar mass and residual homopolymer. Hydrolysis, esterification, imidization, or other reaction of the anhydride groups is post-polymerization modification rather than formation of unmodified SMA.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SMA is an amorphous engineering thermoplastic whose stiffness, strength, and fracture response depend strongly on maleic-anhydride content, molecular mass, glass-fibre reinforcement, weldlines, and the injection-moulding/reprocessing history. In a 2026 open study, unfilled XIRAN SM200 retained similar tensile modulus through five reprocessing cycles while its tensile strength and strain at break changed; a 30 wt% glass-fibre SMA grade showed response governed by fibre volume and fibre-length loss, and weldlines reduced strength and fracture toughness. A separate full patent reports that preparation route, residual polystyrene, and anhydride fraction can also change the properties of commercial and experimental SMA. As one deliberately narrow endpoint, first-processed injection-moulded XIRAN SM200 in the recycling study had tensile strength 27.0 ± 0.3 MPa and strain at break 18.8% under DIN EN ISO 527 type 1A testing (modulus captured at 1 mm/min and the test continued at 5 mm/min). Those values describe that unfilled commercial grade and specimen protocol only, not reinforced or compositionally different SMA grades.
sections.processing:
Styrene–maleic anhydride (SMA) is an amorphous thermoplastic that can be converted by injection molding, melt extrusion, and melt spinning, and it is frequently melt compounded with impact modifiers, other thermoplastics, fibres, or particulate fillers before shaping. Pellet or powder feed uniformity, pre-drying where required by the grade, melt temperature, shear and residence time, filler dispersion, mold or die temperature, weld-line placement, cooling, and regrind history all affect flow and the finished article. The anhydride groups can react with suitable co-reactants, so moisture, contamination, and intentionally reactive blend partners should be controlled rather than treating SMA as an inert styrenic resin. Reprocessing can change melt flow, while injection shear can shorten reinforcing fibres; those effects depend on composition and cannot be inferred from the neat copolymer name alone. Copolymerization and deliberate derivatization belong in Synthesis; compounding, molding, extrusion, spinning, cooling, and clean production-scrap reprocessing belong here.

A Corning patent demonstrates article-conversion routes with commercial XIRAN SMA and describes melt spinning, twin-screw extrusion, and injection molding. Its bounded 250 g SMA–magnetite trials dry-blended the components, allowed melting for about 2 min in a Brabender mixer held at 250 °C, mixed for 5 min at 50 rpm, and cooled the discharged blend on foil; these settings apply only to those 10–40 wt% magnetite batches. In a distinct study, Taha, Schach, and Stricker pre-dried the commercial XIRAN SM200 and 30 wt% glass-fibre XIRAN SGH60 materials at 80 °C for 3 h to measured moisture contents of 0.046–0.078%, injection-molded them on a DEMAG 420 machine, and air-cooled the specimens at 23 °C. For SGH60, their two mold configurations used 240–265 °C barrel zones, a 260 °C nozzle, an 80 °C mold, and 20 s residual cooling, with different maximum injection and holding pressures for the film- and pinpoint-gated tools. The authors state that both commercial materials were SMA/ABS blends of undisclosed composition, so these numbers are not a family window for neat SMA.

sections.properties: Composition and anhydride content control compatibility, hydrolysis sensitivity, and thermal response.
sections.applications: SMA is used as a compatibilizer and engineering-thermoplastic component.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Recycling studies report specified SMA materials and histories.

sections.overview: Styrene–methyl methacrylate copolymer is a transparent thermoplastic copolymer containing styrene and methyl-methacrylate units. Composition allows properties to be tuned between polystyrene-like and acrylic-like behavior.
sections.nomenclature: SMMA abbreviates styrene–methyl methacrylate copolymer; MS is also used in product contexts. The name denotes a copolymer and should not be treated as a synonym for either polystyrene or PMMA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–methyl methacrylate copolymer (SMMA) is made by free-radical copolymerization of styrene and methyl methacrylate (MMA). Bulk and solution processes yield a homogeneous resin stream that is devolatilized after reaction, while suspension processes disperse the monomer phase in water and recover solid beads. In a cited solution process, a styrene/MMA mixture is polymerized homogeneously with methanol as solvent; a soluble peroxide or azo initiator can generate radicals, and n-dodecyl mercaptan, n-octyl mercaptan, or an alpha-methylstyrene dimer can serve as a chain-transfer agent. A distinct suspension patent charges styrene and MMA into water stabilized with tricalcium phosphate and an extender such as potassium persulfate or sodium alkylbenzene sulfonate; agitation and stabilizer level control bead size, while lower temperature and a larger water fraction manage the heat release of MMA-rich recipes. Other documented variants include continuous bulk or solution reactors followed by removal and recycle of residual monomers and solvent. Because styrene and MMA do not incorporate at identical rates, starting ratio, staged feed, residence time, and conversion determine composition drift and residual-monomer burden. Initiator concentration, temperature, solvent or aqueous-phase recipe, chain transfer, and reactor sequence control conversion and molar mass. SMMA denotes the binary copolymer; rubber grafting or adding acrylonitrile produces a different material family.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SMMA is an amorphous, transparent styrene/MMA copolymer used in optical and injection-moulded parts. Its mechanical response is consequently grade- and molding-history-dependent: the available manufacturer material identifies low residual stress in molded parts and low water uptake as useful attributes, while datasheet results also vary with grade, thickness, test speed, temperature, and conditioning. Neither source establishes a composition-independent family range or a directional/oriented-film response. As one tightly bounded current example, Resirene CET 116, an injection-molding SMMA grade, is reported at 5 mm/min under ASTM D638 with 55 MPa tensile strength at break, 2.5% break elongation, and 2.90 GPa tensile modulus; its 3.175 mm notched Izod value is 16 J/m under ASTM D256. These are average laboratory values for CET 116, with specimen conditioning and geometry beyond the named standard not supplied, rather than values for all SMMA compositions or forms.
sections.processing:
Styrene–methyl methacrylate (SMMA, or MS resin) is supplied in compositions and grades for injection molding and extrusion, including transparent molded articles and extruded optical sheet or light-guide panels. Melt compounding followed by injection or compression molding is also possible for blends. Feed cleanliness, optional pre-drying, melt and tool temperature, shear, residence time, weld-line placement, cooling rate, and post-forming stress relaxation matter because contamination, bubbles, flow orientation, or residual stress can compromise an otherwise transparent article. Extruded strands and sheet can retain flow-induced orientation, while slower hot pressing and cooling can relax it; the magnitude depends on composition, blend partner, thickness, and thermal history. Polymer manufacture belongs in Synthesis; pellet drying, melt mixing, extrusion, molding, cooling, and orientation control belong here.

Denka identifies TX-100S as an injection-molding MS grade and TX-800LF and TX-820 as extrusion grades. Its grade sheet gives a bounded setup for TX-100S: pre-dry at 70–80 °C for 3–4 h, use 190–240 °C cylinder and 220–240 °C nozzle temperatures, and hold the mold at 40–70 °C. Those supplier settings are for TX-100S, not all styrene/MMA ratios or optical products. In a distinct study, Yamaoka and Kimura extruded SBS/MS blends and then injection- or compression-molded the extrudates. They observed strong extensional-flow orientation after die exit and substantially more relaxation after compression molding and slow cooling. That morphology result belongs to their 10–40 wt% MS blends and shows why cooling and forming history should accompany any reported SMMA property or optical result.
sections.structureAndMorphology: SMMA is a styrene/methyl-methacrylate copolymer with composition-dependent amorphous morphology.
sections.properties: Transparency and stiffness depend on monomer ratio, molecular weight, and additives.
sections.applications: SMMA is used in transparent molded and sheet applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Supplier technical data describe individual grades.

sections.overview: Poly(methyl methacrylate) is a transparent acrylic thermoplastic produced from methyl methacrylate. It is widely used in glazing and molded optical applications.
sections.nomenclature: PMMA abbreviates poly(methyl methacrylate). Acrylic is a broader material descriptor, so it should not be treated as a precise synonym for PMMA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) is the vinyl-addition polymer of methyl methacrylate (MMA). Conventional free-radical routes initiate MMA with peroxide or azo radicals in bulk, solution, suspension, or emulsion; initiator loading, temperature, conversion, chain transfer, and heat removal determine the attainable molar mass and dispersity. Controlled-radical routes such as atom-transfer radical polymerization (ATRP) retain the same PMMA backbone but use an alkyl-halide initiator with a catalyst/ligand or photoredox catalyst system to manage radical concentration and chain ends. Published aqueous AGET-ATRP and visible-light organocatalyzed ATRP examples demonstrate this control in emulsion or polar organic media. These examples do not establish one universal formulation for commercial PMMA, and casting, extrusion, polishing, and other article conversion steps are excluded.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PMMA is an amorphous, glassy thermoplastic at ordinary room temperature. Unmodified material is comparatively stiff and strong but has limited resistance to sharp notches and impact; tensile damage commonly develops through craze initiation, craze growth, and eventual crack propagation. Its response is viscoelastic: creep and stress relaxation increase with load duration, and stiffness falls while ductility generally rises as temperature approaches the glass-transition region. Molar mass and its distribution, tacticity and residual monomer, plasticizers or rubber-impact modifiers, casting versus extrusion or injection molding, thermal history and annealing, residual molding or forming stress, molecular orientation, section thickness, notch or surface damage, loading rate, test temperature, and load duration can all alter the measured response. Solvent exposure or absorbed liquids can interact with tensile stress to promote environmental crazing, so conditioning and chemical environment are consequential context.

A bounded molding-grade example is Röhm's PLEXIGLAS 8N, an amorphous PMMA supplied as pellets for injection molding. Its public product information reports typical values of 3300 MPa tensile modulus under ISO 527 at 1 mm/min, 77 MPa stress at break and 5.5% strain at break under ISO 527 at 5 mm/min, and 20 kJ/m² Charpy unnotched impact strength under ISO 179/1eU at 23 °C. The document does not disclose specimen molding history, specimen geometry, or pre-test conditioning, and labels the data as typical rather than specification limits. These figures therefore characterize that named grade and stated tests, not the whole PMMA family.
sections.processing:
Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) molding compounds are converted principally by injection molding and extrusion, while extruded or cast sheet can be thermoformed. Annealing can relieve forming and machining stresses, and finishing, assembly, and welding are common downstream operations. Feedstock drying, melt and mold temperature, screw selection, cooling rate, wall-thickness transitions, and residual-stress control should be developed for the particular grade and optical or dimensional requirement rather than transferred between PMMA products without qualification.

For a bounded injection-molding example, Röhm describes PLEXIGLAS 8N as an amorphous PMMA pellet grade for optical and technical parts and specifies a three-zone general-purpose screw for engineering thermoplastics. Its February 2020 product sheet recommends predrying at no more than 98 °C for 2–3 h in a desiccant dryer, a melt temperature of 220–260 °C, and an injection-mold temperature of 60–90 °C. These values apply to PLEXIGLAS 8N and are guidance rather than a specification or a family-wide PMMA window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PMMA is a glassy amorphous vinyl polymer with methyl methacrylate-derived side groups. The rigid pendant ester groups restrict chain mobility and give transparent articles when molecular mass, residual stress, and inclusions are controlled.
sections.properties: PMMA provides optical clarity, weathering resistance, surface hardness, electrical insulation, and useful stiffness. It is more brittle and less heat-resistant than many engineering thermoplastics, and solvent exposure can cause swelling or crazing.
sections.applications: PMMA is used in transparent sheets and glazing, light guides and optical parts, signage, lenses, displays, medical and laboratory components, coatings, and molded housings. Grades are tailored for casting, extrusion, injection molding, impact modification, or optical performance.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Residual stress, notch geometry, molecular mass, copolymer or impact modifier, colorant, thickness, UV exposure, and solvent contact affect clarity and cracking. Drying and thermal residence also matter; a commercial optical grade is not representative of every PMMA formulation.

sections.overview: Polyacrylonitrile is a nitrile-bearing polymer made from acrylonitrile. It is a major precursor polymer for acrylic fibers and carbon fibers, and its microstructure and molecular weight strongly affect fiber processing.
sections.nomenclature: PAN abbreviates polyacrylonitrile. The name denotes the acrylonitrile homopolymer, whereas many commercial acrylic fibers are copolymers and should not automatically be treated as identical to PAN.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) is the radical-addition homopolymer of acrylonitrile. It can be made by aqueous emulsion or precipitation polymerization using a persulfate-based initiator system, or by solution polymerization in a PAN solvent such as dimethylformamide, dimethylacetamide, dimethyl sulfoxide, or thiocyanate-containing media. Radical initiator type and amount, monomer concentration, temperature, solvent composition, and oxygen exclusion determine polymerization rate, molar mass, and whether the polymer stays dissolved or precipitates. The term PAN here means the acrylonitrile homopolymer; acrylic fibers and carbon-fiber precursor copolymers often contain comonomers and have distinct composition and downstream stabilization/carbonization steps, which are outside this entry's synthesis scope.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) mechanics are strongly form-dependent: precursor-fiber molecular weight and comonomer content, spinning/coagulation history, draw ratio, fiber diameter, void content, crystallinity, and orientation must be retained with any tensile value. In one single-fiber study of 97:3 acrylonitrile/methyl-acrylate copolymer precursor, the high-molecular-weight fiber after a total draw ratio of 18 had tensile strength 241 ± 7 MPa and elongation at break 12.49 ± 1.71%; the undrawn counterpart was 126 ± 3 MPa and 62.26 ± 9.36%, respectively. Independent work on ionic-liquid-spun textile-grade PAN likewise reports that draw ratio changes the fiber tensile response. These fiber results do not define bulk PAN or all PAN copolymer precursor grades.
sections.processing:
Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) is normally solution-spun because conventional PAN grades cyclize or degrade before providing a broad, stable melt-processing interval. Established article-conversion routes include wet spinning, dry spinning, dry-jet wet spinning, gel spinning, electrospinning, and phase-inversion casting or spinning of membranes; specially modified copolymers can also be melt-spun. For wet and dry-jet wet precursor fiber, a filtered and degassed spinning dope is metered through a spinneret, coagulated by solvent–nonsolvent exchange, washed to remove residual solvent, drawn in hot water, oiled where required, dried/densified, and steam-drawn. Dope solids and viscosity, spinneret pressure and temperature, air-gap stability, coagulation-bath composition and temperature, solvent diffusion, jet stretch, total draw, washing, drying, and steam stretch control voids, skin–core structure, diameter, orientation, and filament breaks. Stabilization and carbonization that convert PAN to carbon fiber are downstream chemistry, not PAN article shaping, and are outside this Processing account.

Ahn, Yeo, and Lee review wet, dry-jet wet, gel, electrochemical wet, and modified melt-spinning routes and identify dope viscosity, thermodynamic affinity, air-gap jet stretch, coagulation, and drawing as key controls rather than prescribing a family-wide window. Cao and co-workers provide a bounded pilot-line example for their PAN–2 wt% itaconic-acid copolymer in DMSO: a degassed and precisely filtered dope containing 20% polymer was gear-pumped to the spinneret at 60 °C; coagulation-stage draw ratios were 2 for dry-jet wet spinning and 0.7 for wet spinning, followed by washing, hot-water stretching, drying/densification, and steam stretching. Total draw ratios were 20 and 9.8, respectively. These values describe those matched pilot processes and dope, not all PAN compositions or spinnerets.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PAN is a nitrile-bearing vinyl polymer often converted into oriented precursor fibers.
sections.properties: Fiber behavior depends on molecular weight, comonomers, drawing, and stabilization route.
sections.applications: PAN is used for acrylic textiles and carbon-fiber precursors.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Spinning studies address specified precursor compositions and conditions.

sections.overview: The poly(alkyl acrylate) family comprises vinyl-addition polymers of alkyl acrylate esters. The ester alkyl group, comonomers, and molecular architecture distinguish individual members, so the family does not have one fixed composition or property set.
sections.nomenclature: Poly(alkyl acrylate) is used as a family name for acrylic ester polymers, including poly(n-butyl acrylate) and related members. The family excludes poly(acrylic acid), methacrylate polymers, and any one crosslinked or copolymer formulation as silent synonyms for all poly(alkyl acrylates).
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The poly(alkyl acrylate) family comprises vinyl-addition polymers of alkyl acrylate esters; the alkyl ester substituent and any comonomer identify the particular family member or copolymer rather than a single interchangeable resin. Conventional free-radical polymerization may be carried out in bulk, solution, dispersion, or emulsion, with initiator, solvent, regulator, temperature, feed, and reinitiation determining the resulting architecture and molar-mass distribution. A patent example explicitly uses n-butyl acrylate and 2-ethylhexyl acrylate with AIBN in acetone under nitrogen and a thioester regulator; it is an acrylic copolymer example, not a synthesis prescription for every neat poly(alkyl acrylate). Plasma-initiated chemical-vapor deposition is a separate thin-film route: short atmospheric-pressure plasma pulses fragment alkyl-acrylate monomers, and the fragments can initiate or terminate competing radical/plasma pathways. Plasma-film chemistry should likewise not be generalized to bulk polyacrylate production.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(alkyl acrylates) span soft, generally amorphous acrylic-ester materials whose tensile response is set by ester-side-chain identity, molar mass, copolymer or hard-segment content, and—when a rubber or coating is cured—crosslink density and crosslink chemistry. Temperature relative to the material's glass transition, strain rate, physical aging, orientation, and fillers or other formulation components also matter; an uncrosslinked liquid or pressure-sensitive adhesive cannot be compared directly with a network elastomer. In one room-temperature tensile study at 100 mm min−1, 6% chemically crosslinked poly(n-butyl acrylate) networks incorporating 6% of a PEG-based crosslinker gave an elastic modulus of 3.82 ± 0.13 MPa, tensile strength of 0.63 ± 0.17 MPa, and strain at break of 0.19 ± 0.05; the corresponding UPy-containing network gave 5.57 ± 0.08 MPa modulus and reached 4.5 MPa and 0.8 strain without fracture before the apparatus load limit. Those values describe the named 6%-crosslinked poly(n-butyl acrylate) rubbers and their particular reversible crosslinker, not the whole poly(alkyl acrylate) family. A separate open study likewise distinguishes viscous poly(n-butyl acrylate) with a low density of UPy groups from higher-UPy materials that could be compression-molded into tensile dog-bones, underscoring the role of physical association and specimen preparation.
sections.processing:
Poly(alkyl acrylate)s are usually converted as soft films, pressure-sensitive adhesive layers, latex coatings, solution-cast sheets, and plasma-deposited conformal coatings rather than as unsupported high-temperature melt articles. Coating and casting require control of polymer concentration or latex solids, viscosity, wetting, wet-film thickness, evaporation rate, coalescence, residual solvent or water, and any crosslinking step. In plasma-initiated chemical-vapor deposition, monomer delivery, discharge power, substrate position and temperature, pressure, and residence time couple film growth to polymer formation; the reaction mechanism belongs in Synthesis, while substrate deposition and film conditioning belong in Processing.

Two open studies bound different routes. Loyer and co-workers deposited several poly(alkyl acrylate) films by atmospheric-pressure plasma-initiated chemical-vapor deposition and showed that monomer structure and operating conditions affected deposition and chain termination. In a solvent-casting example, Fage and co-workers made poly(butyl acrylate)-graft-polystyrene films from 20 mL of a 3 wt% toluene solution in 10 cm Petri dishes, evaporated solvent for 24 h at room temperature in a fume hood, water-immersed the dishes for 2 h to release the films, and vacuum-dried them at 50 °C for 24 h, obtaining about 100 +/- 10 micrometre films. That recipe is specific to the graft copolymers and test-film geometry and is not a family-wide coating window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(alkyl acrylates) are side-chain-variable acrylic polymers that can be soft, glassy, or physically crosslinked.
sections.properties: Glass transition and elasticity depend on ester alkyl group, molecular weight, and crosslinking.
sections.applications: They are used in coatings, pressure-sensitive adhesives, and elastomeric films.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Family examples such as PBA cannot define every alkyl-acrylate chemistry.

sections.overview: Polyacrylamide is a polymer of acrylamide with pendant amide groups. It is commonly used in water-soluble form or as a crosslinked hydrogel, with molecular weight and crosslink density controlling material behavior.
sections.nomenclature: PAM abbreviates polyacrylamide. The canonical name refers to the acrylamide homopolymer; copolymer and hydrogel formulations need separate qualification.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyacrylamide is the linear radical-addition homopolymer of acrylamide. Aqueous solution and adiabatic gel polymerizations use water, acrylamide, and a radical initiator system; peroxides, persulfates, azo initiators, and redox couples are documented choices. Monomer concentration, pH, initiator identity and loading, heat removal, and dilution or dissolution after gel polymerization affect conversion, solution concentration, and molecular mass. Mildly alkaline aqueous routes have also used free ammonia or ammonium hydroxide alongside a radical catalyst to produce water-swellable, dispersible polymer. Copolymers containing acrylic acid or sulfonated comonomers, and intentionally crosslinked hydrogel articles, are outside the homopolymer boundary unless separately named.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Reported polyacrylamide (PAAm) mechanics commonly concern hydrated, cross-linked networks rather than a single dry-resin grade. Network cross-linker content, monomer concentration at gelation, entanglement density, equilibrium water content, specimen geometry, and loading mode/rate can all change the response. In an equilibrium-swollen PAAm-gel series tested in tension, the 2% cross-linker specimen (10 × 20 × 3 mm dumbbell) had a Young's modulus of 56 ± 7 kPa, break stress of 22 ± 3 kPa, and break strain of 62 ± 6%; the reported 1–9% cross-linker series spanned 19–157 kPa in modulus. A separate PAAm hydrogel study found that increasing monomer concentration at fixed 5.0 mol% cross-linker raised tensile modulus from 9.6 to 196.7 kPa (1.0 to 5.0 mol/L AAm), while swelling reduced fracture stress and strain. These are gel-network measurements under their stated preparation and test conditions, not general values for all PAAm forms.
sections.processing:
Polyacrylamide is article-processed mainly from water-based solutions, inverse emulsions, or hydrogel precursor mixtures rather than as an ordinary thermoplastic melt. Important operations include emulsion inversion and solution make-up for coating, papermaking, and water-treatment dosing; casting between plates or in molds; photopolymer vat printing of hydrogel articles; and, for selected high-molecular-weight grades or blends, solution spinning and electrospinning. Commercial-emulsion handling requires gentle storage agitation and low-shear transfer, followed by strong localized mixing only where emulsion first contacts dilution water so individual particles invert and dissolve. Water hardness, pH, temperature, concentration, aging time, dissolved iron, oxygen, and order of addition govern fisheyes, incomplete dissolution, viscosity loss, and solution life. Hydrogel shaping additionally requires control of resin rheology, oxygen inhibition, exposure dose, layer release, washing, and swelling after cure.

The SNF handbook's numbers are guidance for its inverse-emulsion products, not for every polyacrylamide. It specifies indoor storage at 5–30 °C, minimal shear during pumping and storage, water below 30 °C for make-up, emulsion addition into water, and about 5 g/L active polymer (10–15 g/L commercial emulsion) as an efficient inversion concentration; harder water above roughly 300–400 ppm as CaCO3 slows inversion. As a distinct shaped-hydrogel example, Wang and Li printed their stated acrylamide/bis-acrylamide, tartrazine, and LAP resin at room temperature by DLP using 100 µm layers, 8 s first-layer and 7 s subsequent exposures, then rinsed the parts and post-exposed them for 10 min under a 15 W, 365 nm lamp. Those settings belong to that formulation and printer, and the article-forming exposure schedule is reported here as Processing even though the underlying network chemistry belongs in Synthesis.

sections.overview: Poly(acrylic acid) is PAA, the vinyl-addition polymer of acrylic acid. It may be prepared by radical polymerization, and later neutralization or crosslinking produces material states distinct from the linear acid polymer.
sections.nomenclature: PAA is the abbreviation for poly(acrylic acid). The record denotes the acrylic-acid homopolymer; polyacrylate salts, acrylic-acid copolymers, crosslinked PAA hydrogels, and a particular neutralized formulation are not aliases for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) is the vinyl-addition polymer made from acrylic acid; a common route is free-radical polymerization in water or another appropriate medium. A bounded aqueous example removes oxygen with nitrogen and uses the potassium persulfate/sodium thiosulfate redox pair to initiate acrylic-acid polymerization; this is a low-molar-mass PAA preparation rather than a universal PAA recipe. PAA can also be made indirectly when tert-butyl acrylate is radical-polymerized and its ester groups are acid-cleaved. In one patent example, AIBN and a protected aminoethanethiol chain-transfer agent are used in toluene before acid treatment converts the poly(tert-butyl acrylate) product to amino-terminated PAA. Initiator system, medium, conversion, and chain-transfer-agent amount are route controls for molar mass and end groups. Those linear-polymer routes are distinct from later crosslinking used to make a PAA hydrogel.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Poly(acrylic acid) (PAA) mechanics are especially state-dependent: dry polymer, neutralized aqueous network, and swollen hydrogel are different materials. In hydrogels, crosslink chemistry/concentration, ionization and pH, water content, fillers, temperature, and strain rate control modulus, strength, and extensibility. An open tensile study reports a neat PAA hydrogel at 152 kPa Young's modulus, 119 kPa tensile strength, and 969% elongation at break; adding 0.05% GO-based covalent crosslinker gave 161 kPa, 248 kPa, and 4078%, respectively. A separate open pH-sensitive acrylic-acid hydrogel study likewise reports that network crosslinking and swelling change tensile response. These hydrogel endpoints do not represent dry PAA or a universal polymer value.
sections.processing:
PAA is commonly converted from aqueous solution into hydrogel films, molded gels, superabsorbent networks, patterned or layered actuators, and substrate coatings. For network articles, the shaping operation may be coupled to cure in a flat mold or template; the underlying polymer-forming chemistry belongs in Synthesis, while filling, heat or radiation exposure, demolding, washing, swelling, drying, and patterning belong in Processing. Solution neutralization, viscosity, degassing, crosslinker and initiator distribution, mold heat transfer and exotherm, layer-to-layer interpenetration, residual-sol removal, and hydration history govern cavitation, uniformity, swelling, adhesion, and final dimensions.

Lee and co-workers provide a bounded flat-film example. They degassed an 80%-neutralized acrylic-acid formulation by nitrogen bubbling for 1 h, filled an 11.5 x 15 x 0.1 cm glass template, and heated it on a 55 °C plate for 2 h before demolding a freestanding film; sequentially casting a second formulation made adhered bilayers, and crosslinker loading controlled swelling and curvature. In a distinct PAA/graphene-oxide-crosslinker experiment, the authors sonicated the crosslinker/initiator dispersion for 30 min, mixed it into the formulation, filled a two-plate glass mold separated by a 2 mm PTFE spacer, and held it at 58 °C for 4 h under inert atmosphere before demolding. These conditions apply only to the reported formulations and mold geometries.

sections.properties: Swelling and mechanics are pH-, ionic-strength-, and crosslink-density-dependent.
sections.applications: PAA is used in responsive hydrogels and adhesive or absorbent systems.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Graphene-oxide and bilayer-film results concern specific composites and conditions.

sections.overview: The thermoplastic polyester family comprises melt-processable linear polyesters commonly made by step-growth esterification or transesterification of bifunctional diacids or esters with diols. PET and PBT are representative members; crystallinity and formulation distinguish individual materials and grades.
sections.nomenclature: Thermoplastic polyester is a family name rather than one fixed composition. PET, PBT, and related linear polyester members fall within the boundary, while segmented copolyester elastomers, wholly aromatic liquid-crystalline polyesters, unsaturated-polyester thermosets, and a single commercial grade are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The principal thermoplastic-polyester families are linear step-growth polymers made from bifunctional diacids or diesters and diols. Representative semiaromatic members pair terephthalic acid or dimethyl terephthalate with ethylene glycol for PET, 1,3-propanediol for PTT, or 1,4-butanediol for PBT; copolyesters introduce additional diacids or diols to alter crystallization and transition temperatures. Manufacture generally has two reaction stages. Direct esterification of a diacid releases water, whereas ester interchange of a dialkyl ester releases methanol and forms hydroxy-terminated oligomers. Melt polycondensation then proceeds at higher temperature and reduced pressure while excess glycol is removed, shifting the equilibrium toward high molar mass. One cited PET process directly esterifies terephthalic acid with ethylene glycol and uses cobalt-, manganese-, and antimony-containing components during polycondensation. A distinct continuous PBT process transesterifies dimethyl terephthalate with excess 1,4-butanediol using a titanium catalyst, then precondenses and polycondenses under subatmospheric pressure while recovering and recycling butanediol-rich vapors. Monomer purity, near-equimolar functional-group balance, catalyst and stabilizer choice, temperature, vacuum, residence time, and removal of condensates control conversion, molar mass, color, and side reactions. Segmented copolyester elastomers, wholly aromatic liquid-crystalline polyesters, and unsaturated thermoset polyester resins use related ester chemistry but have distinct feedstocks or network formation and are treated separately.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Thermoplastic polyesters cover chemically and mechanically distinct materials, from rigid semicrystalline PET-, PBT-, PTT-, PEN-, and PCT-type engineering resins to amorphous copolyesters and highly oriented aromatic liquid-crystalline members. Rigid semiaromatic grades commonly combine tensile stiffness and strength with dimensional stability and useful creep resistance; depending on temperature, crystallinity, molecular orientation, and impact modification, they may yield and draw extensively or fail in a notch-sensitive manner. Amorphous or heavily comonomer-modified grades generally trade some stiffness, chemical resistance, and high-temperature load retention for transparency or toughness, while wholly aromatic liquid-crystalline copolyesters have a separate, strongly anisotropic response. A single family property range would therefore obscure consequential differences in chemistry, morphology, formulation, and material form.

Mechanical response is governed by backbone rigidity and comonomer sequence, molar mass and chain degradation, crystal fraction and lamellar morphology, physical aging, thermal history, and uniaxial or biaxial orientation. Glass or mineral reinforcement raises modulus and load retention but introduces fiber-orientation, weld-line, and transverse-strength effects; impact modifiers, plasticizers, flame retardants, nucleants, recycled content, and blends can shift the stiffness–toughness balance. Although many engineering polyesters absorb relatively little moisture in service, hot-water aging and moisture present during melt processing can hydrolyze ester chains and reduce strength or ductility. Temperature relative to the glass transition, loading rate and duration, notch geometry, specimen thickness, conditioning, and molding or drawing direction must accompany comparisons.

As one bounded numerical example, BASF reports typical values at 23 °C for uncoloured Ultradur B 4520, an unreinforced PBT standard injection-molding grade. ISO 527-1/-2 measurements give a tensile modulus of 2400 MPa, yield stress of 55 MPa and yield strain of 3.7% at 50 mm/min, with nominal strain at break greater than 50%; ISO 899-1 gives a 1000 h tensile creep modulus of 1200 MPa at no more than 0.5% strain and 23 °C. The same sheet lists ISO 179/1eA notched Charpy impact strength of 5 kJ/m² at 23 °C. These are grade-datasheet typical values, not specifications or representative values for PET, copolyesters, reinforced compounds, oriented film or fiber, or the full thermoplastic-polyester family.
sections.processing:
Thermoplastic polyesters span semicrystalline PET and PBT, amorphous or modified copolyesters, and grades engineered for distinct melt strength and crystallization behavior, so no single processing window represents the family. Important conversion routes include injection molding; profile, pipe, tube, sheet, cast-film and monofilament extrusion; fiber spinning; extrusion coating; thermoforming of extruded sheet; extrusion blow molding; and injection or reheat stretch-blow molding of suitable PET and copolyester grades. Grade selection must match flow, melt strength, crystallization rate, transparency, orientation, heat setting, and the intended cooling or reheating sequence.

Feed preparation is central because moisture hydrolyzes polyester chains in the melt, reducing molecular mass and viscosity even when visible bubbles are absent. Pellets, color concentrate, and regrind should be dried to the grade supplier's limit, moved through a closed dry-air system, and protected from condensation and reabsorption. Processing controls include screw design and speed, shear heating, melt temperature, residence time, back pressure, hot-runner or die stagnation, injection/hold pressure, gate freeze, mold and cooling temperature, extrusion filtration and take-up, sheet gauge, preform reheat uniformity, axial and hoop stretch, parison strength, blow pressure, quench, heat setting, and annealing. Cooling rate and orientation determine crystallinity, clarity, shrinkage, warpage, and dimensional stability. Stoppages require temperature reduction or purging, and regrind should be checked for viscosity loss rather than assigned a universal recycle fraction. Polymerization and solid-state molecular-weight build belong in Synthesis; pellet drying, melting, shaping, orientation, cooling, and heat setting belong here.

BASF's Ultradur guide directly documents injection molding and extrusion of its PBT grades into film, pipes, profiles, sheet, monofilaments, fibers, and coated products, and it ties moisture, residence time, mold temperature, shear, cooling, and regrind history to hydrolysis, degradation, crystallization, and warpage. Eastman's separate guides establish extrusion blow molding for its high-viscosity PET-family copolyesters and thermoforming for named extruded Eastar, Tritan, and Eastalite sheets. For one bounded injection example, Unitika lists its own homogeneous and copolymerized PET molding resins: crystalline material is dried at 130 °C for 8 h or 140 °C for 6 h; its example uses 255–290 °C nozzle/cylinder settings depending on resin type, 150 rpm screw speed, an 8 s injection, 16 s cooling, and 27 s total cycle with chilled molds in the 15–30 °C range. These are supplier examples for those Unitika PET products and mold setup, not family-wide polyester settings.

sections.overview: Poly(ethylene terephthalate) is an aromatic thermoplastic polyester made from ethylene glycol and terephthalate-derived units. It is a major polyester material used in fibers, films, and packaging.
sections.nomenclature: PET is the standard abbreviation and PETE is also used. The canonical name identifies the ethylene-terephthalate homopolymer and should not be used as a synonym for all thermoplastic polyesters.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is a terephthalate polyester made from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid or a terephthalate diester such as dimethyl terephthalate. The ester route performs ester interchange with ethylene glycol to form hydroxyethyl terephthalate intermediates and methanol, then melt polycondenses while removing ethylene glycol. Direct esterification from terephthalic acid similarly forms oligomer before polycondensation, with removal of water needed to advance esterification. Manganese, zinc, cobalt, and antimony catalysts are documented source-specific choices for ester interchange or polycondensation. These route variants produce PET; they do not establish a single universal catalyst package or reactor sequence.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PET is a semicrystalline polyester whose stiffness, strength, and ductility vary markedly with intrinsic viscosity or molar mass, crystallinity and morphology, orientation from drawing or stretch-blow processing, copolymer/contaminant content, and thermal, moisture, and aging history. Test temperature and strain rate are especially consequential near the glass-transition region; hydrolysis, thermo-oxidative processing, physical aging, and repeated recycling can change chain length and the balance of brittle and ductile response. In an open study of filament-based printed recycled bottle-grade PET with no intentionally added HDPE, a single printed specimen gave a Young's modulus of 1.7 ± 0.3 GPa and maximum tensile stress of 44.8 ± 7.7 MPa, whereas a three-print specimen gave 2.1 ± 0.1 GPa and 47.9 ± 3.2 MPa. Those figures apply only to that recycled feedstock, print construction, and tensile protocol—not virgin PET, bottle preforms, drawn film, or fiber. A second open study of post-consumer recycled PET further compares physical aging and crosshead-speed effects, so its results should likewise remain tied to its recycled feedstock and conditioning.
sections.processing:
Poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) is converted into injection-molded parts and bottle preforms, injection-stretch-blow-molded containers, extruded sheet, film, profile and strapping, thermoformed packaging, and melt-spun fibers and nonwovens. Grade intrinsic viscosity, copolymer content, additives, recycled-feed contamination, and thermal history distinguish bottle, sheet, fiber, film, and engineering-molding feeds. PET is hygroscopic: pellets and clean regrind must be dried and protected from reabsorption because melt moisture causes hydrolytic molecular-mass loss. Melt temperature, shear and residence time also affect discoloration and acetaldehyde; rapid cooling retains transparent amorphous preforms or sheet, while mold temperature, reheating, biaxial stretch, draw ratio, cooling, and heat setting control crystallinity, orientation, shrinkage, and barrier performance.

Celanese's polyester manual directly covers injection molding plus profile, tube, monofilament, melt-blowing, and other extrusion routes and emphasizes that Impet PET grades require especially careful drying. The U.S. International Trade Commission independently documents preform injection followed by stretch blow molding, as well as sheet extrusion, thermoforming, and strapping. As one bounded injection example, Unitika's published homogeneous PET-resin setup uses 270-290 °C at the nozzle and front/middle cylinder, 250-270 °C at the rear, a 15-30 °C mold, 150 rpm screw speed, and 16 s cooling; it warns that mold temperatures above 40 °C can prevent complete solidification in that process. Those settings are Unitika's example for its disclosed resin categories, not a universal PET window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PET is a semicrystalline aromatic polyester with ethylene terephthalate repeat units. Crystalline lamellae, amorphous tie chains, and orientation develop during cooling and stretching, producing different morphologies in bottles, fibers, films, and molded articles.
sections.properties: PET provides useful strength, stiffness, transparency in amorphous forms, barrier behavior, dimensional stability, and electrical insulation. Crystallinity, molecular mass, acetaldehyde or moisture history, orientation, and additives influence thermal, optical, and transport properties.
sections.applications: PET is used in beverage bottles, food packaging, films, fibers, textiles, strapping, electrical insulation, and engineering compounds. Amorphous and oriented grades are selected for clarity, barrier, drawability, or dimensional stability.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PET is susceptible to hydrolysis during melt processing if insufficiently dried and can suffer crystallization, warpage, acetaldehyde generation, and thermal degradation. Intrinsic viscosity, comonomer, crystallinity, orientation, reheating, contamination, and recycled content make article-specific qualification necessary.

sections.overview: Glycol-modified poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PETG) is a copolyester made from terephthalate, ethylene-glycol, and glycol-modifier components such as cyclohexanedimethanol. The modification is used to suppress the crystallization behavior associated with unmodified PET and yields an amorphous copolyester in documented grades.
sections.nomenclature: PETG identifies the glycol-modified PET copolyester family, not all PET or every copolyester containing a glycol. The identity of the glycol modifier and the resulting copolymer composition define the material boundary; a particular commercial PETG grade remains a narrower formulation within that family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Glycol-modified poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PETG) is a terephthalate copolyester, commonly made by melt copolycondensing terephthalic acid or a terephthalate ester with ethylene glycol and a glycol comonomer such as 1,4-cyclohexanedimethanol (CHDM). It is not PET merely blended with a glycol. A documented PETG laboratory route esterifies terephthalic acid, ethylene glycol, and CHDM with titanium tetraisopropoxide, then raises temperature and reduces pressure for polycondensation. A separate patent describes a PETG route from DMT, ethylene glycol, and CHDM through ester-exchange intermediates followed by polycondensation. Acid/ester feedstock choice, CHDM fraction, catalyst, and vacuum/temperature sequence are grade-specific; extrusion, thermoforming, and other shaping operations follow polymer synthesis and are not included.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PETG is usually an amorphous glycol-modified copolyester, so unfilled material commonly combines a glassy tensile response with substantial post-yield ductility and useful impact resistance rather than the crystallinity-controlled response of conventional PET. Its mechanical outcome is not a single grade-independent value: glycol comonomer content and molecular weight, moisture and drying history, sheet versus filament versus printed-part form, cooling/thermal history and physical aging, orientation, and filler or blend morphology all matter. In additively manufactured parts, raster orientation, interlayer bonding, voids, build temperature and annealing add further anisotropy and processing dependence. Rigid fillers or a second polyester can raise strength and modulus while reducing elongation if interfaces are poor.

For a bounded neat-resin example, Wang and co-workers tested dried SK Chemicals PETG K2012, compression-molded as 0.5 mm sheets after melt mixing at 230 °C and 50 rpm for 8 min, hot pressing at 230 °C and 20 MPa for 8 min, then water cooling at about 100 °C/min. After 48 h in a drying oven, five dumbbell tests at 5 mm/min gave tensile yield strength 44.38 ± 0.62 MPa, tensile modulus 1076 ± 35 MPa, and elongation at break 223.0 ± 10.2%. Test temperature and the applicable tensile standard were not reported. Independently, Eastman reports for 3 mm Spectar™ Clear copolyester sheet, tested at 23 °C and 50% relative humidity unless noted, ASTM D638 yield strength 48 MPa, break strength 53 MPa, modulus 1800 MPa, and 340% break elongation; the grade, sheet form, and supplier's limited-testing disclaimer prevent treating this as a PETG family range.
sections.processing: PETG is an amorphous thermoplastic commonly converted by extrusion, sheet or film forming, thermoforming, and injection molding. Moisture control is important before melt processing. Autodesk's Moldflow guidance recommends reducing PETG moisture below 0.04%, drying at approximately 65 °C for 4 h without exceeding 66 °C, and treating 220–290 °C as a grade-specific melt-temperature range; it lists 10–30 °C mold temperature, 30–130 MPa injection pressure, and high injection speed provided embrittlement is avoided. In an open PETG/PGA study, neat PETG pellets were vacuum-dried at 45 °C for 12 h, melt blended at 230 °C for 8 min at 50 rpm, then compression molded at 230 °C and 20 MPa for 8 min and rapidly water-cooled under pressure to make 0.5 mm sheets. Those conditions describe the named K2012 laboratory material and a software processing guide, not a universal PETG window; comonomer content, molecular mass, residence time, moisture, and thermal history can change the result.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PETG is a copolyester based on terephthalate units in which a glycol comonomer such as cyclohexanedimethanol disrupts the regularity of PET chains. The reduced packing efficiency suppresses crystallization relative to ordinary PET and gives predominantly amorphous, transparent articles.
sections.properties: The amorphous structure supports clarity, impact resistance, thermoformability, and relatively low haze. PETG remains sensitive to thermal history, orientation, residual stress, and moisture during processing; properties such as chemical resistance and heat distortion are grade- and formulation-dependent.
sections.applications: PETG is used for clear sheets, packaging, display and point-of-sale parts, thermoformed trays, medical and laboratory components, and additive-manufacturing filament. Its combination of transparency and ease of forming is useful where ordinary crystalline PET would be less forgiving.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PETG can soften or deform at temperatures below those used for higher-heat engineering plastics and may be sensitive to solvents, stress cracking, and moisture-related hydrolysis during processing. Glycol composition, intrinsic viscosity, additives, drying, cooling rate, and forming history must accompany comparisons between grades.
