sections.overview: Solution styrene–butadiene rubber is styrene–butadiene rubber produced by solution polymerization, commonly using organolithium initiation. The process route enables control of microstructure and functionalization relevant to compounded-rubber performance.
sections.nomenclature: S-SBR abbreviates solution styrene–butadiene rubber. It is a process-defined SBR subfamily and is distinct from emulsion SBR; it does not name every styrene–butadiene rubber material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Solution styrene–butadiene rubber (S-SBR) is made by copolymerizing styrene and 1,3-butadiene in a dry hydrocarbon solvent, usually by anionic polymerization with an organolithium initiator such as n- or sec-butyllithium. Water, oxygen, and other protic impurities terminate the living chains and are therefore excluded. Because styrene and butadiene have different propagation behavior, a polar randomizer or an alkali-metal alkoxide can promote statistical styrene placement and also alter the fraction of 1,2- versus 1,4-butadiene units. One cited patent combines organolithium with an alkali-metal alkoxide in an alkane solvent to prepare random rubber at controlled styrene content. A distinct patent uses n-butyllithium, tetrahydrofuran or potassium tert-amyloxide as randomizer, and silicon tetrachloride or tetraethyl orthosilicate as a coupling agent. Monomer feed profile, randomizer level, temperature, initiator concentration, and hydrogen-free chain transfer or termination determine composition, vinyl content, molar mass, and sequence distribution. Living ends may be coupled into branched architectures or reacted with functional end-group modifiers before antioxidant addition, solvent removal, and drying. Sulfur crosslinking with an accelerator and activator package subsequently creates the elastomer network; article cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Solution styrene–butadiene rubber is an amorphous random diene copolymer whose useful mechanical response normally refers to a compounded and vulcanized network, not the uncured polymer gum. Above its formulation-dependent glass transition, a cured S-SBR compound can undergo large, substantially recoverable tensile deformation with pronounced rate-, temperature-, and strain-amplitude-dependent hysteresis. Unfilled S-SBR does not provide the strain-crystallization reinforcement of natural rubber, so tensile strength, tear, abrasion, fatigue, hardness, and modulus are commonly governed by sulfur crosslinks and by carbon-black or silica reinforcement. Tire-tread formulations deliberately balance wet traction, rolling-loss hysteresis, heat buildup, wear, and crack resistance rather than maximizing one static endpoint.

Styrene fraction and sequence, 1,2-vinyl versus cis/trans 1,4-butadiene microstructure, molar mass and distribution, branching and chain-end or backbone functionalization set glass transition, chain mobility, and filler affinity. Oil extension and plasticizer, S-SBR/BR or other rubber blending, silica or carbon-black loading, surface area and dispersion, silane type and dosage, mixing temperature and silanization, sulfur/accelerator chemistry, crosslink density and sulfur rank, cure time and temperature, antidegradants, moisture on silica, oxidative aging, test temperature, loading rate and strain history all change the observed response. Reinforcing filler can raise modulus and wear resistance, while too much filler networking or crosslinking can reduce extension and strength; polymer–silica coupling and functionalization can reduce filler–filler hysteresis while improving load transfer.

A bounded tread-compound example used oil-extended Trinseo SLR4630 S-SBR (25 wt% styrene, 63% vinyl within the butadiene fraction, and 37.5 phr oil), 60 phr Ultrasil 7000GR silica, 4.8 phr TESPT silane, and 0.9 phr sulfur with the reported activator/accelerator package. The silica–silane mix was held for 3 minutes at 145 °C, the sheet was press-vulcanized at 160 °C for 1.2 times its measured t90, and ASTM D412 tension was run at 500 mm/min. That formulation gave Shore A 57, stress at 100% and 300% elongation of 1.7 and 7.3 MPa, tensile strength 14.6 MPa, and elongation at break 460%. Raising sulfur alone to 1.5 phr in the same 60-phr-silica system raised Shore A to 61 and M300 to 10.1 MPa but reduced tensile strength to 13.5 MPa and break elongation to 370%. These are compound-specific results, not properties of neat S-SBR, other microstructures, carbon-black compounds, blends, or commercial tire treads.
sections.processing: Solution-SBR (SSBR) is converted as a compounded elastomer: plasticize the rubber, incorporate filler and coupling/activating chemicals under controlled shear and temperature, sheet the intermediate, add sulfur and accelerators in a cooler finishing stage, and then press-mold or otherwise shape and vulcanize the compound. In an open silica-filled S-SBR tire-tread study, the rubber was premixed for 30 s at 15 rpm; silica, silane, zinc oxide, and stearic acid were added during the first stage, silanization was held for 3 min at 145 °C, and the batch was dumped at 145 °C. After sheeting, sulfur and accelerators were added in stage 2 and the compound was dumped below 100 °C; 60/80 phr silica and 0.9–1.5 phr sulfur formulations had 160 °C rheometer t90 values of 14.7–18.2 min, and hydraulic-press vulcanizates used 160 °C for 1.2×t90. An independent silica-filled SSBR/BR study used a 70 rpm initial rotor speed and 160 °C cure testing for 30 min, with tensile specimens cured for 30 min. These are filler-, sulfur-package-, and machine-specific examples; keeping curatives out of the hot silanization stage limits scorch risk, and SSBR manufacture in solution is outside this Processing section.
sections.structureAndMorphology: S-SBR is solution-polymerized styrene–butadiene rubber with tunable microstructure and end functionalization.
sections.properties: Filler interaction and vulcanizate response depend on polymer design and compound formulation.
sections.applications: It is used in silica-filled tire compounds.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Sulfur-variation results apply to stated silica-filled formulations.

sections.overview: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber is a carboxyl-functional styrene–butadiene copolymer material, commonly supplied as a latex or compounded rubber. The carboxyl functionality distinguishes it from unmodified styrene–butadiene rubber.
sections.nomenclature: XSBR denotes carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber. The name describes a functionalized styrene–butadiene copolymer family rather than one fixed styrene, butadiene, or carboxyl-group composition; it does not make ordinary SBR an alias for this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber is made by aqueous free-radical emulsion copolymerization of styrene and butadiene with an ethylenically unsaturated carboxylic-acid comonomer. The acid component can be selected from acrylic, methacrylic, itaconic, maleic, or fumaric acid; its identity, proportion, and any crosslinking comonomer define the particular latex rather than a single universal composition. One patent example starts an itaconic-acid, surfactant, and seed-latex aqueous charge with persulfate, then feeds styrene and butadiene; tertiary-dodecyl mercaptan is included during the feed as a chain-transfer control. A separate staged patent route uses batch and continuous emulsion-polymerization charges of styrene, butadiene, acrylic and itaconic acids, anionic emulsifier, and persulfate/redox initiation; it specifically uses the chain-transfer agent and the late acid-monomer addition to control gel content. These are route-specific latex examples, not a general formulation for every carboxylated SBR.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Mechanical response in the accessible evidence is formulation- and material-state-dependent: an unvulcanized latex film, a filled film, and a sulfur-cured tire compound are not interchangeable XSBR states. Visakh and co-workers used an XSBR latex containing 59% styrene (47% dry-rubber content) as an unvulcanized control and as the matrix for cast films with 4.1–9.0 wt% crab-chitin whiskers. In nanoindentation creep at 23 °C (Berkovich tip, 0.05 mN maximum load, 200 s hold; 20 tests per sample), their fitted Burgers-model constants for the unannealed neat XSBR control were K1 = 48.664 N/m and K2 = 80.901 N/m. Those surface-creep fit parameters are not a bulk Young’s modulus; the authors also found that annealing neat XSBR at 100 °C for 90 min did not show the increased indentation resistance observed for the higher-chitin films. In a separate sulfur-cured tire-compound example, 50 phr of a named carboxylated SBR was combined with 50 phr E-SBR, 127 phr N330 carbon black, 95 phr paraffinic oil, zinc oxide, sulfur, and accelerator. The reported compound had tensile strength 8.7 MPa, elongation at break 673%, 300% ring modulus 3.32 MPa, and Shore A hardness 61 at 23 °C; stress–strain data were obtained on a Zwick 1445 tester. This is a filled, oil-extended, sulfur-cured blend—not a neat-XSBR property—and the document does not give tensile specimen geometry, test speed, or statistical basis. These bounded examples should therefore not be combined into family-wide ranges.
sections.processing: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber (XSBR) can be compounded and vulcanized as solid rubber, or used as a waterborne latex for sprayed and dried coatings. Formulation, filler loading, and final cure are article-specific. In a laboratory ENR/XSBR experiment, latex blending preceded coagulation; recovered rubber was mixed with ZnO, stearic acid, CBS, and sulfur, sheeted on a cold two-roll mill, and compression molded at 130 °C for its measured t90. Those conditions apply to that ENR-30/XSBR blend, not all XSBR compounds. A separate carpet-backing patent demonstrates wax-modified XSBR latex sprayed onto wet, skinned foam then dried at 130 °C for 12 min; its 10% solids coating and 60 g/m² dry application rate are example-specific, and heavier coatings can crack on bending and lengthen drying.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Carboxylated styrene–butadiene rubber (XSBR) is a styrene/butadiene latex copolymer containing an acid comonomer; finished materials are commonly filled and vulcanized rubber networks.
sections.properties: Its response depends on the carboxylated-latex composition and on compounding, cure, and filler choices rather than on an intrinsic XSBR value.
sections.applications: A documented latex formulation uses carboxylated SBR with wax for carpet spray coating.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Published creep, tensile, and dynamic results describe named chitin-filled, tire-tread, or coating formulations and their stated test methods; they do not define all XSBR grades.

sections.overview: Nitrile butadiene rubber is an elastomeric copolymer of butadiene and acrylonitrile. Its bound acrylonitrile content is a central compositional variable in NBR production and material behavior.
sections.nomenclature: NBR abbreviates nitrile butadiene rubber. The name identifies the acrylonitrile–butadiene rubber family and should not be treated as a synonym for butadiene rubber without nitrile comonomer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is the synthetic copolymer of acrylonitrile and 1,3-butadiene. Commercially relevant routes use aqueous free-radical emulsion polymerization with emulsifier, initiator, and often a molecular-weight regulator, followed by coagulation and recovery of the latex polymer. Acrylonitrile feed and staged butadiene addition influence bound acrylonitrile content and the copolymer’s composition; they are not universal values for all NBR grades. One continuous patent describes incremental butadiene feeds during free-radical emulsion polymerization, while another identifies the binary aqueous-emulsion route and a carboxylated-NBR terpolymer variant. Hydrogenation of NBR produces HNBR, a different material, and finished-article vulcanization is excluded from this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is a cured acrylonitrile--butadiene elastomer, so tensile, modulus, tear, and compression response are compound rather than raw-polymer constants.  Acrylonitrile content and polymer Mooney viscosity, carbon-black or mineral reinforcement, plasticizer, sulfur/peroxide cure system, cure time and temperature, specimen geometry, temperature, strain rate, and ageing environment can all change a reported result.  Two 34%-acrylonitrile supplier compounds demonstrate the required limits.  Astlett NBR B6240 (34% bound acrylonitrile, ML1+4 42 at 100 °C) is tested in ASTM D3187 compound with 40 phr HAF black, 3 phr zinc oxide, 0.7 phr TBBS, and 1.5 phr sulfur; after 35 min at 145 °C, it reports ASTM D412 tensile strength 285 kgf/cm², elongation 600%, and 300% modulus 120 kgf/cm².  Separately, Kumho KNB 35L has 34 ± 2% bound acrylonitrile and a stated ASTM D3187/D412 test compound cured at 150 °C for 40 min in a press with carbon-black IRB #7; it lists tensile strength at least 220 kgf/cm², elongation at least 420%, and 300% modulus 150 ± 30 kgf/cm².  These are deliberately non-interchangeable compound-and-cure examples, not an NBR family range.
sections.processing: Nitrile butadiene rubber is normally converted as a compounded elastomer: the gum is mixed with reinforcing filler, zinc oxide, stearic acid, sulfur, and an accelerator, then shaped by extrusion, calendering, or molding and vulcanized. The Astlett B6240 sheet identifies that grade as suitable for extrusion and calendering and gives an ASTM D3187 compound of 100 parts B6240 NBR, 40 parts HAF carbon black, 3 parts zinc oxide, 1 part stearic acid, 0.7 part TBBS, and 1.5 parts sulfur; its stated cure example is 35 min at 145 °C. A separate Kumho KNB 35L sheet gives a different bound-acrylonitrile grade and an IRB #7 carbon-black compound press-cured at 150 °C for 40 min. The formulations and cure cycles are named-grade test recipes, so they should not be generalized across NBR grades, acrylonitrile levels, filler systems, or article thicknesses.
sections.structureAndMorphology: NBR is an acrylonitrile–butadiene elastomer whose nitrile content sets a central composition variable.
sections.properties: Oil resistance, low-temperature response, and mechanics depend on bound acrylonitrile, molecular weight, filler, and cure.
sections.applications: NBR is used in oil-resistant seals, hoses, and molded rubber products.

sections.overview: Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is the modified nitrile-rubber material obtained by selective hydrogenation of NBR's diene-derived unsaturation. The nitrile-containing copolymer backbone remains the starting material boundary while catalyst and hydrogenation conditions control the modification.
sections.nomenclature: HNBR is not a synonym for unmodified nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR): it specifically denotes hydrogenated NBR. Residual unsaturation, acrylonitrile content, and a subsequent vulcanized network are separate grade or formulation descriptors that should accompany any particular HNBR material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is a chemically modified nitrile-butadiene rubber, made by selectively hydrogenating the residual carbon–carbon unsaturation in NBR rather than by a new acrylonitrile/butadiene copolymerization. NBR itself is the acrylonitrile–butadiene copolymer precursor. Documented solution-hydrogenation routes contact dissolved NBR with hydrogen and noble-metal catalysts, including rhodium, ruthenium, or palladium systems; catalyst and ligand choice, solvent, hydrogen pressure, and conversion determine the degree and selectivity of hydrogenation. A heterogeneous palladium/rhodium catalyst patent and an open-access report on metathesis/hydrogenation provide complementary examples. Hydrogenation of nitrile groups is a different, more extensive modification and should not be assumed for conventional HNBR. Vulcanization of the finished rubber is a separate formulation step and is not included here.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is used as a cured elastomer; its tensile and recovery response is governed by acrylonitrile content, residual unsaturation and crosslink density/cure, reinforcement and plasticizer package, temperature, and ageing history.  An open study of sulfur-vulcanized HNBRs containing 34 or 36 wt% acrylonitrile and varied crosslink density reports an amorphous room-temperature state without strain-induced crystallization; stretching instead orients amorphous segments, with the orientation influencing tensile strength, strain hardening, toughness, and recovery.  A bounded compound example is M-Seals HNBR-F/101, a black nominal 75-Shore-A material: the supplier's standard-test-specimen record gives 71 Shore A hardness, 22.70 MPa tensile strength and 346% ultimate elongation by ASTM D412/C, plus 21% compression set after 22 h at 150 °C by ASTM D395/B.  The data sheet expressly cautions that standard specimen results are not directly comparable with finished parts.
sections.processing:
Hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR) is converted as a compounded elastomer: the polymer is masticated and mixed with carbon black or other fillers, plasticizer/process aids, antioxidants, metal oxide, coagent, and a sulfur, sulfur-donor, or peroxide cure package. Internal mixers and two-roll mills are used; staged addition of curatives and strong cooling are important because HNBR compounds build heat and premature scorch would reduce processing safety. Shaped compounds can be extruded, injection-, transfer-, or compression-molded, then vulcanized and, where specified, post-cured. Cure choice and temperature are formulation- and peroxide-specific; oxygen exposure can cause surface reversion in pressureless peroxide cures.

A supplier guide describes a common two-pass internal-mixer sequence: masterbatch discharge near 140 °C, then addition of cure chemicals and second discharge near 100–110 °C, followed by cooled milling. In an independent HNBR-4307 hose-compound study, rubber was thin-pass plasticized on a two-roll mill, ingredients were added in stages, the compound was press-vulcanized at 170 °C for its measured T90, and samples were secondarily cured at 165 °C for 4 h. Those conditions apply to that carbon-black/plasticizer/DCP/TAIC formulation and recycled-powder variants, not to every HNBR grade. Selective hydrogenation of NBR is upstream Synthesis; compounding, shaping, and crosslinking the article belong here.
sections.structureAndMorphology: HNBR is made by selective hydrogenation of nitrile–butadiene rubber, converting much of the residual carbon–carbon unsaturation while retaining polar nitrile groups. The resulting elastomer has a saturated backbone with composition-dependent residual unsaturation and acrylonitrile content.
sections.properties: Hydrogenation improves resistance to heat, ozone, and oxidative aging relative to conventional NBR while the nitrile groups retain useful resistance to oils and fuels. Cure response, hardness, compression set, swelling, and low-temperature flexibility vary with hydrogenation level, acrylonitrile content, filler, and crosslink system.
sections.applications: HNBR is used in automotive and industrial seals, O-rings, hoses, belts, diaphragms, and dynamic sealing components exposed to heat, oil, fuel, ozone, or pressure cycling. Peroxide-cured and sulfur-compatible grades are selected for different service and compression requirements.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: HNBR is not equally resistant to every fluid: polar solvents, strong acids or bases, steam, and extreme low temperatures can remain limiting. Residual unsaturation, acrylonitrile level, cure package, filler, post-cure, temperature, pressure, and compression history must be retained when comparing grades.

sections.overview: Carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber (XNBR) is a nitrile-rubber-derived copolymer/terpolymer that incorporates an unsaturated carboxylic-acid comonomer alongside butadiene and acrylonitrile. The carboxyl functionality enables ionic as well as covalent network formation in formulated latex or rubber articles.
sections.nomenclature: XNBR identifies carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber and is not interchangeable with unmodified nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR). Acid-comonomer level, latex grade, crosslinker, and any filler define narrower materials; a dipped or vulcanized XNBR article is a formulation-specific network rather than the base copolymer alone.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber (XNBR) is an NBR-derived terpolymer/latex in which butadiene and acrylonitrile are copolymerized with an unsaturated carboxylic-acid comonomer. A public patent describes latex polymerization of butadiene, acrylonitrile, and methacrylic acid; the cited recent study likewise frames NBR as an emulsion copolymer and examines carboxylation. Acrylonitrile level and acid functionality are composition variables that affect the resulting latex and cured network.
sections.mechanicalProperties: The carboxyl groups permit ionic as well as covalent network formation, so XNBR mechanical behavior is particularly sensitive to crosslinker, filler, latex grade, and specimen history. An open latex-glove study compared sulfur- and magnesium-oxide-crosslinked XNBR composites and found crosslinker choice and modified-bentonite loading changed tensile, tear, puncture, and abrasion results. These are formulation- and specimen-specific observations, not a general tensile specification for every XNBR latex or compound.
sections.processing: XNBR is commonly handled as a latex for compounding, coating, dipping, film formation, and subsequent crosslinking. The patent describes aqueous terpolymer latex preparation and industrial latex uses, while the recent phase-transfer study varies catalyst chemistry during rubber preparation and then vulcanizes and tests samples. These sources illustrate that pH, solids, cure chemistry, coagulant or dipping conditions, and drying/film-forming history are formulation-specific processing controls rather than fixed family-wide settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Carboxylated nitrile butadiene rubber is an acrylonitrile–butadiene elastomer containing carboxyl-functional comonomer units. The functional groups alter interfacial interactions and cure behavior relative to unmodified NBR.
sections.properties: XNBR is a composition- and cure-dependent elastomer; nitrile level, carboxyl content, latex formulation, crosslinking, and fillers influence mechanical and barrier-related response.
sections.applications: Carboxylated nitrile-butadiene rubber latex is used in protective glove and oil-contact composite applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The glove study evaluates specific XNBR-latex composite formulations, and the phase-transfer study compares a selected catalyst route. Their outcomes should not be generalized to all XNBR latexes or finished vulcanizates.

sections.overview: Butyl rubber (IIR) is the low-unsaturation copolymer of isobutylene with a small amount of isoprene. Its polyisobutylene-rich backbone gives low gas permeability, while the isoprene-derived unsaturation permits vulcanization.
sections.nomenclature: IIR and isobutylene–isoprene rubber identify the same copolymer boundary in this record. Halobutyl rubbers are chemically modified derivatives made after IIR production and are not synonyms for unmodified butyl rubber; a filled and vulcanized compound is likewise a separate formulation state.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Butyl rubber (IIR) is the cationic copolymer of isobutylene with a small amount of isoprene. The isoprene supplies sparse unsaturation that permits vulcanization while the polyisobutylene-rich backbone produces the characteristic low gas permeability. Industrial accounts distinguish low-temperature cationic manufacture from later halogenation used to make halobutyl grades.
sections.mechanicalProperties: IIR combines flex durability with very low gas permeability, but its tensile and dynamic response depends on molecular mass, isoprene level, fillers, plasticizers, and cure system. The cited industrial review treats impermeability as a characteristic of IIR and halobutyl; it does not establish one transferable tensile-strength value. Compound test values should therefore remain tied to the named formulation and test conditions.
sections.processing: IIR is compounded and vulcanized for air-retaining rubber articles, including inner tubes and tire-related components. The published industrial accounts cover the polymerization/manufacturing process and commercial types; they should not be read as a universal mixer or cure recipe. In practice, grade viscosity, filler loading, and cure package set the usable mixing, shaping, and vulcanization conditions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Butyl rubber is an isobutylene–isoprene copolymer with an isobutylene-rich backbone and low unsaturation from isoprene. The small unsaturated fraction permits vulcanization while the backbone structure contributes to low gas permeability.
sections.properties: IIR is an elastomer known for low gas permeability and damping-related behavior, but response depends on isoprene content, molecular architecture, filler, cure state, and compound formulation.
sections.applications: Butyl rubber is used in tire innerliners, inner tubes, sealants, and other air-retention applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The industrial sources cover manufacturing and rubber-family behavior rather than one standardized compound. Finished-property claims must specify the particular IIR grade, curing system, and filled or unfilled formulation.

sections.overview: Bromobutyl rubber (BIIR) is a modified butyl rubber made by brominating the residual unsaturation in isobutylene–isoprene rubber. The modification adds cure reactivity while retaining the low gas permeability associated with the butyl-rubber backbone.
sections.nomenclature: BIIR identifies brominated butyl rubber, not unmodified butyl rubber (IIR) or the separately halogenated chlorobutyl material. Bromine content and starting-IIR microstructure remain grade-defining variables, while a vulcanized BIIR compound is a formulation-specific network rather than the base modified polymer alone.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Bromobutyl rubber is made in two stages: butyl rubber is first produced by cationic copolymerization of isobutylene with a small amount of isoprene, then the residual unsaturation is brominated. The published rubber-industry account treats solvent halogenation of IIR as the industrial route; bromine content and the starting IIR microstructure remain grade-defining variables.
sections.mechanicalProperties: BIIR is valued for low gas permeability and for the cure reactivity introduced by bromination. Reported compound properties vary strongly with cure package and hardness: one supplier sheet gives a tensile-strength maximum of 18 MPa and elongation-at-break maximum of 650% for its compounds, while a separate technical specification reports grade-specific Mooney-viscosity and bromine-content ranges. These are supplier/compound examples, not intrinsic constants.
sections.processing: Bromobutyl is compounded and vulcanized for articles such as tire inner liners, tubes, technical rubber goods, and pharmaceutical closures. The reaction-introduced halogen allows cure systems different from those of unmodified IIR, but compound selection governs mixing and cure response. Supplier documents describe continuous bromination of butyl rubber and state that compound hardness changes final behavior; article-processing conditions must therefore be established for the selected BIIR grade and formulation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Bromobutyl rubber is a brominated derivative of butyl rubber, retaining an isobutylene-rich backbone with a low level of reactive halogenated unsaturation. Curing converts the compounded material to a formulation-specific network.
sections.properties: Bromobutyl combines low gas permeability associated with butyl rubber and reactivity introduced by bromination. Final properties depend on bromine content, grade, curatives, filler, and vulcanization conditions.
sections.applications: Bromobutyl rubbers are used in tire-innerliner, sealing, and other air-retention rubber applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The industrial review discusses butyl-rubber families, whereas the data sheet gives values for a named bromobutyl product. Grade-specific specification values must not be generalized to all BIIR compounds or vulcanizates.

sections.overview: Chlorobutyl rubber is a chlorinated derivative of butyl rubber, an isobutylene–isoprene elastomer. Its halogen functionality distinguishes it from the unhalogenated parent rubber.
sections.nomenclature: CIIR is the customary abbreviation for chlorobutyl rubber. It is distinct from unhalogenated butyl rubber (IIR) and from bromobutyl rubber; those related elastomers are not synonyms for this chlorine-functionalized material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chlorobutyl rubber is a chemically modified butyl rubber. Its parent elastomer is an isobutylene–isoprene copolymer made by low-temperature copolymerization; an NPTEL course example describes methyl chloride as the polymerization medium and 1–3% isoprene in the feed description. Chlorination is then a separate post-polymerization reaction: the parent rubber is dissolved in an inert hydrocarbon, commonly hexane, and contacted with chlorine. The cited industrial patent makes clear that hydrogen chloride accompanies chlorine incorporation, so chlorine charge and removal or neutralization are route controls. Vulcanization belongs to subsequent rubber compounding and is not part of the synthesis claim here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Chlorobutyl rubber (CIIR) is an elastomeric butyl-rubber derivative whose tensile, compression-set, stiffness, and damping response are compound properties rather than family constants. Open experimental work describes CIIR as a comparatively high-damping rubber, but its dynamic response varies with temperature and excitation frequency; reinforcing filler, oil or resin additions, crosslink system, and blending with other rubbers further change the result. In particular, a CIIR reference compound had a loss-factor peak at subzero temperature and substantially lower damping above 0 °C, while CIIR/NBR/CPE blends changed both tensile response and temperature-dependent damping.

A bounded tensile example is the reference CIIR compound reported by Roshan-Tabari and co-workers: 100 phr CIIR, 30 phr carbon black, 20 phr paraffinic oil, 3.5 phr coumarone resin, 2 phr sulfur, 5 phr zinc oxide, 1 phr stearic acid, and 3 phr accelerators. Before ageing, it had tensile strength at break of 7.0 ± 0.9 MPa and elongation at break of 762 ± 91% by ISO 37; after 168 h at 70 °C, the corresponding values were 8.1 ± 0.7 MPa and 720 ± 51%. The paper does not report the ISO 37 specimen geometry or tensile-test temperature. These values describe that filled and cured reference compound, not unfilled CIIR or a universal chlorobutyl-rubber range.

A commercial lining sheet further illustrates formulation specificity: Polycorp 1055 is explicitly a blended chlorobutyl lining with a soft natural-rubber tie gum. Its press-cured ASTM D3182 sample-sheet data specify a minimum ASTM D412 tensile strength of 900 psi and minimum elongation of 400%, with face hardness 55 ± 5 Shore A. Those minimum values do not define the CIIR family or a neat chlorobutyl grade.
sections.processing: Chlorobutyl is converted as a compounded, vulcanizable elastomer into hose, tire-inner-liner or sidewall, belt, sheet, roofing, and wire-insulation articles. Fillers, plasticizers/softeners, tackifiers, stabilizers, pigments, and cure ingredients should be mixed to homogeneity before shaping. In a filled chlorobutyl hose example, an 1100 cm³ Banbury mixed compound and cure ingredients for 4–6 min; approximately 2.3 mm sheet was applied to a steel mandrel and steam-autoclave cured at about 150 °C for 40 or 60 min. This is a formulation/article example, not a universal schedule. A separate carbon-black/ZnO/stearic-acid compound was vulcanized at 160 °C for 30 min, illustrating compound-dependent cure conditions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Chlorobutyl rubber is butyl rubber whose residual isoprene-derived unsaturation has been chlorinated, yielding a modified isobutylene/isoprene elastomer.
sections.properties: Its reported tensile and damping behavior belongs to specified vulcanized compounds and changes with temperature, frequency, fillers, and cure formulation.
sections.applications: Chlorobutyl rubber is directly documented in rubber lining sheet and hose-compound applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited results are for named blends or filled vulcanizates and specified test conditions; chlorine content, parent-IIR grade, compound formulation, and cure prevent family-wide property values.

sections.overview: Polychloroprene rubber is an elastomer made by polymerization of chloroprene. Its chlorine-bearing diene-polymer backbone distinguishes it from polybutadiene and supports use in specialty rubber compounds.
sections.nomenclature: CR abbreviates polychloroprene rubber, and chloroprene rubber is an equivalent common name. “Neoprene” is a commercial name and should not be used as the canonical family name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polychloroprene is produced by free-radical polymerization of chloroprene (2-chloro-1,3-butadiene), most commonly in alkaline aqueous emulsion. Water, emulsifier, radical initiator, and a chain-transfer or sulfur-based modifier are used to manage latex stability, conversion, molar mass, branching, and crystallization behavior. A historical example uses an azo initiator and an alkane thiol in aqueous dispersion. A separate sulfur-free route uses a persulfate/dithionite initiator and a combination of xanthogen disulfide and bis(acylaminophenyl) polysulfide transfer agents, then stops polymerization, removes residual monomer, and isolates the polymer. These are formulation-specific examples; not all polychloroprene uses the same transfer package. Copolymerized chloroprene grades should retain their comonomer limitation, and vulcanization is network formation after polymer manufacture rather than the chloroprene-polymerization step.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Polychloroprene is normally used as a formulated and crosslinked elastomer, so the mechanics of an uncured gum, a dense vulcanizate, an adhesive film, and an open- or closed-cell foam should not be combined. A dense cured compound can undergo large, nonlinear, substantially recoverable deformation with hysteresis and rate-dependent stiffness. Chain regularity and crystallization can add green strength or time- and temperature-dependent stiffening, while the crosslink network controls low-strain modulus, set, strength, tear, and fatigue. Grade modification and molar mass, crystallization rate, metal-oxide and accelerator cure chemistry, cure time and temperature, crosslink density, carbon-black or mineral reinforcement, plasticizer and antioxidant loading, foam density and cell structure, fabric reinforcement and orientation, specimen thickness and notch, temperature, strain rate, cyclic history, oil or water exposure, and ozone or thermal aging are all consequential. Oxidative aging can continue crosslinking and raise stiffness while reducing extensibility before chain scission or cracking dominates.

A bounded compound example is Denka DCR-30, a mercaptan-modified, very-slow-crystallizing polychloroprene grade. Denka's one-sheet test formulation contains 100 parts DCR-30, 1 part antioxidant, 4 parts calcined magnesia, 5 parts zinc oxide, and 0.35 part 2-mercaptoimidazoline, cured at 141 °C for 25 minutes. For that formulation the supplier lists 500% modulus of 1.0–4.0 MPa, tensile strength of at least 14.0 MPa, and elongation at break of at least 750%. These are descriptive formulation-control values, not neat-polymer constants or universal design allowables; specimen geometry, tensile rate, conditioning, and scatter are absent from the sheet. Independently, compression and dynamic-mechanical tests on a commercial black, 5 mm polychloroprene sheet showed increasing stress with rising strain rate or falling temperature, a largely rubbery response down to about −40 °C, and a sharp transition toward glassy behavior below that range. That study's filled commercial sheet and compression geometry are separate from the DCR-30 tensile formulation and should not be numerically merged.
sections.processing: Polychloroprene (CR, neoprene) is processed as a compounded elastomer by mastication, internal or two-roll mixing, calendering, extrusion, compression/transfer/injection molding, and subsequent vulcanization. Cure packages commonly use metal oxides and accelerators; scorch safety, compound viscosity, mold venting, section thickness, and heat removal control the balance between flow and premature cure. Denka's DCR-30 grade sheet gives a bounded test formulation containing 100 parts DCR-30 with 4 parts calcined magnesia and a 141 °C × 25 min cure; the values are for that mercaptan-modified, very-slow-crystallizing grade and formulation. A separate polychloroprene vulcanization patent describes conventional kneaders, rolls, internal mixers, and mixing extruders, a 16 min example mixing sequence, and vulcanization preferably at 140–210 °C under optional pressure, while emphasizing that the exact temperature/time pair depends on formulation, mold, and thickness. Chloroprene emulsion polymerization belongs in Synthesis; this section covers compounding, shaping, vulcanization, and post-cure conditioning.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polychloroprene is a chlorinated diene elastomer made by polymerizing chloroprene. Its backbone retains controlled unsaturation and chlorine-containing repeat units, and crystallization or crosslinking can develop during storage, stretching, or vulcanization.
sections.properties: Polychloroprene offers useful ozone, weathering, oil, flame, and abrasion resistance together with elastomeric flexibility. Crystallization, molecular architecture, filler, plasticizer, and cure system affect modulus, resilience, compression set, and low-temperature behavior.
sections.applications: The directly supported application form is a mixed and vulcanized polychloroprene rubber compound shaped into rubber goods. Hoses, belts, cable jackets, and other articles require the selected compound, cure, and service environment to be retained.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polychloroprene can crystallize during storage or strain and can show limited resistance to some fuels, aromatic solvents, strong oxidants, or high temperatures. Grade type, crystallization state, cure package, filler, aging, and test temperature must accompany service comparisons.

sections.overview: Ethylene–propylene rubber is the binary EPM/EPR copolymer of ethylene and propylene. It is a saturated elastomeric copolymer whose compound properties depend on molecular composition, fillers, oils, and the selected crosslinking formulation.
sections.nomenclature: EPM is the abbreviation used for ethylene–propylene rubber; EPR is also used in the cited literature for the binary copolymer. The record excludes EPDM, which adds a diene, as well as a particular vulcanized compound or an ethylene/propylene copolymer with a different modifier scope.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–propylene rubber (EPR, also called EPM) is the binary coordination copolymer of ethylene and propylene; it is distinct from EPDM because no diene feedstock is used. Conventional solution routes use a vanadium compound with an alkylaluminum cocatalyst, whereas metallocene catalyst systems offer an alternative documented route. One patent describes passing the two monomer gases into dry n-hexane containing vanadium oxychloride and an alkylaluminum catalyst, followed by catalyst removal and solvent flashing. A later patent describes metallocene catalysts for EPR production and contrasts them with vanadium-based production. Catalyst selection, monomer ratio, solvent, and process conditions are route-dependent; sulfur or peroxide vulcanization of a finished rubber article is not part of binary EPR synthesis.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–propylene rubber (EPM) is a saturated elastomer whose useful mechanical response is established after compounding and crosslinking, rather than being a single resin constant. Ethylene content and Mooney viscosity vary across commercial ethylene–propylene grades; in filled vulcanizates, filler/oil loading, cure chemistry, crosslink density and crosslink type, and specimen history govern strength, modulus, extensibility, compression set, and dynamic response. A peroxide network favors thermally robust carbon–carbon links, whereas the cited hybrid sulfur–peroxide study found that a mixed network can change the stiffness–extensibility balance; those findings are formulation-specific.

A bounded research example is Dutral CO 38 EPM (72 wt% ethylene; Mooney 60 MU) compounded with 70 phr N550 carbon black and 10 phr paraffinic oil. Its EPM6 formulation also contained 3 phr ZnO, 1 phr stearic acid, 1 phr sulfur, and 5 phr peroxide. Dumbbells punched from 2 mm compression-molded sheets gave a mean tensile strength of 15.7 MPa when tested at ambient temperature by ASTM D412 at 500 mm/min. This is a result for that cured, filled compound and test protocol—not a general EPM specification.
sections.processing:
EPM/EPR is normally compounded with fillers, oils, and a selected cure package before extrusion or molding; processing behavior varies with ethylene content, Mooney viscosity, oil extension, and filler loading. ENEOS lists EPM/EPDM grades with distinct processability choices: some have excellent extrusion characteristics, some high-speed vulcanization or unplasticized compounds, and others retain extrusion performance at high filler loading. These product-line descriptors support grade selection but do not define one family-wide extrusion or cure schedule.

A bounded high-ethylene EPM/EPDM cable-coating example used an ASTM D2230 tube extrusion test with a 50-mm device, 70 °C screw temperature, 90 °C head temperature, and 20 rpm; the reported samples were subsequently vulcanized at 160 °C for 20 min. The patent treats EPM and EPDM together, so the extrusion and cure settings are an equipment-, compound-, and specimen-specific example rather than a universal EPM recipe.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EPM is a saturated ethylene–propylene copolymer elastomer; it lacks the diene cure sites of EPDM and therefore requires curing approaches suitable for its saturated backbone.
sections.properties: EPM provides weather- and heat-resistant elastomer behavior, but molecular composition, filler, crosslinking, and compound design determine the finished response.
sections.applications: EPM is used in weather-resistant rubber compounds, seals, and related industrial elastomer products.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited crosslink study treats a designed composite, while product information groups EPM and EPDM offerings. Its values or application details must not be transferred between the two rubber classes.

sections.overview: Ethylene–propylene–diene rubber is the EPDM terpolymer of ethylene, propylene, and a nonconjugated diene such as ethylidene norbornene, dicyclopentadiene, or vinylidene norbornene. The diene-derived unsaturation supports subsequent vulcanization of formulated rubber articles.
sections.nomenclature: EPDM is the abbreviation for ethylene–propylene–diene rubber. The diene comonomer is the defining boundary: binary EPM/EPR is excluded, and a cured EPDM compound, reclaimed rubber, or reinforced membrane is a formulation/article state rather than a separate synonym for the terpolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–propylene–diene rubber (EPDM) is produced by coordination terpolymerization of ethylene, propylene, and a diene, commonly a nonconjugated diene such as ethylidene norbornene (ENB), dicyclopentadiene, or vinylidene norbornene. An open review describes the family as catalytic coordination terpolymerization and surveys Group IV catalyst systems; a separate patent identifies solution or slurry Ziegler–Natta manufacture using vanadium compounds such as VOCl3, V(acac)3, or VCl4 with aluminum cocatalysts. A specific historical solution example charges a diene feedstock before ethylene and propylene in a vanadium/organaluminum-catalyzed solution. Diene selection, catalyst chemistry, and monomer conversion govern the product architecture. The retained unsaturation may subsequently support formulation-specific vulcanization, but cure-agent packages and curing schedules do not define EPDM synthesis and are excluded here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–propylene–diene rubber (EPDM) is a vulcanizable terpolymer, so its tensile, tear, hardness, elastic recovery, and aging response are properties of a particular cured compound and construction. Relevant variables include ethylene/propylene balance, diene type and content, cure system and crosslink network, carbon-black/filler and oil loading, reclaimed-rubber fraction, and thermal or weathering exposure. An open study of a Keltan 8550 ECO sealing compound found that replacing virgin polymer with devulcanized EPDM changed network structure: increasing reclaimed content raised Shore A hardness but reduced tensile strength and elongation; reducing the accompanying carbon black and softener partially changed that response. This trend should not be read as a general EPDM value.

A bounded product example is FlexWhite EPDM roofing membrane. The 60 mil membrane, listed at 1.549 mm actual thickness, reported 9.2 MPa tensile strength and 420% ultimate elongation by ASTM D412, Die C; the corresponding 90 mil product reported 11.0 MPa and 495%. These are specific reinforced membrane constructions, not properties of unfilled EPDM resin or every EPDM compound.
sections.processing:
EPDM articles are made from compounded rubber by internal or two-roll mixing, extrusion or calendering, and heat/pressure vulcanization; the cure schedule must be matched to the diene, curative package, section thickness, and target article. A public GenFlex reinforced-membrane process flow lists mixer → extrusion → calendering (with optional scrim) → curing with heat/steam and pressure → trimming and packaging. This is a membrane manufacturing route, not a universal requirement for every EPDM product.

A laboratory EPDM formulation study illustrates bounded feed and cure handling. EPDM, zinc oxide, stearic acid, carbon black, and naphthenic oil were charged sequentially to an internal mixer at 90 °C and 60 rpm; sulfur and accelerator were added in a second stage at 50 °C. After more than 16 h storage, the compound was press-vulcanized at 170 °C under 15–20 MPa. Those temperatures, pressure, dwell history, and formulation apply to the tested vulcanizates; other extrusion profiles, peroxide cures, and thick sections require separate rheometry and heat-transfer validation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: EPDM is an ethylene–propylene elastomer containing a low level of diene-derived unsaturation that enables sulfur or peroxide crosslinking. The selected diene and cure system affect network structure.
sections.properties: EPDM is valued for weathering and thermal-oxidative resistance, but vulcanizate behavior depends on diene content, filler, curatives, reclaimed-rubber content, and aging exposure.
sections.applications: EPDM is used in roofing membranes, seals, hoses, and weather-resistant rubber articles.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The membrane declaration concerns a specific reinforced roofing product, and aging studies concern formulated vulcanizates. Their values and aging results are not general EPDM-family properties.

sections.overview: Acrylic rubber is the ACM family of alkyl-acrylate copolymer elastomers. Its cure-site comonomer and selected cure system are formulation variables, so a finished vulcanized network is not a single, composition-invariant ACM material.
sections.nomenclature: ACM is used here for acrylic rubber as a family name, rather than for one specified alkyl-acrylate copolymer or cured compound. Cure-site chemistry and the resulting crosslinked network remain part of the particular grade or formulation, not alternate names for the family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Acrylic rubber (ACM) is a family of specialty elastomers made by free-radical copolymerization of alkyl acrylates. Industrial ACM uses emulsion polymerization and incorporates a small amount of a cure-site comonomer; the particular cure-site chemistry and cure system are part of the formulation rather than a universal ACM recipe. Reported ACM composite preparations also apply chemical crosslinking after compounding, illustrating that the final network must be specified when discussing a finished material.
sections.mechanicalProperties: The family is used where an elastomeric response is needed together with heat and oil resistance, but tensile and dynamic behavior depend strongly on cure state, fillers, and blend morphology. A high-damping ACM composite study shows that sliding-graft additions and vulcanization change the measured damping and mechanical response; those results describe that formulated composite, not neat ACM. Cure-site selection and vulcanization therefore preclude treating one compound's tensile response as an ACM-family value.
sections.processing: ACM is commonly compounded and shaped as an uncured elastomer, then vulcanized with a cure system matched to its cure-site comonomer. Industrial literature describes emulsion-polymerized ACM and its curing systems, while an ACM composite study uses two-roll-mill compounding and vulcanization for a specific formulation. Mixing, molding, and cure conditions should consequently be taken from the named compound or supplier guidance rather than transferred across ACM grades.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Acrylic rubber is an alkyl-acrylate copolymer elastomer. A small cure-site comonomer is incorporated into the polymer, and vulcanization converts the formulated rubber into a network whose structure depends on the cure system.
sections.properties: ACM is valued as an elastomer with heat- and oil-resistant behavior, but its final response is governed by acrylate composition, cure-site chemistry, crosslink density, fillers, and other compounding ingredients.
sections.applications: Industrial ACM is used for oil- and heat-resistant rubber articles, including automotive sealing applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Reported ACM properties cannot be treated as neat-family constants: the industrial source distinguishes cure-site and cure-system choices, while the cited composite study concerns a separately formulated, chemically crosslinked ACM composite.

sections.overview: Ethylene–acrylic elastomer is the AEM rubber family based on ethylene and alkyl-acrylate comonomers, with cure-site chemistry used in suitable grades. It is an elastomeric copolymer material whose final network and properties depend on the cure formulation.
sections.nomenclature: AEM is the abbreviation used for ethylene–acrylic elastomer. The record covers ethylene/alkyl-acrylate elastomer copolymers, including specified cure-site variants; it excludes the thermoplastic ethylene–acrylic acid copolymer (EAA), ethylene–methacrylic acid copolymer (EMAA), and a particular cured compound as synonyms.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–acrylic elastomer (AEM) is an ethylene–alkyl-acrylate copolymer family, not the acid copolymer EAA. A manufacturer reference identifies a common AEM composition as ethylene, methyl acrylate, and a small amount of a carboxylic-acid-containing cure-site monomer. A historical DuPont patent supplies one bounded polymerization example: ethylene, a C1–C8 alkyl acrylate, and an optional cure-site monomer react in an inert solvent with boron trifluoride and a free-radical initiator. The cure-site is relevant only for formulations intended to be subsequently crosslinked; it should not be treated as mandatory for every ethylene–acrylate copolymer, and cure schedules are outside this synthesis record.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Ethylene–acrylic elastomer (AEM) is an ethylene/acrylate rubber, commonly with a small cure-site comonomer, whose mechanical behavior is determined after vulcanization. Ethylene-to-acrylate balance controls low-temperature behavior, while cure-site chemistry, crosslink density, filler, plasticizer, hardness, and heat or fluid ageing control tensile, tear, damping, and compression-set results. An openly available AEM technical chapter notes that most commercial AEM materials include a third cure-site monomer enabling diamine crosslinking, so base-polymer composition alone does not define finished-part mechanics.

A bounded AEM technical-sheet example describes an ethylene/methyl-acrylate AEM family with 8–40% methyl acrylate and reports, for its stated test material, 100% tensile stress 6.00 MPa, tensile strength 16.0–16.4 MPa, elongation at break 260–280%, Shore A hardness 63–64, and compression set 16% after 70 h at 150 °C. Tensile values are labeled ASTM D412, hardness ASTM D2240, and compression set ASTM D395. These are supplier test-sheet values for that material, not a universal AEM range. A separate compound supplier reports 60- and 70-Shore-A AEM compounds at 13.8 MPa tensile strength with 450% and 400% elongation, respectively, further showing the formulation and hardness dependence.
sections.processing:
Ethylene–acrylic elastomer is converted as a compounded and vulcanized rubber. The selected AEM grade is mixed with filler, plasticizer or process aid, antioxidant, and its compatible cure package in an internal mixer or on an open mill, sheeted or pelletized, then extruded, calendered, compression-, transfer-, or injection-molded and cured. Cure chemistry is grade-dependent: acid-cure-site terpolymers commonly use diamine systems and may require post-cure, whereas ethylene/methyl-acrylate dipolymers can use peroxide/coagent systems. Ingredient compatibility, stock temperature, dispersion, scorch safety, venting, oxygen inhibition, article thickness, and post-cure requirements must therefore be qualified together.

DuPont's bounded Vamac DP examples were mixed in a small laboratory internal mixer, sheeted on a roll mill, and press-cured for 10 min at 177 °C. The same guide describes extrusion-head temperatures around 70 °C for its dipolymer compounds, pressure of at least 0.41–0.55 MPa during autoclave cure to avoid sponging, nitrogen purging because oxygen inhibits peroxide cure, and 160–190 °C molds. These values apply to the cited Vamac dipolymer compounds and equipment; diamine-cured AEM terpolymers use different packages and usually different cure/post-cure schedules.
sections.structureAndMorphology: AEM is an ethylene/alkyl-acrylate elastomer that may include a cure-site comonomer. The final vulcanizate structure depends on the particular dipolymer or terpolymer and cure system.
sections.properties: AEM balances elastomeric flexibility with heat and oil resistance, but its response depends on composition, crosslinking, fillers, and compound formulation.
sections.applications: Ethylene–acrylic elastomers are used in automotive seals, hoses, and O-rings.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Manufacturer and handbook guidance differentiate AEM grades and cure systems. Values in a named seal or Vamac compound cannot be extended to all AEM materials.

sections.overview: Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber is the CO elastomer made by polymerizing epichlorohydrin (chloromethyloxirane). It is a synthetic rubber material whose formulation and vulcanization determine the properties of a finished article.
sections.nomenclature: CO is the abbreviation for the epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber record; poly(chloromethyloxirane) is an alternate chemical name. The homopolymer boundary excludes ECO, the epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide copolymer, and does not equate a cured compound with the uncured polymer record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber (CO, polyepichlorohydrin) is the ring-opening polymerization product of epichlorohydrin; the resulting repeat units retain chloromethyl side groups. A historical assessment identifies high-molecular-weight CO as a distinct elastomer made from the single epichlorohydrin feedstock. In one modern, source-specific activated-monomer route, epichlorohydrin is added in a controlled manner to a boron trifluoride diethyl etherate/water initiating system in toluene; the report describes operation at 20–40 °C and polymer isolation after conversion. These are polymer-formation examples, not a recommendation of a universal catalyst system or an article cure schedule.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber (CO) is a cured elastomer, so its tensile, elongation, hardness, rebound, and compression-set response belong to a specified vulcanizate rather than to the uncured gum alone. The chlorine-rich CO homopolymer is described as having good oil resistance and low-temperature flexibility but poorer rebound than the ethylene-oxide copolymer. Cure chemistry and crosslink density, carbon-black reinforcement, plasticizer, hardness target, and ageing environment all materially change the measured response; the public EPA report specifically notes carbon black as a tensile-strength improver and plasticizer as a low-temperature-flexibility aid.

A bounded published vulcanizate comparison in that EPA report gives the ECH homopolymer 15.9 MPa tensile strength, 230% ultimate elongation, 82 Shore A hardness, −18 °C low-temperature brittleness, and Lupke rebound 26% at 23 °C and 75% at 100 °C. The report does not identify the complete formulation or the tensile test standard, so these are comparative vulcanizate values, not neat-gum properties or a family range. A separate rubber-compound supplier illustrates the formulation issue: its 50-Shore-A CO/ECO compound 571AG lists 9.7 MPa tensile strength and 400% elongation; because it does not distinguish CO from ECO or disclose a full cure package, it is contextual compound evidence only.
sections.processing:
Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber is converted by conventional elastomer compounding, shaping, and vulcanization. Fillers, plasticizers, process aids, antidegradants, metal oxides, and the selected cure package are incorporated on a mill or internal mixer before extrusion, calendering, or molding. Because many CO cure systems release or generate acidic species, the Vanderbilt handbook emphasizes acid acceptors and pH control; magnesium oxide, calcium carbonate, or calcium oxide may be used in formulation-specific roles to bind hydrogen chloride and support the cure. Mixing sequence and temperature must preserve scorch safety and dispersion, and the chosen press, injection, steam, hot-air, infrared, or microwave cure must be qualified for the compound and article thickness.

A bounded Osaka Soda patent example mixed a stated epichlorohydrin-rubber formulation for 15 min on rolls held at 80 °C, sheeted it, and pressure-molded it at 160 °C and 7.8 MPa for 20 min. The patent also gives a much broader 100–200 °C and 0.5–60 min cure envelope across its examples and cure systems. Neither the roll/mold schedule nor that broad patent envelope is a universal CO production window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: CO is a polyepichlorohydrin elastomer with chloromethyl-bearing repeat units; compounding and curing form a finished rubber network.
sections.properties: Its fuel-, oil-, and gas-resistant elastomer behavior depends on molecular characteristics, cure system, filler, and compound design.
sections.applications: Epichlorohydrin homopolymer rubber is used in seals, fuel-system components, and other specialty elastomer articles.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The EPA assessment and compound guide cover industrial elastomer uses and specified vulcanizates; they do not establish generic properties for every CO grade or cured compound.

sections.overview: Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber is the ECO elastomeric copolymer of epichlorohydrin and ethylene oxide. The comonomer-containing backbone distinguishes it from the epichlorohydrin homopolymer CO; finished performance still depends on formulation and cure.
sections.nomenclature: ECO is the abbreviation used for the epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide copolymer rubber. This copolymer record excludes CO homopolymer and other epichlorohydrin copolymers with different comonomer scopes; a vulcanized ECO compound is a formulation state, not a separate synonym for the base copolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber (ECO) is a copolyether elastomer made by ring-opening copolymerization of epichlorohydrin and ethylene oxide. The historical assessment distinguishes ECO from CO and describes trialkylaluminum/water catalyst systems, with acetylacetone as a catalyst-promoting additive, for epichlorohydrin elastomer manufacture; it also notes that ethylene oxide reacts more rapidly than epichlorohydrin in a cited copolymer operation. An independent patent example instead polymerizes the two epoxides in ether/toluene using an organomagnesium/resorcinol catalyst system, then precipitates and purifies the copolymer. These route examples establish feedstocks and polymer-formation chemistry only; downstream vulcanization is not included here.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber (ECO) is a vulcanized copolyether elastomer whose physical response varies with epichlorohydrin/ethylene-oxide composition, polymer molecular weight, cure chemistry and density, reinforcement and plasticizer loading, hardness target, and ageing medium. Relative to the epichlorohydrin homopolymer, the ethylene-oxide-containing copolymer is described in a public comparison as having better low-temperature flexibility and rebound but lower oil resistance. Zeon likewise presents tensile, elongation, and compression set as values of a ‘typical Hydrin compound’ and a broad compound range, rather than ECO constants.

A bounded vulcanizate example in the EPA comparison reports ECH–ethylene oxide copolymer tensile strength 15.0 MPa, ultimate elongation 320%, Shore A hardness 74, low-temperature brittleness −40 °C, and Lupke rebound 67% at 23 °C and 63% at 100 °C. The source does not give full formulation or tensile-method details, so these are comparative cured-compound values only. Zeon’s current ECO page lists, for a typical Hydrin compound, tensile at break 14 MPa, elongation at break 450%, and compression set 15% after 22 h at 100 °C; the listed across-compound ranges are 8–18 MPa, 150–600%, and 10–25%, respectively. These supplier figures are illustrative formulation ranges, not specifications for every ECO grade.
sections.processing:
Epichlorohydrin–ethylene oxide rubber is processed by compounding the gum with reinforcing or mineral filler, plasticizer and process aid, antidegradant, metal oxides or other acid acceptors, and a cure system, followed by extrusion, calendering, injection molding, or compression molding and vulcanization. The Vanderbilt handbook notes that ECO is compounded broadly like other elastomers but that cure-package acidity and compound pH deserve particular control: acid acceptors such as magnesium oxide, calcium carbonate, or calcium oxide can bind hydrogen chloride and influence cure behavior. Mixing order and stock temperature should therefore be set to obtain dispersion without consuming scorch safety, and cure time must be adjusted for the formulation and article thickness.

A patent example covering an epichlorohydrin/ethylene-oxide copolymer mixed the specified compound for 15 min on 80 °C rolls, formed a sheet, and pressure-molded it at 160 °C and 7.8 MPa for 20 min. The same patent lists press and injection molding plus steam, hot-air, infrared, and microwave heating as possible cure routes and gives a broad 100–200 °C, 0.5–60 min range across its formulations. Those conditions are examples from that cure chemistry, not universal ECO settings.
sections.structureAndMorphology: ECO is a copolyether elastomer containing epichlorohydrin- and ethylene-oxide-derived units. Cure chemistry converts the formulated polymer to a network.
sections.properties: Ethylene-oxide incorporation changes low-temperature and fuel-related elastomer behavior, while final properties remain compound- and cure-dependent.
sections.applications: ECO elastomers are used in seals and automotive fluid-handling rubber components.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The product information describes named Hydrin materials and the EPA report covers industrial elastomer categories; neither should be read as a universal ECO formulation or performance envelope.

sections.overview: Chlorinated polyethylene elastomer is an elastomeric chlorinated-polyethylene material made by chlorinating polyethylene. Its composition depends on the chlorination of the polyethylene starting polymer.
sections.nomenclature: CPE is the general abbreviation for chlorinated polyethylene, while CM is also used for the chlorinated-polyethylene elastomer class. This record is scoped to elastomeric CPE and should not make every chlorinated polyethylene grade an automatic synonym.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chlorinated polyethylene elastomer is obtained by chemical post-chlorination of a polyethylene feedstock, not by an ethylene/chlorine copolymerization. A documented solution route keeps polyethylene dissolved in chlorinated solvent while chlorine is introduced, then recovers chlorinated polyethylene; the cited example limits its stated product range to its selected linear, high-density polyethylene feedstocks and chlorine contents. A separate aqueous-suspension manufacturing example charges HDPE and auxiliaries to water, heats the suspension, and feeds chlorine; its reported sequence includes acid removal, centrifugation, and drying after reaction. These are alternative documented manufacture routes, not a universal recipe or a family-wide elastomer specification.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Chlorinated polyethylene elastomer (CPE, CM) is a chlorine-substituted polyethylene whose tensile and elastic response depends on chlorine content and distribution, molecular-weight/entanglement characteristics, filler and plasticizer package, crosslinking agent and cure, and article form.  A public patent describing wire-and-cable CPE distinguishes uncrosslinked CPE from filled/crosslinked compounds and specifies that its reported ASTM D412 outcomes depend on chlorine content and the chlorination/cure process.  As a narrowly bounded material example, the CPE 135A supplier sheet specifies 35 ± 1% chlorine, Shore hardness no greater than 60, tensile strength at least 8 MPa, and elongation at break 700%; it does not state the test standard, specimen preparation, cure, or temperature, so those numbers are useful only as grade-sheet targets, not a CPE property range.  The patent's separately bounded chlorinated material, made by slurry chlorination at 120--140 °C for 2--5 h, reports for 33--38 wt% chlorine an ASTM D412 tensile strength of 12.5--15 MPa and tensile elongation of 900--1200%; its process-specific results likewise do not establish values for other CPE compounds.
sections.processing: CPE elastomer compounds can be calendered, injection molded, or extruded into cable jackets, hose, tubing, and foam. Molecular-mass distribution and residual crystallinity affect the processability/performance balance; CPE can also be blended or plasticized before conversion. For one CPE/hard-resin composite, heated-shear mixing in an extruder, roll mill, Banbury mixer, or kneader was specified at 130–210 °C, with 210 °C identified as the upper thermal-deterioration limit; these are composite-specific conditions. Its examples used Banbury mixing (120 °C jacket, 80 rpm, 3 min; compound reached 160 °C), roll-sheeting/pelletizing, and 180 °C press molding for 5 min, followed where required by coextrusion or insert molding.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Chlorinated polyethylene elastomer (CPE) is polyethylene modified by chlorination; chlorine content and the starting-polyethylene architecture define the resulting elastomeric material.
sections.properties: CPE properties vary with chlorine level, fillers, crosslinking, and compound design, as reflected in supplier and patent compound data.
sections.applications: CPE compounds are directly reported for wire and cable, hose extrusion, calendering, injection molding, and blend applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Published property ranges and processing conditions are compound- and route-specific; thermal deterioration, cure system, and filler package preclude a universal CPE value or processing window.

sections.overview: Chlorosulfonated polyethylene rubber is a polyethylene-derived elastomer bearing chlorine and chlorosulfonyl functionality. Composition and crosslinking formulation affect the resulting rubber material.
sections.nomenclature: CSM abbreviates chlorosulfonated polyethylene. The name distinguishes this material from chlorinated polyethylene, because chlorosulfonation introduces an additional functional group; commercial names are not treated as canonical family names.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Chlorosulfonated polyethylene rubber is a post-modified polyethylene in which chlorine and sulfonyl-chloride substituents are introduced; it is not simply chlorinated polyethylene. A solution route first chlorinates polyethylene and then reacts the solution with a chlorine/sulfur dioxide mixture. Documented alternatives include solvent-free treatment of finely divided polyethylene in a fluidized bed with gaseous chlorine and sulfur dioxide, optionally preceded by chlorination and assisted by ultraviolet irradiation. In one Dow route, particulate chlorinated polyethylene is contacted with chlorine/sulfur dioxide gas, so its specified polyethylene grade, prechlorination, gas ratio, light exposure, and temperature are example-level controls rather than universal production conditions. Later curing of the rubber is outside this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Chlorosulfonated polyethylene rubber (CSM) develops its useful elastomeric mechanics after compounding and curing. Tensile strength, elongation, stiffness, tear response, hardness, and compression behavior depend on chlorine/sulfonyl-chloride content, cure chemistry and crosslink density, filler type and loading, and the test specimen; a cured-compound result is not an intrinsic property of all CSM grades.

A bounded unfilled-vulcanizate example used CSM43 (43% bound chlorine) crosslinked with iron(II,III) oxide at 160 °C for 15 min. Tensile testing to PN-ISO 37:2017 reported tensile strength at break of 6.97 ± 0.56 MPa and elongation at break of 38 ± 12%. In the same study, CSM29 and CSM35 vulcanizates gave lower tensile strengths (1.61 ± 0.10 and 1.25 ± 0.10 MPa) with different elongation, illustrating the sensitivity to CSM composition and cure network.

For comparison, a supplier’s named acid-resistant CSM compounds 399ES and 399BL (60 and 70 Shore A) list tensile strengths of 12.4 and 13.8 MPa with elongations of 400% and 300%, respectively. Those values are compound-specific and demonstrate why commercial CSM performance must remain attached to the formulation, cure, hardness, and method rather than combined into a family range.
sections.processing: CSM rubber is compounded with fillers, plasticizer/extender, stabilizers, and a cure package, then shaped and vulcanized; dynamically vulcanized CSM/polyolefin blends can be sheeted, compression molded, extruded, or injection molded. One CSM-containing thermoplastic-elastomer patent describes completing cure on a heated two-roll mill or static oven. Its single-Banbury procedure used a 70% load, about 5 min melt blending, then 3 min at 176.7–204.4 °C after addition of cure ingredients; that dynamic-vulcanization procedure is blend-specific. A separate filled/plasticized CSM formulation mixed internally at 65–75 °C for 8–12 min, on an open mill at 75–85 °C for 3–4 min, added accelerators at 88–93 °C for 1–3 min, and ventilated-cooled to 15–35 °C; these values apply only to that formulation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Chlorosulfonated polyethylene rubber (CSPE, also CSM) is chlorinated polyethylene further modified by chlorosulfonation, introducing chlorine- and sulfonyl-chloride-derived functionality.
sections.properties: Measured properties are those of particular CSM29, CSM35, or CSM43 filled vulcanizates and change with composition and cure formulation.
sections.applications: Published CSM sources describe rubber compounds and shaped vulcanized blend articles made by internal mixing, milling, and curing.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Chlorine/sulfonyl functionality, grade, filler, cure system, and test standard govern the reported values; they should not be converted into a single CSPE-rubber property set.

sections.overview: FKM is a family of fluorinated elastomer copolymers whose documented architectures include vinylidene fluoride/hexafluoropropylene dipolymers and related terpolymers. Cure-site monomers or halogen-bearing units can be incorporated to enable particular curing systems.
sections.nomenclature: FKM is a family designation, not a single fluoropolymer composition or cured rubber compound. The VDF/HFP dipolymer and peroxide-curable FKM compositions with additional cure-site monomers are distinct members of the family, so monomer architecture and cure system must remain identified for a specific material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: FKM is a vinylidene-fluoride-containing fluoroelastomer family, not a single fixed copolymer. Documented backbones include vinylidene fluoride (VDF) with hexafluoropropene (HFP), and may add tetrafluoroethylene, ethylene, or perfluorovinyl ethers. A Unimatec patent illustrates aqueous-emulsion manufacture of VDF/HFP and related fluoroelastomer architectures, with a perfluorocarboxylate emulsifier and optional cure-site-forming monomer or bromine/iodine source. Cure-site monomers or halogenated chain ends are composition features selected when later network formation is needed; they should not be confused with the free-radical copolymerization that creates the base FKM. An independent FKM source also distinguishes peroxide-curable terpolymers from VDF/HFP dipolymers lacking those reactive sites.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
FKM is a family of fluorocarbon elastomers whose useful mechanical response follows compounding and cure. Tensile strength, elongation, hardness, compression set, and temperature response depend on fluoroelastomer type, cure system and state, fillers, plasticizers, specimen geometry, and thermal or fluid exposure; compound data cannot be used as an intrinsic FKM family range.

A bounded sheet-compound example is J-Flex A-type FDA-compliant FKM, a 66% fluorine dipolymer. The data sheet reports 64 ± 5 Shore A, tensile strength 14 MPa and elongation at break 250% by ASTM D412, plus 18% compression set by ASTM D395 Method B after 22 h at 200 °C. These values are specific to that cured sheet compound and condition.

An open FKM-compound study printed peroxide-cured FKM tensile bars to ASTM D412-C and used DMA/DSC to establish the processing and cure window. It illustrates that curing route and manufactured form affect the measured elastomer response.
sections.processing: FKM is converted as a compounded, uncured elastomer: polymer gum is mixed with fillers and a cure package, then shaped by compression, transfer, or injection molding and vulcanized. Extrusion can also be used for preforms or specialized additive manufacturing, but the compound must remain below its cure onset until shaping is complete. In an open FKM/FFKM demonstration, Tecnoflon 959 FKM with peroxide and silica was mixed in an internal mixer, single-screw extruded to 1.75 mm filament, and printed on a modified FDM printer. DSC placed the FKM compound's cure onset near 95 °C and completion near 187 °C; the reported printing trial used 130 °C, dry-ice precooling near the drive gears, a short constrained filament path, and a large nozzle to limit premature cure, buckling, and under-extrusion. For a conventional Viton A-201C compound containing MgO, calcium hydroxide, and N-990 carbon black, Chemours reports slabs cured 10 min at 177 °C and post-cured 24 h at 232 °C. These settings are formulation- and equipment-specific rather than FKM-family constants.
sections.structureAndMorphology: FKM is a family of fluorinated elastomer copolymers, commonly based on vinylidene fluoride with hexafluoropropylene and sometimes tetrafluoroethylene or other comonomers. Cure-site units or halogenated chain ends can be included so the rubber phase forms a crosslinked network during cure.
sections.properties: Fluorinated backbones give FKM compounds useful resistance to oils, fuels, heat, and many chemicals, while the cured elastomer remains flexible over a grade-dependent temperature range. Hardness, compression set, tensile response, and fluid resistance are properties of the selected compound and cure system rather than constants of the family.
sections.applications: FKM compounds are used for seals, O-rings, gaskets, hoses, diaphragms, and other components exposed to elevated temperature, fuels, lubricants, or aggressive fluids. Cure-system choice separates general bisphenol-cured grades from peroxide-curable compositions designed for different service environments.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: FKM performance depends on monomer architecture, fluorine content, cure chemistry, crosslink density, fillers, post-cure, and exposure fluid and temperature. Some grades have limited low-temperature flexibility or resistance to hot water, steam, bases, or polar fluids; a commercial FKM compound should not be treated as representative of every family member.
