sections.overview: Perfluoroelastomers are highly fluorinated elastomer families designed to be cured into rubber networks. Their polymer chemistry and cure-site design distinguish them from non-elastomeric fluoroplastics and from partially fluorinated elastomers.
sections.nomenclature: FFKM is the conventional shorthand for perfluoroelastomer. It is a family designation whose detailed copolymer composition and cure chemistry vary; it should not be used as a synonym for every fluoroelastomer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Perfluoroelastomer is a family of curable perfluorinated copolymers, not a single composition. A common architecture copolymerizes tetrafluoroethylene with one or more perfluoro(alkyl vinyl ethers), often perfluoro(methyl vinyl ether), and incorporates a small amount of a functional cure-site monomer. Documented cure-site families include nitrile-functional perfluorovinyl ethers and bromine- or iodine-bearing fluorinated comonomers or chain-end functionality. The base copolymer can be made by aqueous emulsion free-radical polymerization; molecular weight can be adjusted with a chain-transfer agent. The elastomeric network is then formed through the selected cure-site chemistry. This identifies network precursor architecture and polymerization routes without treating a particular curing formulation or schedule as universal.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Perfluoroelastomers are highly fluorinated, crosslinked amorphous elastomers whose useful mechanical response is recoverable deformation rather than high stiffness. In seals they show time-, temperature-, and rate-dependent hysteresis, creep, and stress relaxation, so compression set and retained sealing force are often more consequential than a single tensile strength. They stiffen as temperature approaches the glass-transition region and relax more rapidly at high temperature. Tetrafluoroethylene/perfluoro alkyl vinyl ether/cure-site composition, molecular weight, cure chemistry and crosslink density, post-cure, filler loading and dispersion, and residual volatiles all affect modulus, strength, elongation, hardness, and set. Component geometry, imposed compression, exposure time and temperature, chemical swelling or aging, rapid gas decompression, and surface defects further control service response.

A bounded supplier example is AGC AFLAS FFKM PM-5500, a nitrile-curable tetrafluoroethylene/perfluoro alkyl vinyl ether compound. AGC compared a formulation containing 0.8 parts BOAP curative and 5 parts N990 carbon black per 100 parts polymer with a filler-free formulation containing the same curative; both were press-cured for 20 minutes at 180 °C and post-cured in nitrogen through a schedule ending at 305 °C. For JIS B2401 P-26 O-rings compressed 18% at 300 °C, the reported compression set after 168 hours was 16% for the carbon-black formulation and 21% for the filler-free formulation, increasing after 336 hours to 22% and 28%, respectively. These are in-house typical results for the named recipes, cure schedule, ring geometry, compression, temperature, and duration—not family-wide constants. An industry-coauthored open review supports the family description but does not provide a comparably contextualized independent mechanical endpoint.
sections.processing: Perfluoroelastomers are converted as compounded, uncured elastomers: the gum is mixed with fillers and a cure system, shaped by compression, transfer, or injection molding, and then vulcanized and commonly post-cured. The cure-site chemistry and filler package vary substantially across FFKM compounds, so a family-level schedule is not portable. AGC's AFLAS FFKM PM-5500 information gives a bounded formulation comparison—5 phr N990 versus a filler-free recipe—along with press/post-cure guidance and compression-set testing on a JIS B2401 P-26 O-ring. The independent fluoropolymer review describes fully fluorinated TFE/perfluoroalkyl-vinyl-ether/cure-site elastomers, compounding, and their use as sealing articles, providing family context but not a universal cure recipe. The AGC temperatures, times, formulation, geometry, and test values therefore remain specific to PM-5500 and the named O-ring method.
sections.structureAndMorphology: FFKM materials are highly fluorinated elastomers with cure-site functionality that forms a network on vulcanization.
sections.properties: Resistance and mechanical response depend on copolymer composition, cure sites, compound, and service medium.
sections.applications: Perfluoroelastomers are used for severe-service chemical and high-temperature sealing.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Product data and review conclusions distinguish individual FFKM compounds and cure chemistries; they are not family-wide values.

sections.overview: Tetrafluoroethylene–propylene elastomer is the FEPM fluorinated elastomer made from TFE and propylene, commonly by aqueous radical emulsion polymerization. Cure-site comonomers can be incorporated for subsequent crosslinking, so a cured formulation is not the same record as the base copolymer.
sections.nomenclature: FEPM and TFE–propylene rubber are names used for this copolymer elastomer. The record covers the TFE/propylene backbone and its cure-site variants; FKM/VDF-rich fluoroelastomers, nonfluorinated EPM, and a particular cured compound are excluded.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Tetrafluoroethylene–propylene elastomer (FEPM or TFE/P rubber) is formed by free-radical copolymerization of tetrafluoroethylene and propylene, often with a small cure-site comonomer or halogen-bearing chain-end control. Aqueous semibatch emulsion polymerization is established: deoxygenated water, fluorinated surfactant, buffer, and a persulfate or redox initiator are charged to a pressure reactor, which is pressurized with TFE/propylene feed and replenished as polymerization consumes monomer. The strong cross-propagation tendency produces a substantially alternating fluorocarbon/hydrocarbon backbone, while feed ratio, temperature, pressure, initiator, and chain transfer govern composition and molar mass. One cited patent example adds a fluorinated cure-site monomer during ammonium-persulfate-initiated emulsion polymerization, then coagulates, washes, and dries the latex. A distinct patent prepares TFE/propylene chains in the presence of radical initiator and bromine salt or brominated cure-site species so that the isolated rubber has bromine-bearing terminal or pendant sites. Useful networks are then formed with an organic peroxide, which generates radicals at the cure sites, commonly with a multifunctional coagent such as triallyl isocyanurate to increase crosslink efficiency. Filler and activator packages may be included, but they are formulation choices. Dipolymer, VDF-containing terpolymer, and cure-site-modified FEPM grades must remain distinguished because polymerization and cure chemistry differ. Article shaping and press/post-cure schedules belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Tetrafluoroethylene–propylene elastomer (FEPM) is normally used as a cross-linked rubber compound, so its useful response is a combination of tensile strength and extensibility, tear resistance, hardness, resilience, and resistance to permanent compressive set rather than the properties of the uncured copolymer alone. The alternating TFE/propylene backbone supports retention of rubber properties under heat, steam, bases, and many oils, but low-temperature elasticity is a limitation: an AGC technical brochure lists glass-transition temperatures near −3 °C for its TFE/P dipolymer grades and notes that formulation-dependent brittleness and usable low-temperature limits are not interchangeable. Core TFE/P dipolymers should also be distinguished from supplier grades that add vinylidene fluoride or a cure-site monomer, because those terpolymers can change low-temperature behavior, molding, and compression set.

The principal mechanical variables are TFE/propylene ratio and sequence distribution, molecular weight and raw-polymer viscosity, cure-site chemistry, peroxide and coagent identity, cross-link density, carbon-black type and loading, other fillers and process aids, mixing dispersion, press-cure and post-cure histories, and molded-part geometry. Temperature, strain rate, compression duration, cyclic loading, and thermal aging affect the rubber network. Fluid exposure can change volume, hardness, strength, elongation, and sealing force even when the backbone is chemically resistant, so hot water, steam, acid, base, lubricant, fuel, and amine environments must be reported with concentration, temperature, and time. Moisture by itself is not a single family-wide predictor; hot-water and steam exposure can instead act through compound swelling, additives, cure chemistry, and interfaces.

A formulation series in the AGC brochure isolates one major formulation effect. AFLAS 150P was compounded at 100 parts polymer with 5 phr triallyl isocyanurate, 1 phr peroxide, 1 phr sodium stearate, and 10–50 phr N990 carbon black, then press-cured at 170 °C for 20 minutes and post-cured at 200 °C for 4 hours. Across that series, tensile strength stayed at 16–17 MPa while 100% modulus rose from 2.3 to 9.5 MPa, Shore A hardness rose from 63 to 80, and elongation at break fell from 360% to 210%; compression set after 22 hours at 200 °C changed from 20% to 17% and remained about 28–29% after 70 hours. These values describe those exact supplier formulations and cure schedule, not neat FEPM or a family range. As an independent compound example, SKF's black Ecoflas TFE/P test material is reported as Shore A 85 ± 5, 14 MPa tensile strength, 11 MPa 100% modulus, 150% elongation at break, 15 N/mm tear strength, and 20% compression set after 24 hours at 175 °C, with DIN or ISO methods named for each endpoint. The datasheet does not disclose its full recipe, specimen conditioning, or uncertainty for most values, so it should be used as a grade-level reference only.
sections.processing:
Tetrafluoroethylene–propylene elastomer (FEPM) is converted as a curable rubber compound. Directly supported routes include two-roll, kneader, Banbury or extruder compounding; compression and transfer molding; extrusion of wire insulation, tube, and tape; and molding with heat by extrusion or injection. A typical workflow mixes the gum with filler, processing aid, coagent, acid acceptor where required, and a peroxide package, preforms or extrudes the uncured stock, then press-cures or continuously cures and often post-cures the article. Polymer manufacture and the identity of the cure chemistry belong in Synthesis; mixing, preforming, article shaping, vulcanization equipment, and cure schedules belong here.

Mix cleanliness, gum viscosity, ingredient premixing and dispersion, roll or rotor shear, active cooling, peroxide addition sequence, dump temperature, storage and coagent bleed, remilling, mold release, scorch margin, compound temperature in extrusion, cure-line length, winding speed, part thickness, and staged post-cure heating are important controls. AGC notes that its AFLAS grades cure relatively slowly and may resist mold release; insufficient cure can worsen release. Its guide calls for cooling during milling, keeping rolls below 80 °C, and adding peroxide after the hotter internal-mixer stage or in a cooled second pass. For the named AFLAS 150E extrusion grade, the guide says to keep compound temperature below 100 °C to prevent premature cure and identifies steam autoclaves, fluidized salt baths, oil baths, or electron-beam devices as downstream cure equipment. Its 170–180 °C and 10–20 min compression-molding recommendation is expressly for small parts such as O-rings made from its grades, not all FEPM.

Ukihashi, Yamabe, and Kojima provide a separate bounded conversion example for their Example 11 TFE–propylene copolymer. Example 12 blended 100 parts polymer with 5 parts 2,2'-bis(t-butylperoxy)-p-diisopropylbenzene, 3 parts triallyl isocyanurate, 10 parts magnesium oxide, and 25 parts MT carbon black on a 4-inch roll mill; the compound was press-vulcanized at 150 °C for 40 min and then oven-vulcanized at 200 °C for 20 h. Those settings belong to that patent formulation and are not a universal FEPM cure schedule.

sections.overview: Silicone rubbers are polysiloxane-based elastomer families cured into flexible networks. Their backbone chemistry and crosslinking route distinguish them from silicone fluids and rigid silicone resins.
sections.nomenclature: Q is a class abbreviation used for silicone rubbers, and silicone elastomer is a broad equivalent descriptor. Specific classes such as VMQ and FVMQ are narrower silicone-rubber chemistries rather than aliases for the entire family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Silicone rubbers are elastomeric networks made from linear or lightly branched organopolysiloxanes, most often polydimethylsiloxane-based gums or fluids bearing vinyl, silanol, or other reactive groups. Three major network chemistries are documented. Organic peroxides generate radicals that crosslink suitable silicone gums. Condensation-curing systems react silanol-terminated polysiloxanes with tri- or tetrafunctional hydrolyzable silanes, often using tin carboxylate or amine catalysts and releasing water, alcohol, oxime, acetate, or another leaving product depending on the crosslinker. Addition-curing systems hydrosilylate vinyl-functional polysiloxanes with Si–H-functional crosslinkers using a platinum-group catalyst and release no condensation byproduct. One cited patent describes both peroxide and moisture/condensation formulations, including hydroxyl polymers, multifunctional silanes, and metal-carboxylate catalysts. A distinct patent provides an addition-cure RTV example based on vinyl-bearing organopolysiloxane, organohydrogenpolysiloxane, and a platinum catalyst. Polymer functionality, crosslinker functionality and ratio, catalyst or inhibitor, and filler surface chemistry control network formation. Precursor polysiloxane manufacture is covered by the family record; article-specific mixing, molding, and cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Silicone rubbers are soft, highly extensible crosslinked polysiloxane networks whose tensile response is viscoelastic and usually nonlinear beyond small strain. The siloxane backbone remains mobile far below room temperature, while covalent junctions provide elastic recovery; unfilled or lightly filled formulations commonly have elastic moduli no more than a few MPa and ultimate strains well above 300%. Soft grades generally trade lower modulus and ultimate stress for greater extension. Rate, load duration, and temperature affect stress–strain response, hysteresis, creep, stress relaxation, compression set, and tear propagation, so tensile, tear, hardness, and compression values are not interchangeable family constants.

Molecular weight between crosslinks, crosslinker functionality and stoichiometry, cure chemistry, catalyst level, cure conversion, and post-cure set the network density and defect population. Short strands or over-crosslinking can embrittle the network; incomplete cure, entrained air, residual solvent, poor mixing, and specimen flaws depress ultimate strength. Reinforcing fumed silica and some silicone resins can greatly improve tensile and tear resistance but usually raise modulus and hardness; oils, plasticizers, pigments, flame retardants, conductive fillers, and other additives shift the balance again. Condensation-, peroxide-, and addition-cured RTV, HCR, and LSR products, as well as methyl-, vinyl-, phenyl-, and fluoro-containing families, therefore require grade-specific treatment. Moisture during condensation cure, swelling liquids, thermal aging, test rate, notch geometry, specimen thickness, and processing orientation or voids are also consequential.

As one bounded commercial example, Wacker lists platinum-cured, 1:1 A/B ELASTOSIL LR 3003/50 for molded seals and similar parts at Shore A 50, tensile strength 10.3 N mm⁻² and elongation at break 490% by ISO 37 type 1, tear resistance 26 N mm⁻¹ by ASTM D624 die B, and compression set 13% after 22 h at 175 °C by DIN ISO 815-1. The same product series changes substantially with nominal hardness, and the guide presents typical grade data rather than a universal silicone-rubber range. These values should remain attached to LR 3003/50 and the listed methods and conditioning.
sections.processing: Silicone rubber processing spans solid high-consistency/heat-vulcanizing rubber (HCR/HTV), liquid silicone rubber (LSR), and room-temperature-vulcanizing RTV-2 compounds. HCR/HTV is compounded as a solid feed and can be extruded or coextruded, calendered, or compression-, transfer-, or injection-molded; Wacker describes the extruder screw as homogenizing, compacting, and degassing the stock before die vulcanization, with post-cure selected by grade, part volume, and stabilizer requirements. LSR is metered as two components through a static mixer into a heated mold, while RTV-2 is mixed, degassed, poured or brushed into a mold, and allowed to cure. A Lidor technical brochure describes equal A/B metering, a static mixer, chilled nozzle/cylinder hardware near 20 °C to delay premature vulcanization, and grade-dependent molding cure in seconds at 140–230 °C. For a bounded RTV-2 moldmaking example, SiSiB MR21030 specifies 10:1 A:B by mass, low-speed mixing to minimize air, approximately 90 min working time at 23 °C, vacuum degassing at 30–50 mbar for 5–10 min, and room-temperature cure; it warns that sulfur-containing materials, tin-catalyzed silicones, tin-stabilized PVC, amine-cured epoxies, and some solvents can inhibit platinum cure. Feed temperature, screw/static-mixer cleanliness, mold venting, part thickness, cooling before demolding, residence time, and any post-cure must remain grade-, formulation-, and tooling-specific; silicone network chemistry remains in Synthesis.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Silicone rubbers are crosslinked polysiloxane elastomers.
sections.properties: Modulus and durability depend on base polymer, filler, and cure chemistry.
sections.applications: They are used in medical, automotive, seal, and flexible molded products.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Solid and liquid silicone rubbers have distinct grades and processing.

sections.overview: Methyl-vinyl silicone rubber is a silicone-elastomer class based on vinyl-methyl-siloxane units. It is supplied as a rubber compound and subsequently cured into an elastomeric network.
sections.nomenclature: VMQ is the conventional designation for methyl-vinyl silicone rubber. It distinguishes this vinyl-containing silicone rubber from fluorosilicone rubber (FVMQ) and other silicone-elastomer classes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Methyl-vinyl silicone rubber is an organopolysiloxane gum containing mainly dimethylsiloxane units and vinylmethylsiloxane units; it is a polymer precursor distinct from the subsequently crosslinked silicone article. A documented industrial route ring-opens/equilibrates dimethyl cyclic siloxanes or octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane with a vinyl cyclic siloxane and an end-blocker in the presence of catalyst. Vinyl-ring feed, end-blocker, catalyst, water content, and devolatilization conditions control vinyl content, chain ends, and molecular-weight distribution. One high-vinyl route uses tetramethyltetravinylcyclotetrasiloxane and tetramethyldivinyldisiloxane with tetramethylammonium hydroxide; another uses a tubular polymerizer starting from dimethyl cyclic siloxane. These are source-specific routes. Peroxide or addition curing turns the gum into a network and is deliberately excluded from this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Methyl-vinyl silicone rubber (MVQ) is normally compounded and cured before its mechanical response is measured. Its Si–O backbone supports a wide useful temperature range, but unreinforced silicone has modest tensile, tear, and abrasion strength; reinforcement, cure chemistry, crosslink density, hardness, and temperature are decisive. A specific SKF Ecosil 85 Shore A MVQ sealing compound is reported with DIN 53504 tensile strength of at least 6.5 MPa, elongation at break of at least 130%, and 100% modulus of at least 4.5 MPa; its DIN ISO 34-1 tear strength is 9 N/mm and DIN ISO 815 compression set is at most 20% after 24 h at 175 °C. The sheet limits these values to standardized test specimens and distinguishes nominal batch requirements from general guidance, so they are compound-specific rather than silicone-gum constants. Independent silicone technical data show that commercial grades vary substantially in tensile strength and are selected by hardness, elongation, and service requirements.
sections.processing: Methyl-vinyl silicone rubber (VMQ/MVQ) is converted in formulation-dependent HTV, LSR, or RTV forms by extrusion, calendering/coating, compression molding, transfer molding, and injection molding. The compound normally contains reinforcing silica and a peroxide or platinum cure system; filler level, hardness, cure chemistry, and article thickness determine the usable window. Mesgo's technical page lists extrusion with hot-air, microwave, salt-bath, or steam reticulation, plus calendering/coating and compression or injection molding. A separate VMQ processing guide states that compression or transfer molding is typically carried out at 150–180 °C for a few minutes, followed when needed by post-curing to complete crosslinking and reduce volatiles; the exact schedule varies with mold and wall thickness. These are process-family and guide-level constraints, not a universal recipe for every methyl-vinyl silicone grade.
sections.structureAndMorphology: VMQ is a vinyl-methyl-siloxane elastomer cured into a polysiloxane network.
sections.properties: Final elasticity and thermal behavior depend on vinyl content, fillers, peroxide or addition cure, and compound design.
sections.applications: VMQ is used in molded silicone-rubber seals and flexible components.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Technical sheets report specific compounds, so values cannot be transferred across VMQ formulations.

sections.overview: Fluorosilicone rubber (FVMQ) is a fluorinated silicone-elastomer subfamily built from organosiloxane units that can include trifluoropropyl substitution. Vinyl-containing siloxane units may also be introduced to provide cure functionality in a particular rubber formulation.
sections.nomenclature: FVMQ is narrower than generic silicone rubber: the name identifies fluorosilicone compositions containing fluorinated organosiloxane units. The exact balance of trifluoropropyl-, dimethyl-, and methylvinyl-siloxane units, and any post-cure network, defines a specific material rather than an alternative name for the subfamily.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Fluorosilicone rubber is based on polyorganosiloxane chains bearing fluoroalkyl substituents, commonly 3,3,3-trifluoropropylmethylsiloxane units, and may also contain dimethylsiloxane and low levels of vinylsiloxane units. It is distinct from a fluorocarbon elastomer and from a filler/cure package. Documented raw-polymer routes use ring-opening/equilibration polymerization of fluoroalkyl cyclic trisiloxanes alone or with other cyclic siloxane comonomers. One route uses a fluoroalkyl cyclic trimer and a second trisiloxane in an aprotic solvent with an organolithium catalyst; another describes sequential living polymerization of cyclic siloxanes with alkyllithium or lithium silanolate to make a trifluoropropyl/dimethyl/vinylsiloxane block copolymer. The exact fluoroalkyl fraction, end groups, and vinyl content are route-specific. Silica reinforcement and peroxide or addition cure form formulated rubber articles and are deliberately not treated as universal polymer synthesis steps.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Fluorosilicone rubber (FVMQ) is a cured elastomer, so tensile, tear, hardness, and damping values reflect the gum composition, fluorinated substituent level, reinforcing or non-reinforcing filler, cure chemistry, and cure schedule. An open composition study reports that changing filler and fluorinated-polysiloxane formulations shifts ASTM D412 modulus, tensile strength, and elongation, and that dynamic loss factor also varies with temperature and frequency. Its press-cured examples therefore demonstrate formulation sensitivity rather than a material constant.

A bounded sheet example is Viking Extrusions' VFL60SH 60 Shore A fluorosilicone sheeting, which reports 900 psi tensile strength and 200% elongation by ASTM D412, and 40 ppi tear by ASTM D624 Die B. The supplier explicitly presents these figures as guide values rather than a specification. In separately disclosed press-cured formulation examples (170 °C for 10 min), one cited sample reported 9.1 MPa tensile strength, 540% elongation, 0.95 MPa M100, and 36.4 kN/m tear (ASTM D412 and D624 Mold B); it must remain associated with that patented formulation and cure.
sections.processing: Fluorosilicone rubber is processed as a filled gum or liquid formulation, followed by heat curing or vulcanization. High-consistency compounds can be mixed on a two-roll mill or other mixer, shaped by compression, transfer, or injection molding, and post-cured; addition-cure systems must be protected from premature room-temperature reaction and are often packaged as separate components. A patent example mixed fluorinated polysiloxane, fumed silica, surface-treatment agent, fluorinated hydrosiloxane crosslinker, platinum catalyst, and retardant on a 6-inch two-roll mill, press molded a 2 mm sheet at 165 °C for 10 min under 100 kg/cm², and post-cured at 200 °C for 4 h. The same disclosure gives a broad preferred cure range of 50–300 °C for 1–30 min followed by 100–250 °C post-cure for 0–8 h. An independent fluorosilicone-composition patent reports press curing at 170 °C for 10 min for formulation-specific articles. Filler, viscosity, catalyst, cure system, mold design, and shrinkage make these operating conditions formulation-specific.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Fluorosilicone rubber is a silicone elastomer whose polysiloxane backbone carries fluorinated organic substituents, commonly trifluoropropyl groups. The siloxane chain supplies flexibility while the fluorinated side groups modify compatibility and resistance to hydrocarbon fluids.
sections.properties: Fluorosilicone combines the flexible, low-temperature behavior and weathering resistance associated with silicone elastomers with improved resistance to fuels and oils relative to many ordinary silicone rubbers. Its cured modulus, compression set, and fluid response depend on crosslink chemistry, filler, and post-cure.
sections.applications: Fluorosilicone is used in seals, O-rings, gaskets, hoses, diaphragms, and aerospace or automotive components where silicone-like temperature flexibility must coexist with fuel or oil exposure. It is also supplied as sheet and extrusion stock for selected sealing geometries.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Fluorosilicone is a specialty elastomer rather than a universal chemical-resistant rubber: strong acids, bases, steam, abrasion, and some solvents can remain limiting. Performance varies with fluorinated side-group content, cure system, filler, geometry, compression history, and the particular fluid and temperature.

sections.overview: Polysulfide rubber is a family of sulfur-containing elastomer precursors prepared by condensing sodium polysulfides with di- or polyhalide components. Thiol-terminated liquid polymers can be oxidatively cured into rubbery network materials.
sections.nomenclature: Polysulfide rubber and polysulfide elastomer identify the sulfur-containing elastomer family, not one liquid precursor or cured sealant compound. Chain branching, end-group functionality, oxidant, filler, and coating formulation define particular networked materials and must remain explicit.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polysulfide rubbers are made by condensation of organic dihalides with alkali-metal polysulfides, creating chains whose backbone contains recurring organic groups separated by sulfur sequences. A common feed is bis(2-chloroethyl) formal; ethylene dichloride, propylene dichloride, or other dihalides can change the organic segment, and a small multifunctional halide introduces branching. One cited patent describes aqueous-dispersion condensation of bis(2-chloroethyl) formal and related dihalides with sodium polysulfide, followed by reductive cleavage of a high-molar-mass intermediate with sodium hydrosulfide and sodium sulfite to yield thiol-terminated liquid polymer. A distinct historical patent identifies the same dihalide/polysulfide chemistry and branched liquid precursors. The terminal thiols are then oxidatively coupled into an elastomeric network with curing agents such as lead dioxide, manganese dioxide, zinc peroxide, or organic peroxides; filler and accelerator packages are formulation-specific. Sulfur rank, dihalide mixture, branching-agent level, reductive cleavage, and end-group content control precursor architecture. Article-shaping cure schedules and application equipment remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polysulfide-rubber (PSR) materials span liquid polysulfide oligomers and cured or compounded elastomer networks, so their response is governed by molecular structure, cure chemistry and crosslink density, plasticizer or resin modification, filler loading and interfacial coupling, cure history, temperature, aging, and test rate. A study of PSR with a liquid-polysulfide-oligomer-modified MoS2 crosslinker identifies the inherently limited mechanical response of neat PSR and the importance of crosslinker and filler dispersion. In a separate marine-deck-coating experiment, the polysulfide-rubber-modified formulation designated L1 gave static tensile strength 12.4 MPa, compared with 5.5 MPa for the unmodified coating (L0). This is a formulation-specific, cured coating comparison; it is not a tensile specification for unfilled polysulfide rubber or for sealants cured by other chemistries.
sections.processing:
Liquid polysulfide rubber sealants and molding compounds are article-converted by accurately metering a base and curing component, low-speed mixing to a uniform color, optional vacuum degassing, and prompt pouring, gun application, or tooling into a prepared joint or mold before the pot life expires. Substrates and molds must be clean and compatible with the specified primer or release practice; joint geometry, backing material, adhesion faces, and bead depth control movement accommodation. Mixing speed and time, scraping the vessel walls and bottom, entrained air, batch size, material and ambient temperature, humidity, and elapsed time after mixing govern viscosity, flow, bubble retention, working life, surface tooling, and cure. The applied material should be protected from disturbance and incompatible contamination while it develops a crosslinked network, and demolding or service loading should wait for the formulation's stated cure. Manufacture of the liquid polysulfide prepolymer belongs in Synthesis; metering, mixing, application, and the cure schedule that creates the finished seal or molding belong in Processing.

The numerical schedules are formulation-specific. Sika Polysulphide PG specifies a 95:5 A:B mass ratio, about 5 min mixing with a drill or electric mixer at no more than 500 rpm, about 2 h pot life at 25 °C, application from 5–50 °C, and about one week cure; its joint guidance is 6–50 mm width with width:depth near 2:1. Smooth-On's distinct FMC-201 polysulfide compound calls for thorough separate stirring, combining the two parts for 3 min, optional vacuum degassing to reduce bubbles, and prompt pouring while viscosity is low. Neither schedule is a universal polysulfide-rubber cure window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polysulfide rubber comprises liquid organic polysulfide precursors with thiol end groups that can be oxidatively converted into branched or rubbery networks.
sections.properties: Cured polysulfide-rubber response changes with crosslinker type, MoS2 dispersion, and the complete coating or elastomer formulation.
sections.applications: Polysulfide rubber is directly reported as a marine-deck-coating modifier and as a cured rubber network.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Mechanical values belong to named modified coatings or crosslinked PSR networks; precursor functionality, oxidant, filler, dispersion, cure, and test geometry must remain attached.

sections.overview: Polyisobutylene (PIB) is the polymer produced by cationic polymerization of isobutylene. Lewis-acid/coinitiator systems can control its molecular weight and terminal-group structure, making those variables relevant to a particular PIB grade.
sections.nomenclature: Polyisobutylene and polyisobutene identify the isobutylene homopolymer in this record. PIB is distinct from butyl rubber, which includes an isoprene comonomer; end-functional PIB grades and PIB-containing block copolymers are narrower materials rather than synonyms for the base polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyisobutylene is made principally by cationic addition polymerization of isobutylene. An electrophilic initiating species generated by a Lewis-acid/coinitiator system adds to the electron-rich olefin, and the resulting tertiary carbocation propagates; low reaction temperature suppresses chain transfer and rearrangement when high molar mass is sought. Lewis acids such as aluminum, boron, titanium, or iron halides can be paired with water, alcohol, hydrogen halide, ether, or an organic initiator, with solvent polarity, temperature, monomer concentration, and transfer or termination chemistry controlling molar mass and whether chain ends are exo-olefinic or halide terminated. The cited review compares catalytic systems for controlled and highly reactive PIB, including water/TiCl4/alcohol initiation. A distinct patent example scopes low-temperature slurry copolymerization in a polar diluent with a Lewis acid and initiator; it is included as an industrially relevant isobutylene-polymerization variant and not as evidence that every PIB contains a comonomer.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyisobutylene (PIB) covers low-molar-mass viscous materials through high-molar-mass elastomeric grades, and its mechanical response is controlled by molecular weight/distribution, chain architecture and end groups, temperature and rate, and—when used in a network or block material—crosslink density, hard-block fraction, and processing history. Accordingly, values for a PIB-based block copolymer or polyurethane are not values for neat linear PIB. As a bounded example, a poly(styrene-block-isobutylene-block-styrene) (SIBS) material with number-average molecular weight 33,000 g mol−1 was tested as ISO 37:2017 type-1A dumbbells at 10 mm min−1 and had tensile strength 3.51 MPa. This describes that specific SIBS block copolymer, not a general PIB tensile specification.
sections.processing:
Polyisobutylene (PIB) is commonly article-converted as the elastomeric base or viscosity modifier in solvent-borne and hot-melt pressure-sensitive adhesives, sealants, barrier coatings, and highly filled compounds. Documented application methods include spraying, dipping, spreading, troweling, and coating a carrier film. Production operations therefore center on dissolving or melt-mixing selected molecular-weight grades with lower-molecular-weight PIB, tackifiers, oils, waxes, fillers, and antioxidants, followed by thin-layer application, solvent removal or cooling, slitting, winding, pelletizing, or slab forming. Molecular mass and solids content strongly control viscosity and equipment choice: low-viscosity solutions can use high-shear mixers, while high-viscosity mastics require churns, planetary mixers, kneaders, mills, or Banbury-type equipment. Thin coats and adequate intercoat drying are important because PIB's low permeability can trap solvent and create porosity. Hot processing should minimize air exposure and unnecessary heat history because the oxidation risk rises as low-molecular-weight material is handled near its melt-processing temperature.

Petrie's SpecialChem guide gives formulation-specific rather than universal ranges: it describes about 5–10% solids for spraying, 10–30% for dipping, 25–50% for spreading, and 50–70% for trowel or spatula application, and assigns 50,000–200,000 cP products to jacketed turbine mixers, 200,000–1,000,000 cP products to churns or double-arm planetary mixers, and products above 1,000,000 cP to kneaders, mills, or Banbury mixers. It also reports a typical PIB hot-melt viscosity of 30,000–60,000 cP at 177 °C depending on grade, not a family specification. A distinct industrial example from BUSS uses an 11 L/D continuous kneader: PIB and rubber fractions are melted or masticated by dissipative shear in the first zone, fillers and resins enter the second, and waxes, plasticizers, antioxidants, and optional rework are distributed downstream before hot-cut granulation, rotoforming, or slab molding. That equipment-specific sequence illustrates how short residence, staged feeding, temperature control, and distributive mixing are used for a viscous PIB gumbase formulation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyisobutylene (PIB) is a saturated hydrocarbon polymer from isobutylene; cationic-polymerization conditions control molecular weight and exo-olefinic or chloride chain ends.
sections.properties: PIB mechanical behavior depends on molecular characteristics and on whether it is used neat, as a plasticizer, or in a reinforced or block-copolymer material.
sections.applications: The cited review identifies isobutylene-based polymers in plasticizer and reinforcement contexts.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A SIBS heart-valve study and controlled-end-group synthesis do not define all PIB: block composition, molecular weight, end groups, and article form must remain specified.

sections.overview: Ethylene–octene elastomer is a polyolefin elastomer based on ethylene/1-octene copolymers, with comonomer content and crystallinity governing the balance between elastic and thermoplastic behavior. Commercial grades are melt-processable and may be used neat or in blends, but grade-specific behavior is not a family-wide constant.
sections.nomenclature: POE is the abbreviation used for ethylene–octene elastomer, also described as an ethylene–octene copolymer. The record covers binary ethylene/1-octene elastomer grades; it excludes EPDM (which contains a diene), EPM/EPR (ethylene–propylene), and a dynamically crosslinked blend as synonyms for the neat copolymer family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Ethylene–octene elastomers are coordination copolymers made from ethylene and 1-octene, rather than blends of polyethylene and an octene-containing additive. Molecular catalysts, including metallocene, post-metallocene, and vanadium systems, provide routes whose catalyst/activator pair and monomer feeds influence octene incorporation and molecular-weight distribution. In a documented metallocene solution experiment, ethylene and 1-octene were polymerized in decane with MAO/borate activation and triethylaluminum scavenger; a separate open review reports vanadium/alkylaluminum catalyst systems tested for ethylene/1-octene copolymerization. These are route-specific examples, not a universal elastomer composition or manufacturing prescription. The resulting material is a thermoplastic copolymer; later compounding or crosslinking, when used, is outside this synthesis account.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Ethylene-octene elastomers are semicrystalline thermoplastic elastomers in which octene-derived short-chain branches interrupt polyethylene crystallization. The amorphous, branched segments provide rubber-like extensibility, while small polyethylene-rich crystals act as reversible physical junctions that provide strength and recovery. Their tensile response is therefore nonlinear and viscoelastic, often combining low initial stiffness, very large elongation, strain hardening, hysteresis, and some permanent set; stiffness and recovery can fall rapidly as service temperature approaches the grade's crystal-melting interval. Octene content and comonomer distribution, density and crystallinity, random versus blocky sequence architecture, molecular mass and long-chain branching, entanglement density, crystal size and morphology, cooling and annealing history, orientation, strain rate, test temperature, cyclic history, and oxidative or thermal aging are consequential. Greater crystallinity generally raises hardness, modulus, yield stress, and heat resistance but reduces softness; stretching can reorganize or fragment physical crystals. Fillers, blends, foaming, and interfacial adhesion further change strength, tear, impact response, and set. Peroxide, silane, or radiation cross-linking adds permanent junctions and can improve high-temperature strength, compression set, and dimensional recovery, although excessive cross-linking or phase separation can reduce elongation and melt reprocessability. As one bounded commercial-grade example, Dow's ENGAGE 8150 technical information identifies a density-0.868 g/cm3 ethylene-octene copolymer. Compression-molded specimens tested to ASTM D638 at 508 mm/min had a reported 100% modulus of 2.6 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 9.5 MPa, and ultimate elongation of 810%; the same sheet reports Shore A 70 and Shore D 20 hardness to ASTM D2240 and Type C tear strength of 37.3 kN/m to ASTM D624. These are typical, non-specification values for that grade, not ranges for all ethylene-octene elastomers. The sheet does not state tensile specimen dimensions, conditioning, or test temperature, and its grade-specific results should not be transferred to foams, filled compounds, blends, cross-linked articles, or differently crystallized moldings without new testing.
sections.processing:
Ethylene–octene elastomers are melt-processable thermoplastic elastomers used in compounding/blending with polyolefins and in hose, tube, profile, and injection-molding operations. Dow's ENGAGE processing guide recommends conventional thermoplastic equipment, cooling the feed throat below 50 °C to limit pellet bridging, and fast injection to promote shear thinning; its temperatures are reference starting points that can vary by about ±5 °C and may be increased by at most 20 °C. The advice is grade- and machine-dependent, and should not be treated as a universal POE recipe.

A bounded dynamic-compounding example used ENGAGE 8480 (20 wt% octene) in POE/EPDM blends. EPDM and dicumyl peroxide were first mixed on a two-roll mill at 25 °C for 3 min; the preblend was then combined with POE in a torque rheometer at 110 °C, 40 rpm, for about 6 min, and the temperature was raised to 165 °C for cure during compounding. This two-step sequence was selected to preferentially crosslink the EPDM phase and belongs to the reported blend formulation; neat ethylene–octene resin need not be dynamically crosslinked.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Ethylene–octene elastomers are ethylene-rich copolymers in which octene comonomer disrupts polyethylene crystallinity and produces a soft polyolefin morphology.
sections.properties: Octene content, molecular architecture, crystallinity, and crosslinking determine elasticity, density, and strength.
sections.applications: POE is used as a soft polyolefin modifier and in injection-molded elastomer applications.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: ENGAGE technical information is grade-specific, while the research study examines dynamically crosslinked POE/EPDM blends. Their properties cannot be assigned to neat POE generally.

sections.overview: Styrene–butadiene–styrene is a styrenic triblock copolymer with polystyrene end blocks and a polybutadiene midblock. Its microphase-separated architecture provides thermoplastic-elastomer behavior.
sections.nomenclature: SBS abbreviates styrene–butadiene–styrene block copolymer. The name specifies a block copolymer and should not be confused with random styrene–butadiene rubber.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–butadiene–styrene (SBS) is a triblock copolymer made from styrene and 1,3-butadiene, most commonly by living anionic polymerization under rigorously dry, oxygen-free conditions. In a sequential route, an organolithium initiator such as sec- or n-butyllithium first forms a living polystyryl block in a hydrocarbon solvent; butadiene is then added to form the rubbery midblock, followed by a second styrene charge to complete the linear S–B–S chain. A cited manufacturing example uses cyclohexane, n-butyllithium, and tetrahydrofuran in this sequence. An alternative cited route makes living S–B diblocks and reacts their carbanionic ends with a multifunctional coupling agent; a difunctional coupling event gives a nominal linear SBS architecture, while higher-functionality coupling gives branched or radial material. Initiator concentration and block-feed amounts set molar mass and block fractions, while polar modifiers and temperature influence butadiene 1,2/1,4 microstructure. Polymerization is terminated and the antioxidant-stabilized polymer is recovered from solvent. At service temperature, incompatible polystyrene end blocks associate into hard domains that physically connect the polybutadiene chains; this reversible physical network is intrinsic to the thermoplastic elastomer and is not a covalent cure network.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SBS is a physically crosslinked thermoplastic elastomer: glassy polystyrene-rich domains act as reversible junctions in a rubbery polybutadiene midblock. Tensile and recovery behavior therefore change with styrene fraction and block lengths, butadiene microstructure, molecular mass and linear/radial topology, uncoupled styrene–butadiene diblock content, microphase morphology and orientation, oil/resin/filler formulation, oxidation or UV exposure, molding/casting history, temperature, and loading rate. An open tensile/DMA study of solution-cast SBS/SB blends found the viscoelastic and large-strain response sensitive to diblock content; at equal diblock content the storage-modulus plateau fell more sharply for linear than radial SBS. As one deliberately grade-bounded endpoint, Solprene 4318 is a linear pellet/powder SBS with 32 wt% total styrene (at least 31 wt% block styrene): its listed tensile strength is 3.7 MPa, 300% modulus 1.2 MPa, and elongation above 1000%. The published grade listing does not supply a tensile standard, specimen geometry, conditioning, or temperature, so these values are not a design basis or an SBS-family range.
sections.processing:
Styrene–butadiene–styrene (SBS) is a thermoplastic elastomer that can be compounded and shaped by conventional thermoplastic operations including extrusion, injection molding, blown-film or blow molding where the formulation has adequate melt strength, and solution or hot-melt coating and casting. Heating releases the physical polystyrene-domain junctions so the material can flow and cooling restores the elastomeric network; ordinary shaping therefore does not require vulcanization. Grade architecture, styrene and diblock content, oil and resin loading, filler dispersion, solvent removal, melt temperature, shear rate, residence time, gate or die geometry, cooling time, and regrind history control flow, anisotropy, surface defects, and recovery. Unsaturated SBS is more vulnerable than hydrogenated SBCs to excessive heat and oxidation.

Avient's supplier bulletin says its SBS/SIS-based formulations normally do not require drying and gives a general processing band of 290–350 °F (about 143–177 °C); it warns that processing above 400 °F (about 204 °C) can produce gels and discoloration. It also links low-shear/high-melt-strength behavior to extrusion, blown film, and blow molding, high-shear thinning to thin-wall injection, excessive shear to separation and gate splay, and soft grades to longer cooling before ejection. These are GLS formulation observations, not settings for neat SBS of every architecture. In a distinct actual casting study, Adhikari prepared named linear and radial SBS/SB blends in toluene, evaporated solvent over about 10 days to make roughly 1 mm films, dried them for several further days, and vacuum-annealed them at 120 °C for 48 h. That long solvent-removal and annealing schedule belongs to those laboratory blends.

sections.overview: Styrene–isoprene–styrene is a styrenic triblock copolymer with polystyrene end blocks and a polyisoprene midblock. Its phase-separated architecture supports thermoplastic-elastomer and adhesive formulations.
sections.nomenclature: SIS abbreviates styrene–isoprene–styrene block copolymer. It is a block copolymer, not random styrene–isoprene rubber, and is distinct from SBS and its hydrogenated derivatives.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–isoprene–styrene (SIS) is prepared from styrene and isoprene by living anionic block polymerization. A representative sequential process excludes water and oxygen, charges a dry hydrocarbon solvent and an organolithium initiator, polymerizes styrene to a living hard block, adds isoprene for the rubbery midblock, and then adds a second styrene charge. A polar modifier may be used to adjust anionic kinetics and isoprene microstructure; the living chain is finally stopped with a protic reagent, stabilized, and recovered. A distinct patent example prepares an SIS precursor in cyclohexane with sec-butyllithium before optional selective hydrogenation. Coupling is a route variant: living S–I diblocks can be joined through a difunctional agent to form a nominal linear SIS chain, while multifunctional coupling yields branched or radial architectures. Monomer-charge ratio, initiator level, feed sequence, temperature, modifier, and coupling efficiency control block lengths, molar mass, isoprene microstructure, and residual diblock content. The polystyrene end blocks microphase-separate into hard domains that form a reversible physical network around the polyisoprene phase; SIS does not require covalent crosslinking to meet its family definition.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SIS obtains rubber-like extension and recovery from a polyisoprene midblock physically anchored by glassy polystyrene end-block domains. Its stiffness, strength, stress relaxation, and tack/cohesion balance depend on styrene fraction and block architecture, isoprene microstructure and molecular mass, microphase morphology, oil and tackifier loading, oxidation/UV ageing, compounding and coating or molding history, test temperature, strain rate, and direction. In an open adhesive study, mineral oil and asphaltene/resin components plasticized a 44 wt% styrene SIS grade, reducing moduli and altering tensile/adhesive behavior; formulation could trade cohesive strength against low-temperature or pressure-sensitive flow. As a bounded neat-material example, a 2017 study identifies Kraton D1165P (SIS30, 28.2–31.8 wt% styrene) with 32 MPa tensile strength at break, 1300% elongation at break, and Shore A 48 hardness. These supplier-characterized values do not include tensile specimen geometry, conditioning, or test rate in the accessible paper and must not be applied to oil-extended adhesives, SIS20, blends, or oriented forms.
sections.processing:
Styrene–isoprene–styrene (SIS) is a thermoplastic elastomer that can be compounded and shaped by conventional thermoplastic operations including extrusion, injection molding, blown-film or blow molding where the formulation has adequate melt strength, and solution or hot-melt coating, lamination, and casting. Heating releases the physical polystyrene-domain junctions so the material can flow, and cooling restores the elastomeric network; ordinary article shaping therefore does not require vulcanization. Grade architecture, styrene and diblock content, tackifier and oil loading, filler dispersion, solvent removal, melt temperature, shear rate, residence time, gate or die geometry, coating weight, cooling time, and regrind history control flow, anisotropy, surface defects, tack, cohesion, and elastic recovery. The unsaturated polyisoprene midblock is vulnerable to excessive heat and oxidation, so long hot-melt residence and repeated thermal histories require particular care.

Avient's supplier bulletin says its SBS/SIS-based formulations normally do not require drying and gives a general processing band of 290–350 °F (about 143–177 °C); it warns that processing above 400 °F (about 204 °C) can produce gels and discoloration. It also links low-shear/high-melt-strength behavior to extrusion, blown film, and blow molding, high-shear thinning to thin-wall injection, excessive shear to separation and gate splay, and soft grades to longer cooling before ejection. These are GLS formulation observations, not settings for every neat SIS architecture. In a distinct bounded adhesive experiment, Ilyin and co-workers compounded Vector 4411A SIS (44 wt% styrene) with specified asphaltene/resin and naphthenic-oil contents in a twin-rotor laboratory mixer at 120 °C for 20 min and 60 rpm. They shaped 160 ± 20 µm films between siliconized PET films with a laminator at 120 °C and did not cure the samples. That mixing and lamination schedule belongs to the reported SIS/ARB/oil formulations.

sections.overview: Styrene–ethylene/butylene–styrene is a hydrogenated styrenic triblock copolymer with polystyrene end blocks and an ethylene/butylene midblock. Hydrogenation distinguishes it from the unsaturated butadiene-midblock SBS precursor.
sections.nomenclature: SEBS abbreviates styrene–ethylene/butylene–styrene block copolymer. The slash in ethylene/butylene describes the saturated midblock composition; SEBS is distinct from SBS and SEPS.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–ethylene/butylene–styrene (SEBS) is normally produced by selectively hydrogenating the polybutadiene midblock of an SBS precursor. The precursor is first made by living anionic block polymerization of styrene and 1,3-butadiene in a dry hydrocarbon solvent, either by sequential styrene–butadiene–styrene addition or by coupling living S–B diblocks. Butadiene 1,4- and 1,2-addition units become ethylene-like and butylene-bearing saturated units, respectively, so modifier level and precursor microstructure help set the composition of the hydrogenated midblock. The cited examples use hydrogen with transition-metal catalyst systems, including nickel/aluminum Ziegler-type catalysts, to reduce aliphatic carbon–carbon double bonds while largely preserving the aromatic styrene rings. Hydrogen pressure, temperature, catalyst concentration, and contact time determine hydrogenation extent; catalyst residues are removed or deactivated before isolation and drying. Block-feed ratios, initiator level, and optional coupling control molar mass, styrene fraction, and linear versus radial architecture. SEBS retains the reversible network of microphase-separated polystyrene domains and a saturated rubbery midblock; that physical association, rather than a permanent covalent cure, defines its thermoplastic-elastomer architecture.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SEBS is the selectively hydrogenated analogue of SBS, with polystyrene physical junctions and a saturated ethylene/butylene rubbery midblock. Styrene fraction and block molecular mass, ethylene/butylene sequence distribution, molecular topology, oil/resin/filler and polymer-blend formulation, molding/cooling and flow orientation, temperature, strain rate, and ageing package determine its hardness, modulus, strength, elongation, compression set, and recovery. A full open study of SEBS/HIPS/CaCO₃ shoe-sole blends measured both flow directions and found that increasing HIPS raised modulus, strength, hardness, impact resistance, heat-deflection-related measures, and wear while lowering elongation; those compounded directional results are not intrinsic-SEBS values. As one tightly bounded unfilled-grade endpoint, linear Europrene SOL TH 2314 (31 wt% bound styrene, antioxidant-stabilized) measured on ASTM D4703 compression-molded specimens had 24.0 MPa tensile strength, 550% elongation at break, 4.0 MPa 300% modulus (ASTM D412), and Shore A 70 hardness. This is a typical value for that compression-molded grade, not for oil-extended, filled, blended, oriented, or differently hydrogenated SEBS.
sections.processing:
Styrene–ethylene/butylene–styrene (SEBS) is commonly compounded with oils, polyolefins, styrenic resins, fillers, and stabilizers, pelletized, and converted by extrusion, injection molding, compression molding, blown-film or blow molding, and coextrusion or overmolding. The saturated midblock tolerates more heat than SBS, but usable settings remain grade- and formulation-specific. Molecular architecture, styrene content, oil and filler loading, blend morphology, feed consistency, melt temperature, screw shear and residence time, gate or die design, mold temperature, and cooling control viscosity, dispersion, orientation, shrinkage, and surface quality. High temperature can volatilize oil and trap gas; excessive shear can separate a TPE formulation or create splay, while soft parts require enough cooling to eject without distortion.

Avient's supplier bulletin says SBC TPEs normally do not require drying and places its harder, at-least-40-Shore-A SEBS/SEPS formulations in a general 350–410 °F (about 177–210 °C) processing band; it warns that most such grades can degrade above 460 °F (about 238 °C). Those observations are not a neat-SEBS family window. A distinct bounded study by Banerjee, Ray, and Ghosh processed Kraton G1643 M SEBS and SEBS/polystyrene blends in a conical co-rotating twin-screw microcompounder at 200 °C, 80 rpm, and 3 min residence after filling. Extruded strands were fed directly to a micro-injection machine operated at 210 °C cylinder temperature, 30 °C mold temperature, and 510 bar; neat SEBS received the same history. The authors also observed long relaxation behavior relevant to time-dependent shrinkage after secondary processing, so cooling and stress relaxation cannot be inferred from nominal melt flow alone.

sections.overview: Styrene–ethylene/propylene–styrene is a hydrogenated styrenic block copolymer with styrene end blocks and an ethylene/propylene midblock. Its segmented architecture gives it thermoplastic-elastomer character.
sections.nomenclature: SEPS abbreviates styrene–ethylene/propylene–styrene block copolymer. It is a distinct member of the styrenic block-copolymer family, not a synonym for SEBS or SEEPS.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–ethylene/propylene–styrene (SEPS) is commonly made by selective hydrogenation of a styrene–isoprene–styrene precursor rather than by direct copolymerization of ethylene and propylene between polystyrene blocks. SIS is first formed by living anionic polymerization in a dry hydrocarbon medium using an organolithium initiator: styrene is polymerized for the first end block, isoprene for the midblock, and styrene for the second end block, or living S–I arms are coupled. Selective catalytic hydrogenation then converts the unsaturated polyisoprene segment into an ethylene/propylene-like saturated segment while retaining the polystyrene blocks. The cited sources identify hydrogenated styrene–isoprene block copolymers as SEPS and describe hydrogenation with hydrogen and transition-metal systems; one route-specific example uses a nickel/aluminum Ziegler catalyst in cyclohexane. Isoprene microstructure, styrene/isoprene feed ratio, initiator loading, optional coupling, and degree of hydrogenation control midblock composition, block size, architecture, and residual unsaturation. After catalyst deactivation or removal, the stabilized polymer is recovered from solvent. Polystyrene end-block domains supply a reversible physical network; selective midblock saturation does not itself create a permanent covalent network.
sections.mechanicalProperties: SEPS is the saturated, hydrogenated analogue of SIS: polystyrene end-block domains form reversible physical junctions in a generally noncrystalline ethylene/propylene midblock. Its rubbery extension, modulus, recovery, and thermal/oxidative durability depend on styrene content and block molecular mass, midblock sequence, oil or tackifier extension, fillers and blend partners, casting or molding orientation, thickness, temperature, and loading rate. Kuraray’s SEPS family information distinguishes soft, low-styrene from rigid, high-styrene grades and identifies strong tensile elongation and low-temperature behavior; its listed SEPS grades span 13–65 wt% styrene and Shore A 36–98, illustrating why a single family value is misleading. As one bounded experimental endpoint, dogbone tests on Kraton G1730 SEPS (22% polystyrene) gave a 3.3 MPa modulus; the authors used it as a roughly 860 μm elastomer layer in an LLDPE/SEPS/LLDPE trilayer, tested at 100% nominal strain per minute. This result is specific to that commercial grade, dogbone/test rate, and unfilled layer, not to SEPS composites, oil-extended adhesive grades, or other styrene contents.
sections.processing:
Styrene–ethylene/propylene–styrene (SEPS) is a saturated styrenic thermoplastic elastomer processed as neat pellets or, more commonly, after compounding with oils, polyolefins, fillers, tackifiers, and stabilizers. Applicable conversion routes include extrusion and coextrusion, injection and compression molding, blown film or blow molding for high-melt-strength formulations, film lamination, and orientation or stretch-and-release texturing. Grade architecture, styrene content, oil and partner-polymer loading, feed uniformity, melt temperature, shear rate, residence time, interlayer adhesion, die or mold temperature, cooling, and imposed orientation control flow, recovery, shrinkage, and surface quality.

Avient's bulletin treats SEPS/SEBS formulations as strongly shear-thinning materials that can serve both low-shear extrusion and high-shear injection applications. It says SBC TPEs normally do not require drying, places harder formulations at 350–410 °F (about 177–210 °C), warns of degradation above 460 °F (about 238 °C) for most grades and oil volatilization at high temperature, and notes that soft molded parts need additional cooling before ejection. These are supplier formulation observations, not a universal neat-SEPS window. In a distinct article-conversion experiment, Yang and co-workers relieved residual stress in 50 µm LLDPE face films by heating them to 90 °C, then compression-molded Kraton G1730 SEPS pellets between the films at 133 °C in a platen press, using steel-strip spacers to set the SEPS layer thickness. The resulting trilayers were cut to dogbones and stretched to 50–300% strain at 100% per minute before release to generate a wrinkled surface. That lamination and orientation schedule belongs to the named SEPS/LLDPE construction.

sections.overview: Styrene–ethylene/ethylene-propylene–styrene is a hydrogenated styrenic block-copolymer family with polystyrene end blocks and a mixed saturated midblock. Its block architecture supplies thermoplastic-elastomer behavior.
sections.nomenclature: SEEPS abbreviates styrene–ethylene/ethylene-propylene–styrene block copolymer. It identifies a distinct hydrogenated styrenic-block-copolymer midblock composition and is not interchangeable with SEBS or SEPS.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrene–ethylene/ethylene-propylene–styrene (SEEPS) is made by selectively hydrogenating a styrenic triblock whose unsaturated midblock contains both butadiene- and isoprene-derived units. In a documented sequential route, dry cyclohexane and styrene are initiated with sec-butyllithium, a mixed isoprene/1,3-butadiene charge forms the central block, and a final styrene charge completes an S–(I/B)–S precursor; methanol stops the living chains. Selective hydrogenation with hydrogen and a transition-metal catalyst, exemplified by a nickel/aluminum Ziegler system, saturates the diene-derived carbon–carbon double bonds while leaving the aromatic styrene blocks substantially intact. The hydrogenated butadiene-derived sequences provide ethylene-like units, while hydrogenated isoprene-derived sequences provide ethylene/propylene-like units. The second cited source likewise identifies hydrogenated styrene–butadiene/isoprene block copolymers as SEEPS and describes applicable catalyst systems. Isoprene/butadiene feed ratio, diene microstructure, initiator level, block-feed sequence, and hydrogenation extent control the saturated-midblock composition and residual unsaturation. Catalyst removal or deactivation and solvent recovery follow reaction. Microphase-separated polystyrene end blocks make the reversible physical network; no covalent cure is required by the SEEPS identity.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
SEEPS is a physically crosslinked styrenic thermoplastic elastomer. Below the softening region of its polystyrene end blocks, glassy styrene-rich domains anchor chains while the saturated ethylene/ethylene-propylene midblock supplies rubber-like extension and recovery. Its tensile response is therefore generally nonlinear and highly extensible rather than the yield-and-neck response of a neat semicrystalline polyolefin. The junctions are reversible rather than covalent: cyclic loading, long dwell, or elevated temperature can permit midblock relaxation and chain pullout, producing hysteresis, creep, stress relaxation, or compression set, while sufficient heat and shear soften the styrene domains and permit melt flow. Kuraray's full SEPTON/HYBRAR brochure describes this hard-domain/soft-midblock mechanism and emphasizes that hydrogenation supports heat, weather, and ozone resistance, but it does not establish a family-wide modulus or strength.

Mechanical response varies with styrene fraction, end-block and midblock molecular masses, block architecture and dispersity, the continuity and spacing of styrene domains, and any orientation introduced during extrusion or drawing. Oil or other plasticizer dilutes the midblock and reduces hardness and modulus but can increase softness and extensibility; oil retention consequently depends on grade architecture and compatibility. Added polystyrene or polyolefin can reinforce or aid processing, while fillers, tackifiers, compatibilizers, and crosslinking or reactive modifications change stiffness, tear, set, and interfacial failure. Mixing temperature and shear, cooling history, molded or film orientation, test temperature relative to the soft- and hard-block transitions, loading rate, strain amplitude, cycle count, dwell time, and thermal/UV ageing must accompany comparisons.

A public patent supplies a deliberately narrow compound example rather than a neat-SEEPS value. Its Example 1 contained 9.9 wt% Septon 4055 SEEPS, 49.5 wt% Sibstar E1140B crosslinked-polyisobutylene/HDPE TPV, 19.9 wt% liquid polybutene, 5.5 wt% polypropylene, 5.0 wt% polyphenylene ether, 9.9 wt% calcium carbonate, and minor slip aid and antioxidants. The ingredients were twin-screw compounded through 215/260/215 °C zones at 400 rpm, pelletized, and injection molded at 235 °C. ASTM D412 Die C testing gave 305 psi tensile strength (about 2.10 MPa) and 244% elongation; ASTM D395 Method B compression set was 14.3% after 22 h at 23 °C and 18.4% after 22 h at 70 °C. These values demonstrate how an approximately 10 wt% SEEPS grade can function in one oil-rich, multipolymer seal compound; they are not intrinsic properties of neat SEEPS or transferable to other grades.
sections.processing:
Styrene–ethylene/ethylene-propylene–styrene (SEEPS) is converted mainly as the elastomer phase of compounded thermoplastic elastomers. Typical operations meter SEEPS with polyolefin, process oil or polybutene, stabilizer, filler, and other modifiers into a batch mixer or co-rotating twin-screw extruder; staged liquid injection helps distribute high oil loadings, and the melt is pelletized before injection molding, extrusion, tubing or film formation, foaming, or other thermoplastic shaping. SEEPS grade, styrene content, molecular mass, oil absorption, polyolefin compatibility, solids and liquid feed locations, screw shear, temperature profile, residence time, cooling, and pellet handling govern dispersion, flow, surface quality, and compression set. Polymer manufacture and any dynamic-network chemistry belong in Synthesis; compounding, pelletizing, shaping, and cooling belong here.

Kuraray's technical brochure identifies the SEPTON 4000 series as SEEPS, shows formulation-dependent flow and compound behavior, and establishes that SEPTON materials are supplied for TPE compounding and conversion into varied article forms. A distinct patent gives a bounded operating example for SEEPS-containing Examples 1–3 rather than neat SEEPS: all ingredients except the Indopol polybutene plasticizer entered before zone 1 of a twin-screw extruder, the liquid plasticizer was injected at zone 3, the extruder ran at 400 rpm with zones 1–3 at 215 °C, zones 7–8 at 260 °C, and zones 11–12 at 215 °C, and the compound was pelletized. The pellets were then injection molded on a Boy machine at 235 °C and high pressure. These conditions belong to the patent's multicomponent TPV/SEEPS/polyolefin/PPE formulations and must not be presented as a general SEEPS window.

sections.limitationsAndVariability: SEEPS response depends on grade architecture, oil and other compounding ingredients, formulation ratio, and article-forming route; brochure and compound results are not neat-family constants.

sections.overview: Thermoplastic polyolefin elastomers are uncrosslinked multiphase materials combining a polypropylene-rich thermoplastic phase with a dispersed olefinic elastomer phase. They are made either by melt compounding or by reactor processes that polymerize the elastomer in the presence of polypropylene, and are used in applications such as automotive parts.
sections.nomenclature: TPO is the abbreviation for thermoplastic polyolefin. This family includes compound-grade and reactor-grade PP/olefin-elastomer materials; dynamically vulcanized TPV, neat polypropylene, and one particular filled or molded grade are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Thermoplastic polyolefin elastomer (TPO) is an uncrosslinked multiphase polyolefin material. In compound-grade TPO, a semicrystalline thermoplastic—most often isotactic polypropylene—is melt blended with an olefin elastomer such as EPR, EPDM, or an ethylene–alpha-olefin copolymer. The polymers, antioxidants, and optional compatibilizer, oil, pigment, or mineral filler are compounded under shear until the elastomer is dispersed through a continuous or co-continuous polyolefin phase, then pelletized. Polymer ratio, melt-viscosity ratio, temperature, shear history, feed order, and compatibilizer govern phase continuity and rubber-domain size. A cited open chapter documents internal-mixer and twin-screw melt blending of PP with EPDM, EPR, ethylene–octene, or related rubbers. Reactor-grade TPO is a distinct in-reactor route: one cited patent first polymerizes propylene to polypropylene and then copolymerizes ethylene with propylene or another alpha-olefin in the presence of that polypropylene, producing an intimate heterophasic product without separately blending all polymer phases. Catalyst choice, hydrogen, monomer feeds, stage residence times, and phase fraction control the matrix and rubber composition. These two routes should not be collapsed into one formulation. TPO is not dynamically vulcanized: its rubber phase remains substantially uncrosslinked. If crosslinking is deliberately carried out during mixing, the product belongs to the thermoplastic-vulcanizate family instead.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Thermoplastic polyolefin elastomer (TPO) commonly denotes an uncrosslinked melt blend in which a semicrystalline polyolefin—often polypropylene—provides a load-bearing, melt-processable phase and an EPR, EPDM, ethylene-octene, or related olefin elastomer provides a compliant phase. It is distinct from a thermoplastic vulcanizate, whose rubber phase is dynamically crosslinked. TPO stress–strain response consequently combines polyolefin stiffness and yielding with rubber-particle deformation, cavitation or interfacial debonding, and shear yielding of the matrix. Increasing elastomer content commonly trades tensile modulus, yield stress, and hardness for greater ductility, low-temperature impact resistance, and energy absorption. The absence of a covalently crosslinked rubber network also makes creep, stress relaxation, and permanent set strongly dependent on composition and temperature rather than inferable from hardness alone.

The principal controls are polyolefin grade, molecular mass and crystallinity; elastomer chemistry, comonomer content and viscosity; plastic/elastomer ratio; rubber-domain size, continuity and dispersion; and adhesion across the phase boundary. Compatibilizers can refine domains and improve stress transfer, while talc, clay, fibers, or other fillers can restore stiffness but may reduce elongation or shift impact failure if agglomerated or poorly bonded. The open IntechOpen chapter describes rubber cavitation/debonding followed by matrix shear yielding as important toughening mechanisms and shows why elastomer fraction, filler dispersion, compatibilizer content, feed rate, and screw speed cannot be separated from mechanical results. Injection-flow or extrusion orientation, cooling and crystallization history, weld lines, specimen thickness, notch geometry, test temperature, loading rate, and thermal/oxidative ageing are likewise consequential, especially for impact and cyclic response.

A narrowly bounded commercial example is Sumitomo TPO 8710, described by its manufacturer as a flexible, simply blended, injection-molding TPO. The public product sheet reports 3.7 MPa tensile strength at break and 270% elongation at break by ASTM D412 using Die C at 500 mm/min, together with Shore A 79 hardness by ASTM D2240. Those are typical values for that named grade, not guaranteed specifications. The sheet does not disclose the polymer ratio, molding history, specimen conditioning, or test temperature, so the figures should not be treated as a TPO-family range or compared directly with a filled exterior-grade TPO without matching context.
sections.processing:
Thermoplastic polyolefin elastomers are converted by conventional thermoplastic operations, but the preferred grade depends on melt flow, melt strength, elastomer and filler content, and whether the material is a compounded or reactor TPO. Important supported routes include internal-mixer or twin-screw compounding, pelletizing and injection molding, plus sheet extrusion followed by thermoforming. Specific reactor grades are also sold for calendered soft sheet and film and for mono- or multilayer air-quenched blown film. During compounding, feed order, compatibilizer or masterbatch premixing, filler dispersion, feed rate, barrel temperature, screw speed, shear history, and melt-viscosity balance control rubber-domain size and agglomeration; excessive shear can alter impact behavior even when dispersion improves. Injection molding generally does not require bulk drying because polyolefin TPO is not hygroscopic, but cold pellets can carry surface condensation, so sealed storage and equilibration matter and material showing splay or voids may need conditional drying. Melt temperature, shot size and residence time, fast but stable filling, packing through gate freeze, mold temperature, venting, and balanced cooling govern gloss, weld lines, sink, molded-in stress, shrinkage, and warpage. For thermoforming, a sheet grade with adequate melt strength is needed; uniform multi-zone heating, sheet sag, plug and vacuum timing, tool temperature and finish, cooling fixtures, and removal temperature control wall distribution, surface replication, cycle time, and distortion. Reactor polymerization and formation of the PP/elastomer architecture remain Synthesis operations; Processing covers compounding and shaping an existing polymer material.

The numerical guidance is source-specific rather than a family window. The Plastics Group of America's one-page Polifil guide covers its filled and unfilled TPO molding resins. It says routine predrying is unnecessary, but recommends 82–99 °C for 1–2 h when condensation, old stock, critical appearance, splay, or voids warrant it and warns against drying beyond 24 h. It gives a 204–232 °C stock-melt range, rear-to-nozzle zone settings of 199–210/210–215/215–221/221–227 °C, 50–100 rpm screw speed, and 50–100 psi back pressure; the guide also links continued pack pressure through gate solidification to control of sink and warp. SIMONA PMC's separate sheet-forming guide gives start-up conditions for its TPO practice: 320–360 °F (160–182 °C) sheet temperature, 170–190 °F (77–88 °C) tool temperature, 140–170 °F (60–77 °C) part-removal temperature, and at least 25 in Hg vacuum, with controlled drafts and cooling fixtures. Finally, the open IntechOpen chapter reports a bounded PP/EPDM/clay compounding study that varied feed rate from 0.2 to 1 kg/h, screw speed from 50 to 150 rpm, and barrel temperature from 180 to 200 °C; its modeled optimum of 0.2 kg/h, 150 rpm, and 180 °C belongs only to that nanocomposite study and equipment.

sections.properties: Morphology, toughness, and tensile response depend on blend ratio, compatibilizer, mixing, and rubber phase.
sections.applications: TPO is directly supplied as elastomer grade and prepared by internal-mixer and twin-screw compounding.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Compound- and reactor-grade TPO are distinct; feed, morphology, and grade scope limit property transfer.
