sections.overview: Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate) is PHBHHx, a biosynthesized PHA copolyester containing 3-hydroxybutyrate and 3-hydroxyhexanoate units. The 3HHx fraction is controlled by the organism, pathway, and carbon feed rather than by physically mixing PHB with another polymer.
sections.nomenclature: P(3HB-co-3HHx) and PHBHHx are abbreviations used for this copolyester. The copolymer boundary requires both 3HB and 3HHx units; PHB homopolymer, PHBV, and a blend or modified article are not aliases for this record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate) (PHBHHx) is a bacterial PHA copolyester containing 3-hydroxybutyrate and 3-hydroxyhexanoate units. Its composition is controlled biologically by microorganism/catalytic enzyme choice and carbon feedstocks, not by physically mixing PHB and a separate polymer. Documented routes include engineered Cupriavidus necator production from CO2 and Aeromonas production from vegetable oil, fatty acids, or other C6-derived feedstocks under nutrient limitation. The 3HHx content is a route-dependent outcome, and reported feedstock ratios or gene sets must not be generalized to every PHBHHx material. Following fermentation, intracellular polymer must be recovered and purified by a process appropriate to the organism; article molding is outside this synthesis entry.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyhexanoate) is a semicrystalline thermoplastic polyester whose 3-hydroxyhexanoate units disrupt close packing of the 3-hydroxybutyrate-rich chains. Relative to poly(3-hydroxybutyrate), increasing the 3HHx fraction generally lowers crystallinity, tensile modulus, and tensile strength while increasing extensibility; it can therefore shift from a comparatively stiff response toward a flexible, ductile one. Mechanical behavior also depends on molecular weight, crystallization and physical-aging history, melt temperature and residence time, mold or chill temperature, cooling time, orientation, test rate and temperature, and the presence and dispersion of plasticizers, blend partners, fillers, or pores. Moisture and hydrolytic or thermal degradation can further reduce molecular weight and load-bearing performance.

A bounded melt-processed example used Kaneka Aonilex X151A containing 10.5 mol% 3HHx. Pellets were dried for at least three days at 65 °C, twin-screw extruded at 145 °C and 50 rpm, injection molded into ISO 527-2 type 5A specimens in an 80 °C mold, cooled for 60 seconds, and conditioned at 23 °C and 50% relative humidity for at least three days. At 23 °C and 50% relative humidity with a 20 mm/min crosshead speed, the five-specimen validation run reported 21.4–22.0 MPa tensile yield strength, 320–342% nominal elongation at break, and 883–1007 MPa Young's modulus. The elongation was calculated from the 50 mm grip distance rather than the 20 mm gauge length. These values are limited to this 10.5 mol% grade, process window, specimen, conditioning, and test definition; the same study showed that mold temperature, processing temperature, and test speed materially changed the measured response.
sections.processing:
PHBHHx is shaped by extrusion and compounding, injection and compression molding, film and fiber routes where the grade has sufficient melt strength, solution casting and phase inversion, electrospinning, and filament-based additive manufacturing. Incorporating 3-hydroxyhexanoate generally changes flexibility and crystallization relative to PHB, but the usable window remains composition- and grade-specific. Feed drying, melt and mold temperatures, screw speed and shear, pressure, residence time, cooling and demolding time, crystallization, and post-molding conditioning must be balanced against thermal and mechanical degradation. Slow crystallization or premature demolding can distort an article, while excessive melt temperature and residence can lower molar mass and produce defects.

Vanheusden and co-workers mapped a bounded design space for Aonilex X151A containing 10.5 mol% 3-hydroxyhexanoate. They dried pellets at 65 °C for at least three days, extruded them through an 11 mm, L/D 40 twin screw at a feed setting of 4 rpm, and evaluated melt profiles centered at 145, 152.5, and 160 °C, mold temperatures of 40, 60, and 80 °C, screw speeds of 50, 100, and 150 rpm, and cooling times of 60, 180, and 300 s. Injection used 200 bar for 15 s followed by 150 bar for 10 s. Their preferred validation combination used the lower 140-145 °C profile, an 80 °C mold, 50 rpm screw speed, and 60 s cooling; combinations above 160 °C or with low mold temperature produced deterioration or defective specimens. This window applies only to that grade, machine, and study geometry.

sections.properties: Composition controls flexibility, crystallinity, degradation, and processing window.
sections.applications: PHBHHx is used in biodegradable packaging and biomedical studies.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Copolymer composition and processing route must be specified.

sections.overview: Polylactide (PLA) is a family of aliphatic polyesters commonly made by ring-opening polymerization of lactide, itself obtained from lactic-acid oligomerization and depolymerization. Its composition and stereochemistry influence the properties of a particular PLA material.
sections.nomenclature: PLA and poly(lactic acid) identify the polylactide family, not one stereochemical form, molecular weight, or compounded grade. A plasticized, blended, or reactively modified PLA is a formulation based on the family and should retain those additions in its material description.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polylactides are most commonly made by ring-opening polymerization of lactide, the cyclic dimer derived from lactic acid. Lactic acid is first oligomerized by water removal and the oligomer is depolymerized to lactide; purification and selection of L-lactide, D-lactide, or meso-lactide establish the stereochemical feed. Bulk or solution ring-opening polymerization then uses a catalyst or organocatalyst, usually with an alcohol initiator or chain-transfer agent. Tin(II) 2-ethylhexanoate is a widely used manufacturing catalyst, while zinc-, aluminum-, and organic bases provide alternatives. The cited patent describes the lactic-acid-to-lactide sequence and metal-catalyzed ring opening. A distinct patent demonstrates controlled lactide polymerization with an organic guanidine/alcohol pair. Lactide stereochemistry, monomer-to-initiator ratio, catalyst, and racemization control determine molar mass, end groups, and whether the product is PLLA, PDLA, stereoblock material, or a stereochemically mixed PLA; direct condensation of lactic acid is a lower-molar-mass route variant.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PLA can be relatively stiff and strong but brittle in a glassy state; stereochemistry, molar mass, crystallinity, thermal and ageing history, orientation, strain rate, and blend, plasticizer, or filler formulation can each change the stiffness–ductility balance. An open review identifies this brittleness as the principal mechanical limitation and discusses plasticization, blending, and reactive compounding as routes to tougher formulations. As one tightly bounded example, Ingeo 3051D PLA pellets were hot-pressed into 100 μm films at 190 °C (5 min melt, then 0.5 MPa for 3 min) and water-cooled; room-temperature dog-bone tensile tests at 0.003–0.01 s⁻¹ gave a Young’s modulus of 4.4 GPa and showed yield followed by post-yield softening. That value is for this hot-pressed commercial film and its rate window, not a PLA-family range or a substitute for molded, printed, oriented, or compounded grades.
sections.processing:
Polylactides (PLA) can be converted by injection molding; profile, sheet, cast-film, and blown-film extrusion; injection-stretch and other blow molding; thermoforming; foaming; fiber and nonwoven spinning; melt compounding; compression molding; solvent casting and electrospinning; and fused-filament fabrication. Grade selection is inseparable from route selection because molecular mass, melt-flow rate, D-lactide content, branching, crystallization rate, and additives determine melt strength, drawability, cycle time, and achievable heat resistance. Pellets should be protected from atmospheric moisture and normally dried before melt conversion: water, heat, oxygen, and shear can reduce molecular mass and viscosity. Melt temperature and residence should therefore be kept only as high and long as the grade and operation require, with planned low-temperature purging or shutdown during interruptions. Screw design and speed, mixing sequence, die pressure, draw or blow-up ratio, mold or chill-roll temperature, cooling, annealing, and uniaxial or biaxial orientation govern crystallinity, shrinkage, warpage, gauge, interlayer bonding, and anisotropy.

NatureWorks' Best Practices guide is supplier guidance for Ingeo resins, not every PLA: it recommends drying before extrusion or injection molding, cool dry storage below 50 °C, minimizing pellet exposure, and recognizing that even an interruption shorter than two hours at a controlled temperature below 240 °C can reduce molecular mass and viscosity. Naser, Deiab, and Darras independently document the broader PLA route set and distinguish amorphous from semicrystalline grades. For a bounded injection example, Liparoti, Speranza, and Pantani molded NatureWorks PLA 3251D and 4032D at a 200 °C melt temperature, 2.8 cm3/s average flow rate, and 8 s hold; their trials used 30 or 63 MPa holding pressure and rapidly modulated the instrumented cavity surface from a 30 °C passive condition to selected 50, 100, or 150 °C levels for 1, 8, or 13 s. Those values belong to the two named grades, microfeature mold, and replication experiment rather than defining a family-wide PLA window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polylactide is an aliphatic polyester family whose stereochemistry and crystallinity are set by lactide feed, catalyst, and thermal history.
sections.properties: PLA is often rigid and brittle; plasticization, blending, and reactive compounding can change the stiffness–toughness balance.
sections.applications: Published PLA evidence includes hot-pressed film materials and compounded polymer formulations.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: The cited film modulus belongs to a named Ingeo grade, 100 μm hot-pressed film, and stated tensile rates; stereochemistry, molecular weight, crystallinity, and additives prevent a single PLA property value.

sections.overview: Poly(L-lactide) (PLLA) is the L-stereochemical polylactide polymer made by ring-opening polymerization of L-lactide. Molecular weight, crystallinity, and processing history influence the behavior of a particular PLLA article or scaffold.
sections.nomenclature: PLLA and poly(L-lactic acid) identify the L-lactide-derived member of the broader polylactide family. The name is narrower than unqualified PLA and should not be used for D-lactide, meso-lactide, racemic, or stereoblock materials; a blend or crosslinked scaffold is a separately qualified formulation.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(L-lactide) (PLLA) is the stereodefined polylactide made principally by ring-opening polymerization of enantiopure L-lactide, the cyclic dimer associated with L-lactic acid. Industrial and laboratory routes use catalyst/initiator systems such as tin octanoate, whereas alternative metal complexes can control the opening and stereochemical sequence. Monomer stereochemical purity is central to the PLLA boundary: L-lactide gives the L-rich chain, while meso-lactide or racemic D/L-lactide feeds introduce stereochemical defects or different PLA microstructures rather than simply providing equivalent PLLA feedstock. An open study of L-lactide/meso-lactide mixtures contrasts conventional tin-octanoate melt ROP with a zirconium catalyst that directs stereogradient structures. A separate review documents how the S,S, R,R, meso, and racemic lactide feeds, together with catalyst stereoselectivity, give isotactic, atactic, heterotactic, or syndiotactic poly(lactide) microstructures. These are polymer-formation controls, not molding or annealing instructions.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PLLA is a semicrystalline aliphatic polyester whose tensile and impact response is governed by stereochemical purity, molar mass, crystallinity and crystal form, thermal/aging history, orientation, temperature and rate, and any blend, plasticizer, or filler. These variables can trade stiffness and strength against ductility; porous biomedical scaffolds are additionally controlled by pore structure and porosity. In an open RSC study, NatureWorks 4032D PLLA was vacuum dried, melt-mixed at 190 °C, then injection molded at 200 °C melt and 60 °C mold temperatures. For the neat PLLA control, tested at room temperature under ASTM D638 at 5 mm/min and averaged over at least five specimens, the reported tensile strength was 64.9 ± 2.7 MPa, elongation at break 8.0 ± 0.9%, tensile modulus 2001.6 ± 71.0 MPa, and notched Izod impact strength 16.9 ± 1.4 J/m. This is an injection-molded, high-molar-mass control after that study's thermal history, not a family-wide PLLA range. A separate open review reports that scaffold response varies especially strongly with molecular weight, crystallinity, aging, microstructure, and porosity, so scaffold values must not be compared directly with the molded control.
sections.processing:
PLLA can be melt-extruded, injection or compression molded, thermoformed, melt-spun and drawn, solvent-cast, electrospun, phase-separated into porous scaffolds, and additively manufactured by filament extrusion or melt electrowriting. Hydrolytic sensitivity makes pellet drying important before melt conversion. Melt temperature, shear and residence time must limit molar-mass loss, while mold/bed temperature and cooling determine crystallization, warpage, shrinkage, heat resistance, and interlayer bonding. Solution routes additionally require control of concentration, solvent removal, porosity, and residual solvent; fiber and printed routes depend on draw or raster orientation.

Krug, Zarges, and Heim give a bounded injection-molding comparison of three named PLLA materials. They vacuum-dried Luminy L130 for 4 h at 100 °C and NP HT 202/203 for 4 h at 60 °C. Luminy L130 used a 205/205/215/215 °C barrel-to-nozzle profile, a 40 °C mold, 40 s cooling, and 50.8 s total cycle; the two NP grades used 175/180/185/185 °C and a 25 °C mold, with grade-specific cooling and cycle times. These are specimen-preparation settings for those grades and that Arburg machine; stereochemistry, nucleation, additives, moisture, geometry, and desired crystallinity can require different conditions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PLLA is a stereoregular aliphatic polyester with crystallinity set by molecular and thermal history.
sections.properties: Stiffness, degradation, and toughness depend on crystallinity, orientation, and modification.
sections.applications: PLLA is used in resorbable medical and regenerative-biomaterial systems.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Toughened and injection-molded PLLA outcomes are formulation- and process-specific.

sections.overview: Poly(glycolic acid) is an aliphatic polyester derived from glycolic-acid or glycolide units. It is a hydrolysable polymer used in absorbable medical and other degradable-material contexts.
sections.nomenclature: PGA abbreviates poly(glycolic acid), also called polyglycolide. The name denotes the glycolic-acid homopolyester and is distinct from copolymers such as PLGA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(glycolic acid) (PGA, also polyglycolide) is the aliphatic polyester derived from glycolic acid or, for common high-molar-mass routes, glycolide, its cyclic dimer. Direct melt polycondensation of glycolic acid removes water but is usually limited in molar mass by water removal and the glycolide/polymer equilibrium. High-molar-mass PGA is instead commonly made by ring-opening polymerization (ROP) of purified glycolide; monomer free-acid/water content, catalyst loading, initiator, and thermal history are consequential route controls. One free-access study reports sequential melt–solid glycolide ROP using tin(II) chloride dihydrate and 1-dodecanol; catalyst and initiator concentrations were associated with polymerization rate, end groups, and molar mass. That is a process-specific example, not an assertion that all PGA uses that tin catalyst or an alcohol initiator. PGA is a homopolymer; lactide-containing materials are PLGA/PLA-related copolymers rather than alternate names for PGA.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PGA is a stiff, semicrystalline aliphatic polyester whose practical tensile response is sensitive to molar mass and chain architecture, crystallinity and orientation, thermal and molding history, and hydrolytic moisture exposure. Drawing can substantially increase oriented-specimen strength, while chain extension or branching, blends, and nucleating or toughening additives trade stiffness against ductility; water uptake and hydrolysis make wet or aged results unsuitable as dry-material constants. In one open injection-molding study, neat PGA had a tensile modulus of 6412.10 MPa and elongation at break of 9.8%; adding 0.9 phr of a multifunctional epoxy chain extender produced a modified PGA with 8372.40 MPa modulus and 57.2% elongation. Those values are specific to the study's injection-molded neat and chain-extended formulations and should not be presented as general PGA values. An independent open molecular-dynamics tensile study examined PGA model systems with 1.7%, 2.9%, and 5% water by mass, providing a separate, model-scale indication that water content is a mechanical variable rather than a transferable bulk-test endpoint.
sections.processing:
Poly(glycolic acid) (PGA) can be melt extruded or coextruded into mono- and multilayer film or sheet, injection molded, thermoformed, laminated, and biaxially stretched or stretch-blow molded; drawn monofilament and multifilament are also established article forms. Because PGA is hydrolysis-sensitive, moisture control continues from bag opening through the hopper, and insufficient drying lowers melt viscosity and can compound thermal degradation. Short melt residence, prompt purging after an interruption, moderate screw compression, and controlled cooling/orientation are important because melt degradation, crystallization, and draw history strongly affect the finished article.

Kureha's November 2011 Kuredux technical guide gives grade-family starting guidance, not a universal PGA window: re-dry opened resin at 120 °C for 12 h with −40 °C-dew-point dry air (not more than 24 h), and reject as a starting point resin left about 4 h at 23 °C/60% RH. It lists extrusion zones of 220–240 °C feed, 230–260 °C compression, 250–270 °C metering, and 240–270 °C adapter/die, with a warning not to exceed 280 °C. For its ASTM-family-mold test piece it reports a 230–270 °C cylinder, 90–120 °C mold, 50–100 MPa injection pressure, and 2–3 m/min injection speed. Independently, Gao and co-workers dried one supplied PGA at 60 °C for 8 h, mixed it with 0–0.9 phr Joncryl ADR-4370s at 235 °C and 50 rpm for 10 min, and injection molded that formulation; prolonged 235 °C mixing reduced neat-PGA torque, directly illustrating residence-time degradation. Both schedules remain tied to their named grade or experiment.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PGA is a linear aliphatic polyester with repeating glycolate units and a relatively regular, crystalline chain structure. It can be produced by ring-opening polymerization of glycolide or related routes, and molecular mass and crystallinity depend on catalyst and thermal history.
sections.properties: PGA has high crystallinity, stiffness, barrier performance, and hydrolytic degradability relative to many other aliphatic polyesters. Water access, crystallinity, molecular mass, end groups, and copolymerization strongly control hydrolysis and mass loss.
sections.applications: PGA is used in absorbable surgical sutures and other temporary biomedical devices, drug-delivery systems, tissue-engineering matrices, high-barrier films, and selected blends or copolymers. Its degradation rate is often tuned through composition and morphology.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PGA can be brittle, difficult to process because of a narrow thermal window, and sensitive to hydrolysis during storage and melt conversion. Molecular mass, residual catalyst, crystallinity, specimen thickness, water activity, copolymer content, and sterilization history make degradation and service lifetime application-specific.

sections.overview: Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) is a biodegradable copolyester containing lactide-derived and glycolide-derived units. Its comonomer ratio is an important variable for degradation and drug-delivery performance.
sections.nomenclature: PLGA abbreviates poly(lactide-co-glycolide). The name describes a composition-variable copolymer family, not a single fixed lactide:glycolide ratio, and it is distinct from PLA and PGA homopolymers.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) is a copolyester made by ring-opening copolymerization of lactide and glycolide, not a physical blend of preformed PLA and PGA. The lactide stereoisomer, lactide:glycolide feed and incorporation ratio, catalyst/initiator choice, monomer-to-catalyst ratio, temperature, and conversion all affect the resulting chain composition and molar mass. A high-glycolide study polymerized d,l-lactide and glycolide with tin(II) 2-ethylhexanoate and 1-dodecanol, then varied initiator/catalyst concentration, temperature, and time; its 25:75 L:G material is a composition-specific example. A separate open study emphasizes that high-molar-mass PLGA is obtained by cyclic-dimer ROP rather than direct lactic-acid/glycolic-acid polycondensation, and explicitly evaluates lactide-content variation. Thus PLLA, PGA, and PLGA are related but distinct scopes, and neither a bulk polymerization recipe nor a particle formulation should be generalized to all PLGA compositions.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PLGA is a composition-variable copolyester rather than a single mechanical material. Lactide:glycolide ratio, sequence distribution, molar mass and end groups, crystallinity, thermal and solvent-casting history, orientation, porosity, hydration, and hydrolytic aging all change tensile response. An open review specifically reports that raising glycolide content relative to a more lactide-rich PLGA tends to increase brittleness and lower tensile strength, so named ratios should not be collapsed into one PLGA range. In a separate open thin-film study, solvent-cast PLGA containing 30% glycolide reached a tensile strength of up to 58 MPa; the paper contrasts this result with separately cast PLLA and PDLA films. That endpoint is limited to the reported cast-film composition and study preparation; the available result does not establish a universal PLGA value or a value for a hydrated implant, porous scaffold, or degradatively aged specimen.
sections.processing:
Poly(lactide-co-glycolide) (PLGA) is article-converted by melt injection molding and fiber forming, as well as by solvent casting, particulate-leached casting, emulsion/solvent evaporation, electrospinning, and formulation-specific thermal gelation or photocuring for porous carriers and hydrogels. Solvent routes require complete dissolution and dispersion, controlled casting or droplet/fiber formation, solvent evaporation, and, where applicable, leaching and final drying. Copolymer ratio, molecular mass, end groups, drug/filler content, residual solvent, and thermal history all change viscosity, glass transition, degradation, and solidification, so conditions must be attached to a grade and article geometry.

A bounded injection-molding study used Purasorb PLG 8531, an 85:15 lactide:glycolide grade, in an Arburg 270S/250-70 machine. Four conditions combined melt temperatures of 240 or 210 °C with volumetric flow rates of 25 or 10 cm³/s; the fixed settings included a 25 °C mold, 25 MPa holding pressure, 2 s injection, 90 s cooling, and 100 rpm screw speed. The lower-temperature conditions produced broader birefringence and greater residual stress, while flow rate changed shear, molecular orientation, and failure strain. Those values describe the cited small notched and unnotched test specimens, not all PLGA ratios or medical devices; they also show why rapid cooling, gate/geometry, shear, and post-molding stress cannot be separated from nominal melt temperature.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PLGA is a copolyester of lactide and glycolide whose composition, sequence distribution, molecular mass, and end groups control crystallinity and morphology. Increasing glycolide content generally changes chain packing and water access, while amorphous or partially crystalline domains support tunable degradation.
sections.properties: PLGA is hydrolytically degradable and can be processed into particles, films, fibers, porous scaffolds, and implants. Degradation produces lactic- and glycolic-acid products, and the rate depends on copolymer ratio, molecular mass, crystallinity, geometry, water uptake, and formulation.
sections.applications: PLGA is widely used in biodegradable drug-delivery microspheres, nanoparticles, sutures, tissue-engineering scaffolds, resorbable implants, and temporary medical coatings. It is also studied in barrier and packaging formulations where controlled degradation is desired.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PLGA can undergo autocatalytic hydrolysis, acidic microenvironments, burst release, embrittlement, and dimensional change. Lactide/glycolide ratio, end groups, molecular mass, particle or implant size, porosity, sterilization, residual solvent, and storage humidity must remain tied to any lifetime or release claim.

sections.overview: Polycaprolactone is a biodegradable aliphatic polyester commonly made by ring-opening polymerization of epsilon-caprolactone. It is used in melt-processable materials, including biomedical scaffolds and blends.
sections.nomenclature: PCL abbreviates polycaprolactone. The canonical name denotes the epsilon-caprolactone homopolyester and is distinct from other degradable polyesters such as PLA and PGA.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polycaprolactone (PCL) is the aliphatic polyester most commonly produced by ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone. An alcohol, water, amine, metal alkoxide, or other active-hydrogen compound can initiate a chain, and the initiator functionality determines whether the product is linear, branched, or a multifunctional caprolactone polyol. Tin(II) octoate is a common catalyst, while aluminum complexes, enzymes, and organocatalysts provide alternatives. A continuous-process patent describes ε-caprolactone ROP with active-hydrogen or organometallic initiators and optional catalyst. An open study uses an aluminum phenoxide complex with several alcohol initiators and directly links initiator identity to end groups and molar-mass evolution. Monomer-to-initiator ratio, catalyst, water content, and conversion are architecture controls. Caprolactone copolymers or PCL blocks are distinct from the homopolymer unless their composition is stated.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a semicrystalline, low-melting aliphatic polyester that typically yields and draws to high strain in dense bulk form, but its apparent stiffness and strength vary sharply with molecular mass, crystallinity and cooling history, branching or crosslinking, temperature, hydrolytic aging, blend or reinforcement chemistry, and processing into a dense part, filament, or porous scaffold. At body-relevant temperatures it is closer to its melting transition than at room temperature, so thermal history and service temperature are especially consequential. A bounded bulk example is Perstorp Capa 6800 (Mw 80,000 g/mol): 2 mm compression-molded plaques (170 °C, 4.9 MPa, 1 min, then room-temperature cooling) tested at room temperature to ISO 527-2 at 50 mm/min had 149 ± 25 MPa Young modulus, 13.1 ± 0.2 MPa yield stress, 30.0 ± 1.2 MPa break stress, and 611 ± 25% elongation at break (five repeats). These are not values for electrospun PCL or a scaffold. Independent laser-sintered PCL work shows that build orientation and especially designed porosity reduce tensile modulus and strength markedly compared with near-dense PCL, so scaffold architecture must remain attached to its endpoint.
sections.processing: Polycaprolactone (PCL) is a low-melting semicrystalline thermoplastic converted by melt extrusion, injection/compression molding, fiber spinning, and powder-bed processes such as selective laser sintering; solution electrospinning is also used for scaffold fiber formation. Molecular mass, branching or peroxide modification, powder size, build orientation, and the desired porosity change the usable window. A bounded Capa 6800 example was formed as a compression-molded plaque for tensile specimens, whereas an independent scaffold study used selective laser sintering to fabricate dense and orthogonally porous PCL architectures. The latter route requires control of powder spreading, laser energy, layer fusion, and cooling because insufficient fusion leaves connected porosity while excessive thermal exposure can distort the scaffold. Those are process examples for named PCL feedstocks, not a universal temperature or laser window. Ring-opening polymerization and peroxide functionalization belong in Synthesis; this section covers shaping of supplied PCL resin or powder and post-build conditioning.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polycaprolactone is a semicrystalline aliphatic polyester made from epsilon-caprolactone by ring-opening polymerization or related routes. Its flexible methylene-rich chains form crystalline polyester domains and a relatively low-melting amorphous phase.
sections.properties: PCL is melt processable, flexible, hydrophobic relative to many biodegradable polyesters, and hydrolytically or enzymatically degradable over long times. Crystallinity, molecular mass, copolymer, plasticizer, and geometry control its thermal, barrier, and degradation behavior.
sections.applications: The cited evidence covers compression-molded PCL plaques and selective-laser-sintered dense or porous scaffold architectures. These forms support molded and scaffold applications; drug-delivery, printing, and blends remain grade- and process-specific extensions.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PCL can have low heat resistance, slow degradation in bulk, and limited stiffness without reinforcement. Molecular mass, crystallinity, copolymer content, porosity, water access, sterilization, and processing history strongly affect lifetime and performance.

sections.overview: Poly(butylene succinate) is PBS, an aliphatic polyester made by esterification or transesterification of succinic-acid derivatives with 1,4-butanediol followed by polycondensation. Feed form and molecular-weight-building steps vary among documented routes.
sections.nomenclature: PBS is the abbreviation used for poly(butylene succinate). This record is the succinate polyester; PBSA, PBAT, physical blends, and a particular chain-extended or processed formulation are chemically or materially distinct scopes rather than aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(butylene succinate) is an aliphatic polyester made by step-growth polycondensation of succinic acid, or a succinate derivative, with 1,4-butanediol. The direct-acid route first esterifies the diacid and diol to hydroxyl-terminated oligomers while removing esterification water. Polycondensation then raises molecular weight under reduced pressure in the presence of a catalyst, with removal of volatile 1,4-butanediol helping drive the equilibrium. Dimethyl or diethyl succinate and succinic anhydride are documented alternative acid-side feeds. The cited procedures are route examples; catalyst selection, staged vacuum operation, and any optional chain extension are process-specific and are not universal requirements for PBS.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PBS is semicrystalline, so molar mass, crystallinity, thermal history, chain extension or branching, draw/orientation, and degradation or moisture/temperature exposure control measured mechanics. An open PBS review notes that higher molecular weight can increase tensile strength, while comonomers that lower crystallinity tend to reduce stiffness/strength and increase extensibility. A separate stretching study links changing crystalline morphology and orientation to the PBS tensile/cyclic response.

A bounded film result from one PBS/PBAT study is its neat PBS control: elastic modulus 725.6 ± 15.6 MPa, stress at break 29.6 ± 1.5 MPa, and strain at break 7.1 ± 0.3%. The paper identifies the tested PBS as a specific material (reported Mw 62 kg/mol); these film values are not a general PBS grade range and should not be applied to chain-extended, oriented, blended, or filled PBS.
sections.processing:
PBS can be extruded and compounded, injection or compression molded, blown and cast into film, thermoformed, blow molded, spun into fiber, foamed, and processed by filament-based additive manufacturing. Molar mass and branching select the route: lower-flow molding/extrusion grades and higher-melt-strength film grades are not interchangeable. Drying, melt temperature, shear, residence time, die or mold cooling, crystallization, draw/blow ratio, and repeated heat history influence hydrolysis, degradation, film stability, shrinkage, and final morphology. Nucleants and branching agents may alter both crystallization and melt strength.

Zaverl and co-workers provide a bounded blend example using Biocosafe 1903 PBS and Biocosafe 2003 PBAT. They dried materials overnight at 80 °C, hand-mixed a 60/40 PBS/PBAT skin blend, compounded it in a co-rotating twin-screw extruder at 112 rpm with a 130-150 °C barrel-to-die profile, cooled the strands in water, pelletized them, and molded the skin phase with nominal 185-190 °C zones while studying co-injection temperature, speed, pressure, and mold effects. This is a specific two-polymer co-injection formulation, not a neat-PBS window. The open PBS review likewise makes clear that molecular weight, branching, crystallization, and thermal stability determine whether a grade is suited to injection, extrusion, casting, or film blowing.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PBS is a semicrystalline aliphatic polyester based on succinate and butanediol units.
sections.properties: Crystallinity, molecular weight, blends, and processing influence its mechanics and biodegradation.
sections.applications: PBS is used in biodegradable packaging, films, and molded products.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Film and coinjection studies concern specific formulations and process conditions.

sections.overview: Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) is PBAT, an aliphatic–aromatic copolyester built from 1,4-butanediol, adipic acid, and terephthalic acid or their ester derivatives. The adipate and terephthalate feed balance varies by grade and is not a fixed alternating sequence.
sections.nomenclature: PBAT is the abbreviation for the butylene adipate/terephthalate copolyester. The record denotes a covalent copolymer, not a physical blend of PBS and another polyester; catalyst package, exact sequence distribution, and a filled or processed formulation are not alternate names for PBAT.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) is an aliphatic–aromatic copolyester built from 1,4-butanediol (BDO), adipic acid (AA), and terephthalic acid (TPA), or the corresponding ester derivatives. Common manufacture is staged melt condensation: direct esterification or transesterification first forms oligomers, then high-temperature, reduced-pressure polycondensation removes water, methanol, or excess diol to raise molar mass. Titanium-, tin-, and zinc-based catalysts are reported examples. The AA:TPA feed, BDO excess, catalyst, temperature, time, and vacuum are synthesis controls; the resulting butylene-adipate and butylene-terephthalate sequences should not be represented as a fixed alternating repeat. A separate patent demonstrates both an acid/BDO/titanium-phosphate esterification route and a route that first prepares butylene terephthalate and butanediol adipate then copolycondenses them. These are synthesis examples, not a claim that all commercial PBAT uses their catalyst package or sequence distribution.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PBAT mechanical response is governed by butylene-adipate/butylene-terephthalate composition, molar mass, crystallinity, thermal and processing history, orientation, and any blend, filler, or degradation exposure. Open reviews specifically identify molecular weight, composition, processing pressure/temperature, and crystallinity as controlling variables, so blend or composite data must not be treated as intrinsic PBAT values.

A bounded film example from one PBS/PBAT-blend study is its neat PBAT control: elastic modulus 81.0 ± 2.5 MPa, stress at break 20.1 ± 2.4 MPa, and strain at break 689.5 ± 110.3%. These tensile values apply to that study's film specimen and reported commercial PBAT; its grade, molecular-weight distribution, film processing, conditioning, and test geometry constrain their use.
sections.processing:
PBAT is chiefly compounded and converted into flexible blown or cast film, bags and coatings, and it is also used in injection molding, extrusion coating, sheet/thermoforming blends, and filament processing. Commercial PBAT frequently appears in blends with starch, PLA, or other biodegradable polyesters. Feed moisture, starch plasticization and dispersion, blend ratio, specific throughput and shear, melt and die temperature, screw speed, residence time, blow-up and draw-down ratios, cooling, winding, and storage humidity influence degradation, gels, gauge, bubble stability, orientation, blocking, and mechanical balance.

Thongkham and co-workers provide a bounded TPS/PBAT film study. They compounded virgin PBAT with 20, 40, or 60 wt% thermoplastic starch at 180 rpm and 120-150 °C, pelletized, dried the blends at 45 °C for one day, and blew films on a 25 mm, L/D 30 single screw. Their formulation-dependent film settings used 150-190 °C extrusion, 35-44 rpm, a 140-160 °C die, 3.0-3.5 blow-up ratio, and 5.0-6.5 draw-down ratio; films were sealed against moisture exchange at 30 °C. These are blend- and equipment-specific settings. The processing review further documents that low specific throughput can overheat/degrade TPS/PBAT even while increasing dispersive shear, so temperature, output, and screw speed must be optimized together.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PBAT is an aliphatic–aromatic copolyester combining flexible adipate and rigid terephthalate units.
sections.properties: Composition, crystallinity, blends, and fillers control ductility and biodegradation behavior.
sections.applications: PBAT is used in compostable films and packaging blends.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Biocomposite and blown-film results are formulation- and processing-specific.

sections.overview: Poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) is PBSA, an aliphatic copolyester containing succinate and adipate residues with 1,4-butanediol. It is formed by condensation polymerization, and the relative diacid feed controls copolymer composition.
sections.nomenclature: PBSA is the abbreviation for poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate). The record denotes a covalent succinate/adipate copolymer, not a physical PBS/poly(butylene adipate) blend; PBS homopolymer, PBAT, and modified or filled formulations are separate scopes.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(butylene succinate-co-adipate) (PBSA) is an aliphatic copolyester in which both succinate and adipate residues are incorporated with 1,4-butanediol; it is not a physical blend of PBS and poly(butylene adipate). The cited syntheses charge succinic acid, adipic acid, and 1,4-butanediol to form a prepolymer and then perform condensation poly­merization. The relative diacid feed is a compositional control variable and can change the resulting copolyester, so no single ratio is implied for the entire PBSA name. Additional branching, cross-linking, or chain-extending reactants described in individual sources define modified PBSA variants and are not part of the base copolymer identity.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PBSA is a composition-sensitive aliphatic copolyester. The adipate fraction can lower crystallinity and melting behavior relative to PBS, while molecular weight, film orientation/draw ratio, annealing, filler loading, and environmental exposure further alter tensile response. Independent open studies accordingly describe PBSA as ductile but show that oriented and filled films can be substantially stiffer or less extensible than the neat material.

A bounded neat-PBSA film result from one five-replicate study is Young's modulus 0.29 ± 0.05 GPa, stress at break 21.10 ± 0.50 MPa, and break elongation 400 ± 53%; the same paper reports 32.1% crystallinity for that PBSA. These values are for its particular film and formulation, not for PBSA composites, blends, orientation states, or all succinate/adipate compositions.
sections.processing:
PBSA is a melt-processable aliphatic copolyester used in blown and cast film, extrusion and compounding, injection molding, sheet thermoforming, and blends or composites. Adipate content, molar mass, branching, and blend formulation govern crystallization and melt strength. Pellets and hygroscopic co-components should be dried; melt temperature, shear, residence time, die and chill-roll temperature, draw/blow ratio, cooling and winding must balance homogeneous dispersion against hydrolytic or thermal degradation. Too little melt strength destabilizes film, while repeated heat/shear histories and excessive temperature can lower molar mass.

A bounded cast-film study by Alfano and co-workers used BioPBS FD92PM PBSA in PHBV/PBSA blends. PBSA, PHBV, and compatibilizer were oven-dried at 60 °C for at least 12 h, manually premixed, and fed to an L/D 25 single-screw extruder with a flat die and calender. The profile was 175/175/165/165/165/165 °C at 40 rpm, producing about 500 micrometre sheets. These conditions were selected for those blend compositions and compatibilized films, not neat PBSA generally. The PBS/PBSA review identifies extrusion, injection, casting, and film blowing as established routes and emphasizes that molecular architecture, crystallization, and thermal stability select the suitable process.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PBSA is an aliphatic copolyester with succinate and adipate units that tune chain flexibility and crystallization.
sections.properties: Composition and processing control its mechanical response, hydrolysis, and biodegradation.
sections.applications: PBSA is used in biodegradable films and packaging formulations.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Carbon-chain and film studies apply to specified copolymer compositions and fillers.

sections.overview: Poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate) is an aromatic polyester built from ethylene glycol and 2,5-furandicarboxylate units. Its furan-containing diacid component distinguishes it from terephthalate polyesters.
sections.nomenclature: PEF abbreviates poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate), often shortened to poly(ethylene furanoate). The canonical name specifies the 2,5-furandicarboxylate structure and is not a name for all furan-based polyesters.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate) (PEF) is the polyester from 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA), or a diester thereof, and ethylene glycol. FDCA is a furan dicarboxylic-acid feedstock; its use, rather than terephthalic acid, defines the furandicarboxylate repeat unit. Routes first esterify FDCA with ethylene glycol, or transesterify an FDCA diester, then polycondense the oligomer under reduced pressure while removing low-molar-mass products. Titanium alkoxide and antimony- or germanium-based catalysts occur in the cited examples, and solid-state polycondensation may be used for additional molecular-weight build-up. Those catalyst and finishing choices are source-specific, not a single mandatory PEF recipe.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PEF mechanics depend on molar mass, furan-polyester microstructure, crystallinity/polymorph, thermal history and annealing, strain orientation, and any comonomer or diethylene-glycol content. Open studies find that monomer route and intrinsic viscosity change crystallinity and elastic response, while biaxial stretching induces crystallinity and modifies rigidity; therefore amorphous plaques, annealed material, stretched film, and fibers cannot be pooled.

A bounded high-molecular-weight PEF example (Mn 83,000 g/mol, made by melt polymerization followed by solid-state post-condensation) reported Young's modulus 2,450 ± 220 MPa and maximum stress 35 ± 8 MPa. The paper also studied crystallinity effects with temperature, so these results are not a universal PEF datasheet value or directly transferable to lower-molar-mass, copolymer, or oriented PEF.
sections.processing:
Poly(ethylene 2,5-furandicarboxylate) (PEF) can be converted by melt extrusion and extrusion casting, injection molding of preforms and other parts, stretch blow molding, thermoforming, and fiber spinning. Stretching and shear during these operations alter crystallization kinetics and morphology, so melt temperature, residence time, shear history, cooling, and subsequent uniaxial or biaxial orientation must be developed together. A recent open review also identifies high melt viscosity, shear sensitivity, and the proximity of useful melt processing to thermal degradation as practical reasons not to transfer a PET schedule unchanged to PEF.

For one bounded stretch-blow-molding approach, The Coca-Cola Company's EP 3 194 134 B1 discloses water-conditioning an already injection-molded PEF or PEF-copolymer preform, followed by removal of trapped and surface water and stretch blow molding. Claim 1 gives alternative conditioning ranges of room-temperature water for about 3 h to at least 48 h, water at about 80 °C for up to about 15 h, at least about 65% RH air above about 45 °C for about 0.25 h to at least 72 h, or at least about 85% RH air above about 35 °C for about 0.5 h to at least 44 h. The patent warns that excessive moisture together with heat can produce excessive crystallization. These are claimed options for the disclosed preform process, not a general PEF drying or blow-molding window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PEF is a polyester formed from ethylene glycol and 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid or its ester. The rigid furan-containing aromatic-like diacid unit produces a semicrystalline polyester whose packing and crystallization differ from PET.
sections.properties: PEF can provide high stiffness, useful thermal behavior, and strong barrier performance to oxygen and carbon dioxide relative to conventional polyester benchmarks. Crystallinity, chain orientation, molecular mass, and humidity affect permeability and dimensional response.
sections.applications: PEF is being developed for bottles, films, fibers, packaging, and renewable-content polyester products. Its barrier potential is especially relevant to multilayer or container applications where gas retention matters.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PEF remains sensitive to molecular mass, crystallization rate, hydrolysis, processing temperature, and residual catalyst or moisture. Much evidence is formulation- and process-specific, and PEF should not be treated as a drop-in equivalent for every PET conversion line or application.

sections.overview: Poly(ethylene oxide) is a polyether made from ethylene oxide repeat units. Molecular weight strongly affects its physical form and use, from lower-molar-mass polyethylene glycols to higher-molar-mass PEO polymers.
sections.nomenclature: PEO abbreviates poly(ethylene oxide); polyethylene glycol (PEG) is commonly used for chemically equivalent lower-molar-mass materials. The names should be qualified by molecular-weight scope rather than treated as universally interchangeable.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO), also called poly(oxyethylene) and often termed polyethylene glycol at lower molar mass, is the ring-opening polymerization product of ethylene oxide. Anionic routes combine ethylene oxide with a hydroxyl- or amine-functional initiator and a strongly basic catalyst such as potassium hydroxide; active-hydrogen initiators produce hydroxy-terminated chains or multiple arms according to initiator functionality. Metal-cyanide catalysts are a separately documented ethoxylation route. Thus initiator identity, catalyst system, and ethylene-oxide-to-initiator feed determine architecture and molar mass; they should not be inferred from the bare PEO family name.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
High-molecular-weight poly(ethylene oxide) is a semicrystalline, water-soluble thermoplastic. In a dry film at room temperature its amorphous phase is well above the glass-transition region and the crystals act as physical load-bearing domains, so the material can yield, neck or craze, and deform substantially rather than responding as a rigid glass. It is also strongly viscoelastic and susceptible to creep and rate-dependent fracture. Molecular weight and entanglement density, crystalline fraction and lamellar morphology, solvent-casting or melt history, cooling and annealing, orientation, physical aging, test rate and temperature, and specimen thickness affect modulus, yield, ductility, and wear. Water uptake is especially consequential because it changes crystallinity and chain mobility and can progress to swelling or dissolution; humidity and conditioning must therefore accompany useful PEO mechanical data. Salts, crosslinks, blend segments, and dispersed fillers create mechanically different PEO-based materials.

A bounded neat-film example used Sigma-Aldrich PEO with viscosity-average molecular mass 1,000,000 g/mol. A 4 wt% aqueous solution was cast in glass dishes and vacuum-dried at 80 °C for about 5 hours. The unfilled film had 82% crystallinity by the study's DSC convention. Ten dumbbells with a 2 mm by 20 mm narrow section were pulled at 20 cm/min, giving 760 ± 109 MPa Young's modulus, 14.2 ± 0.9 MPa yield strength, 12.8 ± 0.4 MPa stress at failure, and 86 ± 14% strain at failure. The paper does not report film thickness, tensile-test temperature, or humidity/conditioning, so the values remain specific to that molecular mass and aqueous-cast/dried specimen preparation and are not a general dry-PEO range. A separate NASA study of PEO sliding contacts found molecular-weight, sliding-speed, and load-dependent friction, surface melting, and crack formation, independently reinforcing that load history and molecular size matter without supplying a transferable tensile endpoint.
sections.processing:
Poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO) is commonly converted from solution into cast or doctor-bladed films and coatings, electrospun fiber mats, and solution-derived feed for three-dimensional printing; the appropriate route depends strongly on molecular mass and formulation. For PEO-based solid polymer electrolytes, solution concentration and viscosity, salt or filler dispersion, coating thickness, solvent choice and evaporation rate, and the final vacuum-drying or heat-treatment step control film uniformity and crystallization. Electrospinning additionally requires coordinated control of solution viscosity and conductivity, feed, electric field, collector, and solvent removal. These routes and limitations apply to the cited PEO-containing formulations rather than defining a universal schedule for neat PEO.

As a bounded film-casting example, Xu and co-workers used PEO of viscosity-average molecular mass about 1,000,000 g/mol. They made a 4 wt% aqueous PEO solution, added aqueous cellulose-nanocrystal suspension or cellulose-nanofibril gel to obtain 0–10 wt% reinforcement on PEO solids, homogenized at 100 rpm for 5 min at room temperature, then magnetically stirred at about 100 rpm and 60 °C for 12 h. The mixtures were cast in glass Petri dishes and vacuum-oven dried at 80 °C for about 5 h. That mixing and drying sequence belongs to those PEO/cellulose nanocomposite films and should not be generalized to other molecular masses, solvents, or filled systems.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(ethylene oxide) is a flexible polyether with repeating –CH2CH2O– units. Depending on molecular mass, crystallinity, water content, and salt or polymer interactions, it can occur as a semicrystalline solid, hydrated chain phase, or entangled solution.
sections.properties: PEO is water-soluble, hydrophilic, film-forming, and capable of coordinating cations through ether oxygens. Molecular mass and crystallinity control viscosity, melting behavior, transport, and electrolyte conductivity; moisture and salt strongly alter the response.
sections.applications: PEO is used as a water-soluble binder and thickener, in pharmaceutical and biomedical formulations, solid-polymer electrolytes, membrane and coating systems, dispersants, and electrospinning or fiber formulations. Its solubility and ion coordination enable aqueous and energy-material uses.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: PEO can crystallize, absorb moisture, undergo oxidative chain scission, and lose viscosity under heat, radiation, or strong shear. Molecular mass, end groups, salt identity and concentration, humidity, crystallinity, and blend compatibility must accompany any application claim.

sections.overview: Poly(propylene oxide) is a polyether made by ring-opening polymerization of propylene oxide. Double-metal-cyanide and anionic catalyst systems can produce polyoxypropylene polyols with controlled chain growth and end groups.
sections.nomenclature: PPO, PPG, and poly(propylene oxide) refer to the polyether record boundary here; in polyol contexts PPG emphasizes hydroxyl-terminated material. A crosslinked PPO elastomer or polyurethane soft segment is a network or copolymer formulation made from PPO, not a synonym for the base polyether.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(propylene oxide) (PPO, also poly(oxypropylene)) is the ring-opened polyether from propylene oxide. Anionic ring-opening polymerization with alkoxide/basic initiators is a principal route; common starter choices such as an alcohol, diol, triol, or polyol determine chain-end functionality and whether the product is a linear polyether or a multifunctional polyether polyol. A controlled study uses potassium initiators activated by crown ether in THF and shows that initiator identity affects regioselective ring opening, unsaturation, and molar mass. Double-metal-cyanide catalysts provide a different route for propylene-oxide polyether-polyol formation and can reduce/tune unsaturation and initiation behavior. These route examples do not make a polyurethane network or a CO2/PO copolymer into PPO; such subsequent reactions and carbonate-containing copolymers are separate materials.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PPO/PPG spans low-molar-mass polyether fluids, elastomer networks, and stereoregular solid forms, so it has no single useful bulk tensile value. Mechanical response depends on molar mass and end groups, tacticity/crystallizability, crosslink architecture, fillers or solvent, temperature and strain rate, and whether a sample is a free network, a blend, or a block copolymer. In one open study, an α,ω-diallyl PPO network (PPO Mn 16,500 g mol−1) was photochemically crosslinked with a tetrafunctional thiol and tested at 25 °C. The unfilled network had local tensile modulus 143 kPa at 100% strain and failed at about 170% elongation; treated-fumed-silica-filled networks extended beyond 500% in that study. These numbers describe the specified crosslinked dielectric-elastomer networks, not liquid PPG or uncrosslinked PPO. A second open catalyst study identifies tacticity as a key determinant of isotactic PPO mechanical properties, making stereoregularity and processing history additional scope limits. No open, form-appropriate tensile endpoint for an uncrosslinked commercial PPO/PPG fluid was identified in this focused pass.
sections.processing:
Poly(propylene oxide) (PPO) is commonly encountered as a soft, low-glass-transition polyether rather than a rigid molding resin. Useful articles are therefore often made by solution coating or casting PPO-containing blends, or by mixing a functional PPO with fillers and cure components, casting a thin film, and curing it in place. Molecular weight, end groups, blend partner, solvent removal, filler dispersion, humidity, film thickness, and cure depth must be controlled. The crosslink-forming reaction itself belongs in Synthesis, while formulation mixing, casting geometry, solvent removal, irradiation schedule, and demolding are Processing operations.

A 3M patent directly supports solution and solventless film conversion for PPO-containing adhesive articles: its specified PPO homopolymer or ethylene-oxide/propylene-oxide copolymer can be blended with polyurethane or polyester, dissolved for example in tetrahydrofuran or ethyl acetate, coated onto polyester or paper support, and dried, or the blend can be solventlessly melt cast. These are patent formulations and not neat-PPO molding instructions. For a separate bounded cured-film example, Goswami and co-workers combined 10 g of allyl-terminated Kaneka Silyl ACS003 PPO with 0.244 g tetrafunctional thiol and 0.192 g photoinitiator, mixed at 3500 rpm for 5 min, poured the mixture into an 8 × 10 cm steel mold over Parafilm-lined glass, ventilated it for 45–60 min, and irradiated it at 365 nm and 4.5 mW cm−2 for 45 min in air. Filled versions added fumed silica with 40–60 wt% toluene before mixing. Their films were 80–226 micrometres thick; the neat network was mechanically weak and silica improved handling, while filler choice had to account for UV absorption. The formulation and cure schedule are specific to that study.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PPO is a polyether whose tacticity and molecular weight depend on polymerization route.
sections.properties: It is often used as a flexible polyol; crosslinked systems have formulation-dependent mechanics.
sections.applications: PPO is used in polyurethane and dielectric-elastomer formulations.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Crosslinked-elastomer results are not properties of neat PPO.

sections.overview: Poly(tetramethylene ether glycol) is a hydroxyl-terminated polyether diol made by ring-opening polymerization of tetrahydrofuran. It is supplied in molecular-weight grades and commonly serves as a soft-segment precursor in urethane and copolymer elastomers.
sections.nomenclature: PTMEG, PTMG, and PTHF are names used for this tetrahydrofuran-derived polyether glycol. The hydroxyl-terminated precursor is distinct from a polyurethane or other copolymer elastomer made from it; molecular-weight grade and end-group state should be retained for a specific material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(tetramethylene ether glycol) (PTMEG) is a hydroxyl-terminated polyether produced by cationic ring-opening polymerization of tetrahydrofuran (THF), followed by termination or hydrolysis that furnishes terminal hydroxyl groups. Strong-acid catalyst systems activate THF; water or 1,4-butanediol can act as chain terminators, so catalyst loading, water content, and terminator concentration help set molar mass and functionality. One cited route uses a reusable sulfonic-acid-functional polymeric catalyst with water or 1,4-butanediol. A distinct route uses fuming sulfuric acid together with a lithium halide, then quenches with water and hydrolyzes sulfuric-ester chain ends. These are catalyst-specific manufacturing examples rather than a universal PTMEG formulation, and THF copolymers containing other cyclic ethers are outside the homopolyether boundary unless separately identified.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PTMEG is commonly supplied as a low-molar-mass, hydroxyl-terminated polyether diol used as a soft segment, not as a finished load-bearing homopolymer article. The supplied material can be a waxy solid at room temperature and becomes a low-viscosity liquid near 38 °C; grade molar mass, moisture, temperature, and its conversion into a polyurethane, copolyester, polyamide elastomer, or spandex fiber therefore determine the useful mechanical response. The hard-segment chemistry, isocyanate:hydroxyl ratio, chain extender, crosslink density, cure, blend composition, and final geometry are consequential variables in such products. A public patent gives one deliberately bounded endpoint: an 80:20 PTMEG 2000/Polyol B mixture reacted with MDI to 6% free NCO, chain-extended with 1,4-butanediol, cast as a 1/4-inch plaque and heat-cured, reached 410% elongation in its ASTM D412 tensile test. This is a cured mixed-polyol polyurethane elastomer, not a value for unreacted PTMEG. No open, form-appropriate standalone tensile endpoint for a commercial PTMEG polyol was identified in this focused pass.
sections.processing:
Poly(tetramethylene ether glycol) (PTMEG) is normally a reactive polyol feed rather than a self-supporting article material. Its article-conversion relevance is chiefly in PTMEG-segmented polyurethane elastomers: liquid systems are metered, mixed without entrained air, vacuum-degassed where needed, cast, reaction-injection-molded, transfer-molded, or sprayed, then cured and post-cured; thermoplastic grades can be pelletized and extruded or injection molded into film, sheet, tubing, or elastomeric components. PTMEG molecular mass and phase state, moisture exclusion, polyol/prepolymer temperature and viscosity, stoichiometry, mixing energy, pot life, mold temperature, bubble removal, cure time, and demolding strength are formulation-specific controls. Urethane formation and network chemistry belong in Synthesis; metering, mixing, degassing, article shaping, and cure equipment or schedule belong here.

Sugita and co-workers provide one bounded rapid-cast formulation. Their Example 1 used a PTMEG-1000-containing curing side and an MDI-based prepolymer, vacuum-degassed the two liquids, mixed them for 1.5 min at NCO/OH 1.05 without entraining bubbles, cast a 2 mm sheet in a 60 °C mold, and demolded after 10 min; Example 2 used a low-pressure casting machine, a 50 °C sheet mold, and 2 kg/min discharge and demolded after 5 min. A separate Simula patent demonstrates that PTMEG-based urea-extended polyurethane can be cast, granulated or pelletized, and then extrusion-shaped; its PTMEG-1000 example first cast a 72 mil sheet, while the general process describes tubular structures and sheets and warns that moisture introduced with processing aids can cause hydrolysis and swelling. These schedules belong to the patents' exact isocyanate, chain-extender, catalyst, and stoichiometric systems, not to PTMEG generally.

sections.properties: Its molecular weight and end groups control polyurethane-elastomer behavior.
sections.applications: PTMEG is used in polyurethane, spandex, and cast-elastomer systems.

sections.overview: Poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) is PHEMA, the addition polymer of 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA). It is a hydrophilic acrylic polymer that can be prepared as a linear polymer or, with multifunctional crosslinker, as a water-swollen hydrogel network.
sections.nomenclature: PHEMA is the abbreviation used for poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate). The record denotes the HEMA homopolymer; HEMA copolymers, crosslinked PHEMA hydrogels, and a particular porous or biomedical formulation are related materials rather than aliases for the linear polymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (PHEMA) is formed by addition polymerization of the vinyl group in 2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate (HEMA), usually by a radical route. A solution-polymerization example uses AIBN as thermal radical initiator in toluene under nitrogen, then removes residual solvent after polymerization. A different high-pressure-ramp study shows a bounded initiator-free bulk route: pressure first generates radical species from HEMA and rapid propagation follows on decompression. Linear PHEMA and a PHEMA hydrogel must be distinguished: multifunctional dimethacrylate crosslinkers or multifunctional initiator systems produce a network, whereas their amounts and cure conditions belong to the specific gel route rather than to PHEMA homopolymer synthesis generally.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PHEMA mechanics are most commonly reported for hydrated, cross-linked networks, where water content, cross-linker chemistry and concentration, polymerization solvent, network molecular weight, porosity, loading mode, and test timescale dominate the measured response. Open pHEMA-hydrogel studies show both cross-linker-dependent stiffening and time-dependent stress relaxation; nanoindentation and macroscale compression need not return the same modulus because hydration, equilibration, and geometry differ. Values for dried PHEMA, porous scaffolds, copolymers, and filled networks therefore are not directly comparable.

A bounded example is a porous, unfilled PHEMA scaffold tested in compression in one study: compressive modulus 88.7 ± 15.9 kPa and compressive strength 46.5 ± 4.9 kPa. The reported scaffold had 22% porosity and an 84 µm most-frequent pore diameter. These are wet porous-scaffold compression results, not tensile properties or generic values for bulk PHEMA hydrogel.
sections.processing:
PHEMA articles are commonly formed as hydrated or subsequently hydrated networks by casting in a mold, replica molding, particulate-leach casting, phase separation, freeze-drying, gas foaming, and electrospinning. The article-forming sequence has to control formulation homogeneity, mold wetting, cure exposure, porogen packing or surface-pattern replication, demolding, washing, and hydration. Because swelling changes dimensions and stiffness, the water content used during demolding and service is part of the processing specification. Thick or highly porous articles also need a washing schedule that removes residual soluble species without cracking the network.

Two open experiments illustrate bounded schedules. Zasońska and co-workers loaded a solution containing 3.1 g HEMA, 33 mg EDMA, and 24 mg AIBN in 1.7 mL dioxane into a 10 mL syringe packed with 6.75 g ammonium-oxalate needles, held the filled mold at 60 °C for 16 h, removed and trimmed the cylinder, immersed it in saturated NaCl for 24 h to avoid cracking, and water-washed it for 10 days to leach the porogen. In a separate ophthalmic-surface experiment, Krajňák and co-workers poured their H1 PHEMA formulation onto a nanopatterned silicon replica mold, exposed it for 10 min to a 365 nm, 36 W lamp at a 15 cm distance, then hydrated and rinsed the article and kept it in fresh water for two days. These are formulation- and geometry-specific casting/cure examples, not general PHEMA cure windows; the underlying monomer chemistry belongs in Synthesis.

sections.limitationsAndVariability: Reported scaffold properties belong to specified porous and magnetic formulations.

sections.overview: Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) is a thermoresponsive polymer made by radical polymerization of N-isopropylacrylamide. It is commonly converted into temperature-responsive hydrogel materials through physical or chemical crosslinking, where network composition controls the final response.
sections.nomenclature: PNIPAM and PNIPAAm identify the N-isopropylacrylamide polymer. An uncrosslinked PNIPAM chain is distinct from a PNIPAM hydrogel, interpenetrating network, or composite: crosslinker, comonomer, and added polymer must remain stated rather than being absorbed into the base-polymer name.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) is the linear radical-addition homopolymer of N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM). Conventional solution polymerization uses a thermally decomposing azo initiator after deoxygenation; monomer purity, solvent, initiator concentration, conversion, and chain transfer govern molecular mass and dispersity. Reversible addition–fragmentation chain-transfer (RAFT) polymerization offers a controlled route: NIPAM, an azo initiator, and a thiocarbonylthio chain-transfer agent are polymerized in a dry, oxygen-free solvent to give a chain-transfer-functional PNIPAM that can serve as a macro-CTA. Homopolymer synthesis should not be conflated with PNIPAM hydrogels, which deliberately add a difunctional crosslinker to form a network, or with later block-copolymer extension.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PNIPAM is commonly used as a thermoresponsive swollen network or microgel rather than as a dry bulk plastic. Its load response is controlled by covalent or physical cross-link density, polymer concentration and molecular mass, water content and ionic environment, temperature relative to the approximately 32 °C lower critical solution temperature, heating/cooling history, porosity, and any second network or particulate reinforcement. The volume transition changes both stiffness and deformation mode, so a value for a hydrated gel cannot be assigned to linear PNIPAM or to a dry film. In one open study, UV-cured gels made from 5 wt% NIPAM, 0.25 wt% methylene bisacrylamide, and 0.1 wt% photoinitiator in water (monomer:cross-linker 100:5 by mass), then swollen overnight in deionized water, gave a fully swollen compressive bulk modulus of 6.32 ± 1.43 kPa by calorimetry and 4.59 ± 0.52 kPa by osmotic compression. The latter equilibrated for one week against dextran solutions; these values are for that equilibrium, macroscopic gel, not a universal PNIPAM modulus. Independent PNIPAM/HPMC hydrogel work likewise finds that increasing covalent cross-linker raises differential modulus and strength but decreases extensibility, while HPMC association and microphase separation can substantially alter the response.
sections.processing:
PNIPAM articles are most often aqueous gels, microgels, coatings, fibers, or porous scaffolds rather than bulk melt shapes. Conversion routes include casting and curing in tubes or molds, physical or chemical crosslinking, interpenetrating-network formation, electrospinning, cryogelation or freeze-thaw structuring, and drying or lyophilization when a porous dry article is required. Mixing and degassing, filler dispersion, mold heat transfer, crosslink density, cure exposure, extraction of residual soluble material, drying path, hydration, pH, ionic strength, and temperature all affect homogeneity, pore structure, swelling, and dimensional response near the lower critical solution temperature.

For a bounded monolithic-gel example, the HPMC-intercalated PNIPAM study dissolved HPMC in water for 24 h, added NIPAM and bisacrylamide, cooled the mixture to 15 °C, purged with argon, added TEMED and APS, and transferred it into argon-purged 10 or 4 mm internal-diameter glass tubes. The sealed tubes were held for 24 h at 25 °C before demolding, and most specimens were then equilibrium-swollen to extract soluble material. The authors showed that crosslinker and HPMC contents affected phase separation, transparency, swelling, and demolding-state properties; slow air/vacuum drying preserved a nonporous morphology whereas freeze-drying would create porosity. This schedule is specific to those formulations and specimen sizes.

sections.applications: PNIPAM hydrogels are used in responsive biomaterial and separation studies.

sections.overview: Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) is a cationic polymer formed from diallyldimethylammonium chloride monomer. Its permanently charged ammonium groups make it a polyelectrolyte rather than an uncharged vinyl polymer.
sections.nomenclature: PDADMAC and polyDADMAC are common names for poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride). The canonical name includes the chloride counterion and should not be shortened to a generic polyammonium label.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (polyDADMAC) is the chloride-salt cationic homopolymer obtained by free-radical cyclopolymerization of diallyldimethylammonium chloride (DADMAC) in water. DADMAC itself can be prepared from dimethylamine and allyl chloride under alkaline aqueous conditions. During chain growth, the two allyl functions give the characteristic cyclic quaternary-ammonium repeat structure rather than a simple pendant-diallyl vinyl polymer. Aqueous production examples use radical initiators such as persulfate, azo, or organic-peroxide systems under inert-gas control. Monomer purity, initiator concentration, reaction time and temperature, and added salts can change conversion, viscosity, and molecular mass; these are route controls rather than universal grade specifications. Copolymer and graft examples are outside the homopolymer boundary unless explicitly identified as polyDADMAC-containing materials.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PDADMAC is ordinarily handled as a water-soluble cationic polyelectrolyte, so a stand-alone bulk tensile value is not a useful family property. Mechanical response becomes meaningful for a dried film, a layer-by-layer coating, or an ionically complexed hydrogel/saloplastic, where counterion identity and concentration, water content and humidity, pH when the partner is weakly charged, charge stoichiometry, molecular mass, porosity, drying/annealing, temperature, and strain rate govern the ionic cross-link density and relaxation. In an open study of a PSS/PDADMA multilayer (a PDADMAC-containing polyelectrolyte complex film), the equilibrium shear modulus was 0.3 MPa in 1 M NaCl at room temperature; the same composition as a compact, water-rich complex at 37 °C was almost three orders of magnitude softer. This is a complex-film versus compact-complex comparison, not a value for dissolved or neat PDADMAC. A separate open study reports that cast PSS/PDDA complex films made from 2 g/L solutions at 2 M NaCl and dried after 60–70 °C pressing were tensile-tested as 0.5 cm × 4 cm × 2 mm specimens at 1 mm/s; it found PSS/PDDA about three times softer than a PAA/PAH complex and showed that water exposure, salt, and mixing ratio can markedly alter integrity. Its plotted tensile data do not provide a reliable tabulated endpoint for reuse here.
sections.processing:
Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDADMAC, also written PDADMA or PDDA) is normally handled in water rather than melt-shaped as a neat thermoplastic. Article-conversion routes include alternate adsorption with a polyanion to build layer-by-layer coatings and capsules, solution mixing followed by casting or pressing a wet polyelectrolyte complex, and salt-plasticized consolidation into bulk complex articles. Concentration, charge stoichiometry, pH, ionic strength, mixing order and time, substrate preparation, rinse steps, retained water, drying, and applied pressure control deposition, complex mobility, thickness, porosity, and dimensional stability. These routes make PDADMAC-containing complexes or multilayers; their windows must not be presented as neat-PDADMAC melt-processing data.

Two bounded examples show the practical range. Porcel and Schlenoff mixed 20 mL portions of 0.5 M repeat-unit PSS and PDADMAC solutions in 2.5 M NaCl, then centrifuged the precipitated complex at 188,000g for 4 h at 25 °C to form a transparent compact article; they found that more than about 2 M NaCl at room temperature was needed to reshape that PSS/PDADMAC system efficiently, followed by salt exchange to restore ionic cross-links. In a distinct casting study, Gai and co-workers mixed 2 g/L PSS and PDDA solutions containing 2 M NaCl, collected the wet complex, pressed it against a patterned PDMS mold while heating to 60-70 °C, and then dried before mold release. The salt levels, centrifugal field, heat, and pressure belong to those paired-polyelectrolyte experiments.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride) (PDADMAC) is a water-soluble cationic polymer formed from a diallyl quaternary-ammonium monomer. Its charged backbone and chloride counterions make it a polyelectrolyte whose conformation changes with ionic strength and interactions with oppositely charged species.
sections.properties: PDADMAC provides strong cationic charge, water compatibility, flocculation, charge neutralization, and film-forming or complex-forming behavior. Solution viscosity and association depend on molecular mass, concentration, counterion, salt, pH, and the presence of anionic polymers or particles.
sections.applications: PDADMAC is used in water and wastewater treatment, papermaking, mineral processing, textile and surface formulations, and as a cationic component in polyelectrolyte complexes. Its charge makes it useful for binding anionic colloids and macromolecules.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Ionic strength can screen charge and sharply change conformation, viscosity, adsorption, and complexation. Molecular mass, branching or microstructure, residual monomer, counterion, pH, and blend ratio must be retained; a PDADMAC–polyanion complex is not the same material as the neat polymer.
