sections.overview: Poly(p-phenylene vinylene) (PPV) is a family of conjugated poly(arylenevinylene) materials with phenylenevinylene backbone units. Established precursor routes first shape a soluble precursor polymer and then convert it to the conjugated PPV material.
sections.nomenclature: PPV is a family-level backbone designation, not the name of one precursor, substituted derivative, or block copolymer. Precursor composition and the post-shaping conversion step must remain identified when a particular PPV film or fiber is described.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(p-phenylene vinylene) (PPV) has a para-phenylene/vinylene conjugated backbone. A precursor strategy first converts a bis-sulfonium salt derived from a dihalomethylbenzene and tetrahydrothiophene into a soluble polyelectrolyte by base-induced polymerization, then eliminates the pendant groups to generate the conjugated PPV chain. Direct or one-pot variants instead use activated p-xylylene derivatives whose base-promoted elimination furnishes the conjugated arylene-vinylene polymer. The precursor, leaving-group, base, and conversion route determine the specific chain microstructure and are not interchangeable descriptions of every PPV preparation.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PPV is a rigid, conjugated polymer family commonly handled as thin films or highly oriented precursor-derived material; its mechanical response is therefore inseparable from backbone stereochemistry, molar mass, film morphology and crystallinity, molecular orientation, residual precursor or dopant, substrate constraint, and test temperature and rate. The open mechanochemical study of cis/trans phenylenevinylene block copolymers finds the conjugated olefin resistant to cis–trans isomerisation during extensive ultrasonication-driven elongation, while an open DFT study shows that imposed chain stretching changes PPV's structural and optoelectronic response. These studies support sensitivity to chain configuration and imposed deformation, but they are not interchangeable with bulk-film tensile data. A focused search did not identify a suitably open full-text, form-appropriate PPV tensile or modulus measurement; the accessible historical film numbers were confined to paywalled articles, so no numerical family endpoint is reported here.
sections.processing:
Unsubstituted poly(p-phenylene vinylene) (PPV) is difficult to reshape directly because the fully conjugated polymer is poorly soluble and not a conventional melt-processing resin. A practical article-conversion strategy is therefore to cast, coat, or otherwise pattern a soluble precursor polymer into the required film or fiber geometry and then thermally convert the shaped precursor to PPV. Spin coating and drop casting are particularly relevant to thin optoelectronic layers, while localized heating can write PPV features into a precursor film. Solvent choice, precursor concentration, film thickness, atmosphere, heating rate and time, and shrinkage during elimination must be controlled for the selected precursor chemistry; schedules for substituted PPV derivatives should not be transferred to unsubstituted PPV without qualification.

For one bounded unsubstituted-PPV example, Wang and co-workers drop-cast a 0.25 wt% aqueous poly(p-xylene tetrahydrothiophenium chloride) precursor onto cleaned glass or Si(111). Their 1.4 µm reference film was converted by annealing at 280 °C for 5 h under about 200 mTorr vacuum. They also patterned a 100 nm precursor film with a resistively heated AFM probe at 240–360 °C, 20 µm/s, and 30 nN; visible PPV fluorescence began at the lower tip temperature and strengthened as temperature increased. These are the paper's precursor, substrate, film, and nanolithography conditions, not a general PPV coating or annealing window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PPV is a conjugated phenylene-vinylene backbone polymer whose cis/trans structure affects chain planarity.
sections.properties: Optical and electronic response depend on conformation, defects, and processing.
sections.applications: PPV is used in organic light-emitting and electronic-material research.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Film and calculation results concern specified isomers or processing routes.

sections.overview: Poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene] is a substituted poly(phenylenevinylene) conjugated polymer. Its alkoxy side groups improve processability relative to unsubstituted PPV and it is used as an emissive organic-electronics material.
sections.nomenclature: MEH-PPV abbreviates poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene]. It is a specific substituted PPV, not an alternate name for the whole poly(phenylenevinylene) family.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: MEH-PPV is a soluble substituted poly(p-phenylene vinylene) most commonly made by the Gilch route from 1,4-bis(halomethyl)-2-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-5-methoxybenzene. Its methoxy and branched 2-ethylhexyloxy groups are installed before polymerization. One cited open study first etherifies 4-methoxyphenol with 2-ethylhexyl bromide, then bromomethylates the substituted aromatic precursor with paraformaldehyde and hydrogen bromide to obtain the bis(bromomethyl) monomer. Potassium tert-butoxide in tetrahydrofuran under nitrogen generates quinodimethane-type intermediates that polymerize into the conjugated phenylene-vinylene backbone; benzyl bromide is used there as a chain stopper, and the polymer is precipitated with methanol and washed. A distinct patent demonstrates both batch and continuous-flow Gilch polymerization by controlled addition of the same class of bis(halomethyl) monomer to potassium tert-butoxide in tetrahydrofuran. Base/monomer ratio, concentration, addition rate, oxygen exclusion, optional radical-control additives, and monofunctional stoppers affect molar mass, defects, and gelation. Other PPV precursor routes exist, but they are not interchangeable with the specific MEH-substituted repeat unit.
sections.mechanicalProperties: MEH-PPV is a solution-processable conjugated-polymer subfamily normally used as an ultrathin film, nanosheet, fiber, or composite; its apparent modulus and failure response are particularly sensitive to molecular packing/crystallinity, thickness and substrate constraint, solution-casting or interfacial assembly, annealing, orientation, nanofiller volume fraction and dispersion, indentation depth/rate, and viscoelastic creep. A free-standing, water-air-interfacially assembled MEH-PPV nanosheet about 400 nm thick gave an average nanoindentation Young’s modulus of 4.2 GPa (4.1 GPa in spatial modulus mapping), compared with 2.7 GPa reported for the authors’ spun-cast control films. A separate spin-coated-on-glass nanoindentation thesis found 14.5 GPa for its nominally pure MEH-PPV thin-film sample; the substrate/thin-film test geometry and method differ, so the two values are not a transferable material range.
sections.processing:
Poly[2-methoxy-5-(2-ethylhexyloxy)-1,4-phenylenevinylene] (MEH-PPV) is a soluble conjugated polymer converted mainly as a thin functional layer, not by ordinary melt extrusion or injection molding. It is dissolved in a selected organic solvent and deposited by spin coating, wire-bar or blade coating, inkjet or aerosol-jet printing, screen printing, stamping, drop casting, or interfacial spreading; solvent removal then leaves the film. Substrate cleaning and surface treatment, solution concentration, molecular mass, solvent quality and evaporation rate, extended mixing, filtration, oxygen and light exposure, coating shear, spin or web speed, atmosphere, vacuum drying, and any low-temperature anneal control thickness, roughness, chain ordering, defects, and optoelectronic response. Freestanding nanosheets can also be assembled at a water/solvent interface, slowly dried, transferred to flexible substrates, patterned, and wrapped around a device.

Lee and co-workers provide a bounded comparison using Sigma-Aldrich MEH-PPV with number-average molecular mass 70–100 kg/mol. They stirred a 0.5 wt% toluene solution for 48 h at room temperature in a nitrogen glovebox, either spin-coated it at 2000 rpm for 1 min or wire-bar-coated it at 2.5 cm/s with a roughly 360 µm-pitch groove bar, and vacuum-dried both films for 12 h. The bar-induced shear produced more directional molecular ordering than spin coating, so the two settings are not interchangeable universal recipes. In a distinct freestanding-film experiment, Zhang and co-workers spread 1 mL of toluene containing 0.1–15 g/L MEH-PPV over water in a cleaned, plasma-treated dish, used a perforated cover to moderate evaporation, and picked the resulting nanosheet up on PET, paper, aluminum foil, or PDMS. Concentration controlled thickness from several to hundreds of nanometers; those interfacial-assembly conditions belong to that study.
sections.structureAndMorphology: MEH-PPV is a soluble substituted conjugated PPV with alkoxy side chains.
sections.properties: Luminescence and film mechanics depend on molecular ordering and film processing.
sections.applications: MEH-PPV is used in emissive organic-electronics and biosensing studies.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Reported properties are tied to thin-film or nanosheet preparation.

sections.overview: Polyfluorenes are conjugated polymers built from fluorene-derived units. Side-chain and comonomer design tune their optical and electronic behavior for semiconductor and light-emitting applications.
sections.nomenclature: PFo is used for polyfluorene. The canonical record is family-level: substituted and copolymerized polyfluorenes are distinct variants rather than aliases for one fixed homopolymer.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyfluorenes are conjugated polymers built by carbon–carbon coupling of fluorene units, commonly through 2,7-functionalized fluorene monomers; substituents at C-9 are selected before polymerization to control solubility and later functionality. A Yamamoto route reductively couples a 2,7-dihalofluorene with a nickel(0) system. Suzuki polycondensation instead couples a dibromofluorene with a fluorene bis(boronic acid or boronate), or uses an AB monomer bearing both functions, under palladium catalysis and base. The cited nickel patent scopes a catalytic Yamamoto variant for dihalogenated fluorene, while an independent laboratory example uses Suzuki polycondensation of functional fluorene comonomers followed by side-chain quaternization and dialysis. Halogen/boronate placement fixes the principal backbone linkage; monomer functionality, comonomer selection, stoichiometric balance, catalyst system, and end-group treatment govern copolymer sequence, molar mass, and terminal groups.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyfluorene-family materials are conjugated aromatic polymers generally used as thin films or functional membranes, so their measured mechanics are governed by side-chain identity, molecular mass, aggregation/crystallinity, casting or spin-coating history, film thickness and substrate effects, hydrogen bonding or crosslinking, ionic functionalization and hydration, temperature, and test direction/rate. Freestanding-film tensile values and substrate-supported nanoindentation moduli are not interchangeable. In a diarylfluorene semiconductor-film study, unmodified PODPF freestanding films tested at 0.005 N/min had approximately 200 MPa tensile modulus and 7% strain at fracture; 30–40% amide-functional side-chain copolymers reached about 255–400 MPa while elongation rose to 19–25%. Film thickness, tensile specimen geometry, and conditioning were not reported in the cited result, limiting it to those solution-prepared films. An independent polyfluorene-ether-ketone membrane patent reports a room-temperature, 5 mm/min dumbbell-film endpoint of 61.2 MPa tensile strength and 13.4% elongation for its aromatic-side-chain membrane; it is an ionomer/membrane composition, not ordinary polyfluorene resin. These examples show why side-chain chemistry and ion/water state must be retained with any number.
sections.processing:
Polyfluorene electronic and optical materials are commonly converted as thin films from solution, with the cited evidence directly establishing spin coating and drop casting followed by controlled drying, thermal annealing, solvent-vapor annealing, or brief solvent/nonsolvent treatment. The important processing variables are the exact repeat-unit and side-chain chemistry, molecular mass, solvent and concentration, solution and substrate temperature, substrate cleaning and surface activation, dispense and spin conditions, evaporation rate, residual-solvent removal, annealing atmosphere, time and temperature, and any swelling step. These variables can reorganize chain conformation and aggregation after deposition, so the optical morphology of a film cannot be inferred from polymer identity alone. Coating or printing conditions should be developed with the intended substrate and device stack; aggressive solvent exposure can delaminate or dissolve the layer, while oxygen, water, and thermal history may alter electronic performance.

Minion and co-workers give one bounded spin-coating schedule for their chiral-side-chain cPF homopolymer and cPFT2 copolymer: 30 mg/mL toluene solutions were statically dispensed on fused-silica substrates cleaned ultrasonically in acetone and isopropanol for 10 min each and plasma-treated for 3 min at 80 W; films were spun at 1500 rpm for 60 s and annealed for 10 min at 140 °C in a nitrogen glovebox below 0.1 ppm water and oxygen. Perevedentsev and co-workers used a distinct PFO grade and showed that processing itself selected the beta-phase fraction. Their nominally glassy film used 13 mg/mL PFO in toluene at 2300 rpm after both solution and substrate spent 2 min at 100 °C, whereas a high-beta-phase example was drop-cast from 0.2 wt% PFO in decalin and slowly dried for several hours. Other films in that experiment were swollen for seconds to minutes in specified cyclohexane/isopropanol mixtures or exposed to saturated toluene vapor at 35 °C for 24 h, then desiccated for several days. None of these schedules is a family-wide coating recipe.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyfluorenes are conjugated aromatic polymers built around fluorene units, commonly bearing alkyl, aryl, or heteroatom-containing substituents. Chain planarity, side-chain packing, molecular weight, and aggregation determine intrachain and interchain electronic structure.
sections.properties: Polyfluorenes exhibit strong photoluminescence, tunable absorption and emission, semiconducting behavior, and solution processability. Color purity, charge transport, and aggregation depend on backbone defects, side chains, molecular mass, film morphology, and thermal treatment.
sections.applications: The cited processing evidence covers solution-cast and spin-coated polyfluorene films prepared for optoelectronic and photophysical studies. OLED, photovoltaic, sensor, and transistor performance remains dependent on the specific backbone, side chains, film, and device stack.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polyfluorenes can show aggregation, excimer emission, spectral drift, oxidation, and morphology changes during annealing or operation. Regioregularity, chain defects, solvent, concentration, residual catalyst, film thickness, and encapsulation make a device-film result non-universal.

sections.overview: Polycarbonates are polymers containing carbonate linkages in the backbone. The family includes bisphenol-based and other chemistries, with material properties depending on the diol and carbonate-forming route.
sections.nomenclature: PC abbreviates polycarbonate. The name is family-level and does not identify one specific bisphenol polycarbonate grade; polycarbonate copolymers and blends are narrower material records.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polycarbonates are polymers with recurring carbonate linkages. The principal aromatic thermoplastic route uses a dihydric phenol, most commonly bisphenol A, with a carbonate precursor. In interfacial polymerization, aqueous bisphenolate reacts with phosgene in an immiscible organic phase in the presence of base and often a phase-transfer or tertiary-amine catalyst. In a phosgene-free melt route, bisphenol A undergoes transesterification/polycondensation with diphenyl carbonate while phenol is removed under progressively reduced pressure. Two industrial patents explicitly contrast these routes and document catalyst, purity, heat, and volatile removal as controls. Other diols or carbonate precursors give other family members; the monomer identity and any comonomers must therefore be stated rather than treating every polycarbonate as bisphenol-A homopolycarbonate.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Polycarbonates are a chemical family, so no single mechanical profile covers bisphenol-A polycarbonate, aliphatic or alternative-diol polycarbonates, siloxane or polyester copolycarbonates, blends, and reinforced grades. The common engineering reference material—amorphous bisphenol-A polycarbonate—is a glassy thermoplastic that can combine stiffness with large plastic deformation and impact energy absorption. Its tensile response can pass from elastic deformation through yield, post-yield softening and drawing, and strain hardening. That ductility is conditional: lower temperature, faster loading, sharp notches, greater section constraint, molding residual stress or orientation, surface damage, and stress-cracking liquids can shift failure toward brittle cracking. Sustained load also produces creep. Molar mass and distribution, branching, comonomer identity, additives and colorants, glass or carbon fiber, impact modifiers, blend morphology, moisture and hydrolytic chain scission, recycled-content history, thermal or ultraviolet aging, specimen thickness, temperature, strain rate, and injection or extrusion thermal history must therefore remain attached to reported results.

A bounded commercial example is Covestro Makrolon 2405, a low-viscosity general-purpose injection-molding grade. Covestro's table for specimens molded at a 280 °C melt and 80 °C mold reports, at 23 °C and 50% relative humidity, an ISO 527-1/-2 tensile modulus of 2400 MPa at 1 mm/min, yield stress of 65 MPa and yield strain of 6.0% at 50 mm/min, and strain at break of 125%. ISO 899-1 tensile creep modulus is listed as 2200 MPa after 1 hour and 1900 MPa after 1000 hours. These are typical values for that proprietary grade and molding protocol, not a family range; specimen dimensions, resin molar mass, conditioning duration, and statistical scatter are not supplied in the range table. Independently, tests on specimens machined from 12 mm Lexan 141R plate and held at room temperature for more than three days found ductile deformation through about 0.60 true strain in quasi-static tension and a strong, bilinear rise of yield stress with strain rate across 0.0005–4500 s⁻¹. That rate study is specific to Lexan 141R plate geometry and should not be transferred to other polycarbonate chemistries or loading modes.
sections.processing: Polycarbonate (PC) families are melt-processable engineering thermoplastics converted mainly by injection molding, extrusion, thermoforming, and, for suitable grades, material-extrusion filament printing. PC pellets are moisture-sensitive: drying and dry-hopper handling are important because residual water can reduce molecular mass during the high-temperature melt cycle and cause splay or bubbles. Viscosity/flow grade, reinforcement, pigmentation, part thickness, gate design, mold temperature, and residence time all change the practical window. Covestro's bounded Makrolon 2405 example specifies dry-air drying at 120 °C for 2–3 h to at most 0.02% moisture, 280–320 °C melt temperature, 80–120 °C mold temperature, and 50–75% hold pressure relative to injection pressure; these are grade and test-specimen guidance, not family-wide settings. An independent PC filament benchmark dried feed at 120 °C for 4 h under dynamic vacuum before material-extrusion processing, illustrating a different feed form and machine history. Carbonate polymer manufacture belongs in Synthesis; this section covers drying, melt shaping, cooling, and additive-manufacturing conversion.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polycarbonates are polymers containing carbonate linkages in the main chain, with aromatic bisphenol polycarbonates forming the major engineering family. Rigid aromatic segments generally yield amorphous glassy materials, while aliphatic or copolymer variants broaden the family.
sections.properties: Polycarbonates commonly provide transparency, impact toughness, dimensional stability, electrical insulation, and useful heat resistance. UV exposure, stress, solvents, molecular mass, additives, and copolymer or blend composition can alter optical and environmental performance.
sections.applications: The directly supported forms are injection-molded polycarbonate grades and thermoplastic-extrusion specimens. These cover shaped engineering articles and printed or extruded test forms; glazing, medical, and filled-grade uses require application-specific qualification.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Polycarbonate can undergo solvent-induced crazing, hydrolysis or thermal degradation, UV yellowing, and notch-dependent stress cracking. Bisphenol chemistry, molecular mass, additives, drying, molding stress, orientation, and recycled content must accompany any grade comparison.

sections.overview: Polysulfones are a family of aromatic high-temperature thermoplastics built through nucleophilic polycondensation of a bisphenol component with a dihalodiphenyl sulfone. Changing the bisphenol structure produces distinct polysulfone-family members with different chain architectures.
sections.nomenclature: Polysulfone is a family-level term and should not be used as a synonym for one named member such as PSU, PESU, or PPSU. The particular bisphenol and dihalodiphenyl-sulfone components identify a specific polymer; a membrane, blend, or reinforced article adds a separate material state.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: The polysulfone family is commonly prepared by step-growth nucleophilic aromatic substitution between a bisphenol and an activated dihalodiphenyl sulfone. Base converts the bisphenol to a phenoxide, which displaces chloride or fluoride from the aryl-sulfone monomer and builds aryl-ether-sulfone chains. Bisphenol A gives the conventional PSU structure; changing the bisphenol produces related members and must not be treated as an interchangeable repeat unit. Polymerization is conducted under dry inert conditions in a high-boiling polar aprotic solvent, with water removed because it limits molar mass. Near-equimolar functional-group balance, monomer purity, a controlled stoichiometric offset, and monofunctional end caps regulate chain length and terminal groups. One cited open study makes a bisphenol-Z polysulfone from 4,4′-dichlorodiphenyl sulfone and potassium carbonate in dimethylacetamide/toluene, then filters and precipitates the polymer. A distinct patent demonstrates a bisphenol-A/4,4′-difluorodiphenyl-sulfone process using carbonate, a composite ionic liquid, an entrainer, and precipitation. Polyethersulfone and polyphenylsulfone have separate monomer-specific records.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
The polysulfone family comprises several amorphous aromatic sulfone thermoplastics—notably bisphenol-A polysulfone (PSU), polyethersulfone (PESU), and polyphenylsulfone (PPSU)—whose repeat-unit structures and mechanical balances are not interchangeable. In dense molded form they are generally glassy, stiff engineering plastics that can yield and deform ductilely, retain useful stiffness at elevated temperature, and resist creep better than many commodity thermoplastics. Toughness remains conditional: notches, thick or highly constrained sections, low temperature, rapid loading, weld lines, residual molding stress, surface damage, and stress-cracking liquids can promote brittle failure. Repeat-unit rigidity and ether-link density, molar mass, residual solvent or moisture, physical aging and annealing, temperature and loading time, specimen geometry and rate, molding or extrusion orientation, additive-manufacturing voids and raster direction, glass or carbon-fiber content and orientation, mineral fillers, lubricants, colorants, thermal or hydrothermal aging, and chemical environment can all change modulus, strength, elongation, impact response, creep, and wear. Porous phase-inversion membranes and hollow fibers add porosity, pore morphology, skin/support architecture, solvent exchange, drying, plasticization, and filler dispersion as dominant variables; their tensile results should not be treated as bulk-resin properties.

A bounded numerical example is Solvay Udel P-1700, an unfilled commercial PSU grade. The supplier's typical-property table reports ASTM D638 tensile strength of 70.3 MPa, tangent tensile modulus of 2.48 GPa, and elongation at break of 50–100%; ASTM D790 flexural strength and modulus are 106 MPa and 2.69 GPa, and ASTM D256 notched Izod impact is 69 J/m. The same guide reports that 30 wt% glass-fiber Udel GF-130 reaches 107.6 MPa tensile strength and 8.69 GPa tensile modulus but only 2% elongation at break, illustrating the stiffness/ductility tradeoff within one supplier system. These are nominal typical values for named formulations; the table warns that batches vary and does not give complete coupon molding, conditioning, tensile-rate, or scatter details. They are not ranges for PESU, PPSU, membranes, printed parts, or the polysulfone family as a whole.
sections.processing:
Polysulfone-family members such as PSU, PESU, and PPSU are amorphous high-temperature thermoplastics converted by injection molding and extrusion, while selected grades are dissolved and cast as flat membranes or spun as hollow fibers before nonsolvent-induced phase inversion. Grade identity must remain explicit because melt viscosity, glass-transition temperature, solvent compatibility, and hydrolysis or impact behavior differ among family members. Pellets should be kept clean and dry; absorbed moisture or other volatiles can create splay, bubbles, hydrolytic loss, or poor surface finish at the high melt temperature, although a properly vented extruder can remove volatiles in some extrusion lines. Melt processing requires sufficient barrel and screw capability, uniform melting with controlled shear, short and stable residence, streamlined nozzles and dies, suitable injection and hold pressure, hot-runner control, mold venting, and uniform mold or roll cooling. Excess time or temperature promotes discoloration and degradation, while high residual stress, sharp temperature gradients, flow orientation, and uneven cooling can cause warpage or later environmental stress cracking. For membrane conversion, a preformed polymer is dissolved with any pore-former or filler, mixed to a homogeneous dope, filtered and degassed, cast or spun at controlled thickness and evaporation history, immersed in a nonsolvent coagulation bath, then washed and dried. Polymer concentration, solvent/nonsolvent exchange, air gap, bath composition and temperature, additives, and post-treatment determine skin formation, pore size, macrovoids, shrinkage, and defects. Aromatic polycondensation remains Synthesis; melt or solution shaping of the finished polymer belongs in Processing.

Solvay's Udel guide gives PSU-grade handling rather than a family window. It targets about 0.05% moisture before molding or extrusion; its oven examples are 3.5 h after pellets reach 135 °C or 2 h at 163 °C, and its hopper example uses about 3.5 h residence at 135 °C with a dew point no warmer than −32 °C. The guide also notes the vented-extruder alternative. A distinct open review documents polysulfone membrane solution preparation, flat-sheet casting or hollow-fiber spinning, evaporation and coagulation-bath phase inversion. Those solution variables are membrane-formulation controls, not melt-molding settings and not a single universal recipe for PSU, PESU, and PPSU.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polysulfones are aromatic polymers with sulfone-containing backbones; the bisphenol component distinguishes PSU, PESU, PPSU, and other family members.
sections.properties: The family is generally amorphous and glassy, while reinforcement, blend chemistry, physical ageing, and membrane morphology change the response of individual materials.
sections.applications: Polysulfones are directly used in membrane materials, including phase-inversion, blended, grafted, and filled membrane forms.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A PSU datasheet or a named membrane cannot stand for the family: polymer member, molecular weight, reinforcement, solvent/process route, morphology, and ageing must be specified.

sections.overview: Polyisoprene is a family of isoprene-based elastomeric polymers that includes natural rubber and catalyst-made synthetic polyisoprene. Chain microstructure, nonisoprene components in natural rubber, and vulcanization state materially affect the finished rubber.
sections.nomenclature: Polyisoprene is a family term rather than a single natural-rubber or synthetic-rubber grade. Natural rubber and synthetic IR share the isoprene-polymer boundary but differ in source and composition; a branched polymer, a vulcanizate, or a filled compound requires its own qualifier.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Synthetic polyisoprenes are addition polymers of isoprene, and the catalyst system determines the proportions of cis-1,4, trans-1,4, 3,4, and 1,2 units as well as chain architecture. Coordination routes use titanium-, cobalt-, or rare-earth-based catalysts with organoaluminum cocatalysts to favor stereoregular 1,4 addition; anionic routes use organolithium initiators in rigorously dry hydrocarbon or ether media and permit living-chain, block, and branched architectures. The cited patent prepares a neodymium catalyst by staged reaction of a neodymium carboxylate, organoaluminum compound, and dialkylaluminum chloride before polymerizing isoprene to high-cis rubber. An independent laboratory study uses sec-butyllithium in toluene, TMEDA as a polar modifier, and divinylbenzene as a branching agent to make soluble, highly branched polyisoprene. Monomer purity, solvent polarity, catalyst ratios, chain-transfer agents, and quench chemistry control molar mass, microstructure, branching, and end groups. These are synthetic routes; biological formation and latex recovery are treated with natural-rubber entries.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polyisoprenes include natural rubber, synthetic cis-1,4-polyisoprene, trans-rich materials, and formulated/vulcanized elastomers; their mechanics depend on microstructure, molecular weight, nonisoprene components in natural rubber, crosslink system/density, filler and plasticizer package, strain-induced crystallization, temperature, strain rate, aging, and specimen orientation. In a vulcanized natural-rubber versus synthetic-polyisoprene study, strain-induced crystallization began at 250% strain for natural rubber and 350% for synthetic IR; stress upturns occurred at 383% and 450% strain, respectively. Adding liquid-isoprene or naphthenic-oil plasticizers changed crystallinity and tensile strength, with the reported reduction greater for the IR composites. These are specifically formulated and vulcanized rubber-network results, not values for all polyisoprene forms.
sections.processing:
Polyisoprene rubbers are converted through compound preparation followed by shaping and vulcanization. Directly supported operations include internal or Banbury mixing, two-roll milling and sheet formation, press vulcanization, and latex- or solution-dip molding with repeated deposition, drying, leaching, cooling, powdering, and stripping. The choice between dry mixing and solvent-assisted wet mixing affects filler dispersion, dust, energy use, and compound viscosity. For filled compounds, filler moisture and agglomeration, silane or coupling-agent distribution, mixing sequence, rotor or roll shear, dump temperature, solvent recovery, coagulation and drying, sheet gauge, scorch safety, and a rheometer-derived optimum cure time are important. For dipped articles, solution or latex viscosity, degassing, coagulant pickup, withdrawal and form rotation, number of dip/dry cycles, residual-solvent removal, cure heat transfer, cooling, rinsing, and release control thickness and uniformity. Vulcanizing-agent chemistry belongs in Synthesis; compounding, article shaping, and the vulcanization equipment and schedule belong in Processing.

McGlothlin and Schmid disclose several bounded NATSYN 2200 cis-1,4-polyisoprene dip-molding examples. In one, 21 g of the named grade and 0.63 g dicumyl peroxide were dissolved in 700 g tetrahydrofuran, bubbles were allowed to dissipate, a mandrel was dipped and air-dried for 15 min, eight dip/dry cycles were used, the film was finally air-dried 1.5 h, and it was cured for 3 min in a 180 °C molten-salt bath before rinsing, cooling, powdering, and stripping. A separate study by Wang and co-workers used SKI-5 PM cis-1,4-polyisoprene in a wet-mixed silica compound: the silica/TESPT suspension was mixed at 50 °C and 20,000 rpm for 3 min, combined with a 5 wt% IR solution for 30 min at 300 rpm, coagulated in ethanol, micro-extruded, and vacuum-dried at 45 °C. Activators, accelerator, and sulfur were then incorporated on a two-roll mill at 70 °C for 5 min to form about 2.5 mm sheets, which were press-cured at 145 °C and 15 MPa for the formulation's measured t90. Neither schedule is a universal polyisoprene cure.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyisoprene materials comprise isoprene-chain elastomers; natural rubber retains nonisoprene components and a natural network, while synthetic polyisoprene microstructure is catalyst-controlled.
sections.properties: Strain-induced crystallization and tensile response depend on natural source, nonisoprene components, crosslinking, and chain microstructure.
sections.applications: The directly studied materials include vulcanized natural-rubber elastomer compounds.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Natural-rubber results cannot be applied unchanged to all polyisoprenes: biological source, nonisoprene content, cure state, and strain history define the reported response.

sections.overview: Fluoropolymers are a family of polymer materials made from fluorinated monomers and prepared by routes including emulsion polymerization. The family spans chemically distinct materials with different chain structures and compositions.
sections.nomenclature: Fluoropolymer is a collective family term rather than the name of one repeating-unit structure, grade, or product form. Individual materials such as PTFE, FEP, PVDF, and ETFE require their own names and evidence; their shared fluoropolymer classification does not make them interchangeable.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Fluoropolymers are a broad family defined by fluorine-containing polymer structures, not one polymerization route or one monomer. The family includes fluorinated olefin homopolymers and copolymers (for example materials derived from tetrafluoroethylene, vinylidene fluoride, chlorotrifluoroethylene, hexafluoropropylene, or fluorinated vinyl ethers), as well as side-chain-fluorinated polymers. Free-radical emulsion, suspension, solution, and bulk routes are documented for different members; monomer selection, initiator, medium, surfactant or chain-transfer agent, and feed ratios are therefore subfamily- and grade-specific. An open review covers fluorinated-monomer selection and emulsion-polymerization approaches, while a patent gives a bounded radical ethylene/tetrafluoroethylene example with initiator and chain-transfer-agent control. This family-level account does not treat any one PTFE, PVDF, ETFE, FEP, PFA, or fluoroelastomer recipe as universal, and excludes later compounding or article fabrication.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Fluoropolymers span melt-processable thermoplastics, non-melt-processable PTFE, elastomers, ionomers, and functional materials, so no single tensile strength or modulus represents the family. Mechanical response depends first on chemical identity and molecular architecture, then on crystallinity and thermal history, molecular weight/grade, filler or reinforcement, and finished form such as tube, film, coating, molded part, or elastomeric seal. An open comparative review illustrates the scale of this difference: it lists PTFE with a 550 MPa tensile modulus and 300–550% break elongation, but PVDF with 1,040–2,070 MPa and 50–250%, while ETFE is tabulated at 827 MPa and 150–300%. These are literature summary values for distinct fluoropolymers, not a property range for every commercial grade.

A bounded tubing comparison provides a method-tagged endpoint. Parker lists ASTM D638 tensile-strength ranges of 2,000–7,000 psi for PTFE tubing, 2,800–5,000 psi for FEP tubing, 4,000–4,500 psi for PFA tubing, and 4,500–6,200 psi for PVDF tubing. The values are specifically the supplier's general fluoropolymer-tubing comparison, and should not be transferred to other geometries, grades, or fluoroelastomer compounds.
sections.processing: Fluoropolymer processing is member- and grade-dependent. PTFE's high crystallinity and melt viscosity lead to compression or isostatic molding, ram or paste extrusion, and aqueous-dispersion coating/film casting, whereas melt-processable members such as FEP, PFA, ETFE, ECTFE, and PVDF can use thermoplastic extrusion, injection molding, film or sheet forming, and related operations. The open industry review reports FEP injection molding, extrusion, and film casting, PVDF processing around 200–260 °C, and ECTFE processing around 260–300 °C; it also notes that PTFE properties depend on particle size, sintering temperature, and pressure. For a bounded FEP 100 example, Chemours specifies 3 mm pellets, conventional melt extrusion and injection/compression/blow molding, corrosion-resistant high-nickel equipment, and equipment capability to 400 °C. These settings illustrate the family spread rather than a universal fluoropolymer window; melt viscosity, crystalline morphology, residence time, shear, and corrosive fumes require material-specific design and ventilation.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Fluoropolymers are polymers with fluorinated backbones or fluorinated side groups, ranging from highly crystalline homopolymers and copolymers to amorphous specialty materials. Carbon–fluorine-rich structures lower polarizability and surface energy and can strongly change chain packing and intermolecular interactions.
sections.properties: The family can provide chemical resistance, thermal stability, low surface energy, electrical insulation, low friction, and barrier behavior. These attributes are not universal: crystallinity, fluorine placement, comonomer content, molecular architecture, and processing history determine the response of an individual member.
sections.applications: Fluoropolymers are used in nonstick and low-friction surfaces, chemical-process linings, tubing, membranes, wire and cable insulation, coatings, seals, and high-purity fluid-handling components. The appropriate material depends on melt processability, service temperature, chemical environment, and required mechanical response.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Many fluoropolymers are expensive, difficult to process, or sensitive to high-temperature residence and contamination. Some require sintering or specialized equipment, while others creep under load or have limited adhesion and low-temperature toughness; family-level descriptions must not substitute for a specific grade or chemistry.

sections.overview: Polyurethanes are a family of urethane-linkage polymers formed by reacting polyols with di- or polyisocyanates. Isocyanate-ended prepolymers, chain extenders, catalysts, and water or other blowing components define the network or foam ultimately produced.
sections.nomenclature: PU is a family-level designation, not a single composition, foam density, elastomer, coating, or adhesive. The polyol type, isocyanate, chain extender, crosslinking level, and any blowing formulation distinguish individual polyurethane materials and must remain stated.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polyurethanes are produced by polyaddition of compounds bearing hydroxyl groups with di- or polyisocyanates, forming urethane linkages without a small-molecule condensation product. Common soft-segment feedstocks are polyether and polyester polyols; common isocyanates include methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, toluene diisocyanate, hexamethylene diisocyanate, and isophorone diisocyanate. Predominantly difunctional reactants plus short diol chain extenders can give linear thermoplastic polyurethane, whereas polyols or isocyanates with functionality above two create crosslinked foams, coatings, adhesives, and elastomers. A one-shot route mixes the reactive components together; a prepolymer route first reacts excess diisocyanate with a polyol and then chain-extends or crosslinks the isocyanate-terminated intermediate. Tertiary amines and organometallic catalysts such as tin carboxylates accelerate urethane formation. One cited patent documents conventional polyol/polyisocyanate chemistry and preformed tin-complex catalysts. A distinct patent covers water-stable titanium, zirconium, or hafnium catalyst systems, polyether/polyester polyols, polyisocyanates, chain extenders, and prepolymer variants. Water can react with isocyanate to generate urea linkages and carbon dioxide in foamed systems. Formulation-specific blowing, molding, and cure schedules remain Processing details.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
The polyurethane family covers mechanically dissimilar materials: flexible and rigid cellular foams, rubber-like segmented elastomers, thermoplastic polyurethanes, cast thermoset networks, coatings, and adhesives. In many solid segmented polyurethanes, mobile polyol-derived soft segments provide compliance while hydrogen-bonded or crystalline urethane-rich hard domains provide reinforcing physical crosslinks; covalent crosslinking can add permanent network restraint. Elastomeric grades can show nonlinear viscoelasticity, hysteresis, cyclic softening, and strain hardening, whereas highly crosslinked or rigid grades trade extensibility for stiffness. Cellular foams instead respond through cell-wall bending or stretching, collapse or buckling into a stress plateau, and eventual densification, so apparent density and cell structure can outweigh the neat matrix response. Polyol chemistry and molecular weight, isocyanate symmetry, chain extender, hard-segment fraction and ordering, NCO/OH ratio, crosslink density, hydrogen bonding and microphase separation, fillers or fibers, plasticizers, blowing level, open- versus closed-cell content, cell size and rise-direction anisotropy, cure and post-cure, moisture and hydrolytic history, temperature, loading rate, cyclic history, and specimen geometry are all consequential. Values from foams, elastomers, and coatings must therefore remain separate.

Patel and co-workers provide a bounded cellular example. They tested commercial Sawbones polyurethane foams as 9 mm-diameter cylinders, 3.9 or 7.7 mm long, in unconstrained quasi-static compression at 0.0033 s^-1 with no preload or preconditioning. The 0.09 g/cm^3 open-cell rigid foam gave Young's moduli of 0.08–0.93 MPa and yield strengths of 0.01–0.07 MPa; the 0.16 and 0.32 g/cm^3 closed-cell ASTM Grade 10 and 20 foams together gave moduli of 15.1–151.4 MPa and yield strengths of 0.9–4.5 MPa. Cylinder length affected the apparent result, and cores were taken in a preferred cellular orientation. These measurements demonstrate density-, cell-, orientation-, and geometry-sensitive foam behavior, not intrinsic constants for dense polyurethane or for the family.
sections.processing:
Polyurethane conversion must be organized by material subgroup rather than treated as one melt-processing window. Flexible and rigid foams are shaped by metering and mixing a polyol-side formulation with an isocyanate side, dispensing into an open or closed mold or by spray, and controlling cream, rise, gel, demold, and post-cure. Cast elastomers, coatings, adhesives, and reaction-injection-molded parts likewise use reactive mixing and an article-forming cure, whereas already polymerized thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) is dried and injection molded or extruded into film, sheet, tubing, profiles, cable jackets, and molded parts. For reactive systems, component identity and exact mass or volume ratio, moisture exclusion, preconditioning temperature, filler or pigment agitation, catalyst and blowing-agent distribution, mix quality, degassing, shot size, mold release, tool temperature, pressure, venting, exotherm, and cure/post-cure schedule control bubbles, cells, density, skin, knit lines, shrinkage, scorching, and conversion. Foam lines additionally depend on nucleation, pour pattern, cavity fill and venting, heat removal, and safe control of the rising exotherm. TPU processing depends on desiccant drying, moisture-protected transfer, shear and residence control, melt and mold or die temperature, cooling, drawdown, orientation, annealing, and blocking. Network-forming reaction chemistry and manufacture of polyurethane resin belong in Synthesis; here the reactive operation is included only as the shaping and cure schedule performed in the mold, on the substrate, or in the foam cavity.

The open family review directly documents foam, cast elastomer, coating, adhesive, reaction-injection-molding, and thermoplastic routes and shows why chain extender, catalyst, blowing agent, filler, and crosslinking choices define a formulation rather than a universal process. Two independent supplier examples bound practical settings. Honeywell's hand-mix foam evaluation guide conditions the named polyol premix near 10 °C, calls for 3–10 s mixing after isocyanate addition (5 s in its example), and requires prompt pouring for the rise test. Lubrizol's injection guide covers its Estane, Pearlthane, Isoplast, and Estaloc TPU portfolio from about 70 Shore A to 90 Shore D and advises allowing molded parts to rest 48 h before a 122 °C paint bake to reduce distortion from molded-in stress. The foam and TPU examples describe different polyurethane subgroups and cannot be combined into a family-wide window.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polyurethanes are urethane-linkage polymer families built from polyols and di- or polyisocyanates; prepolymer, chain extender, crosslinking, and blowing chemistry determine the particular architecture.
sections.properties: Foam compression response depends on cell structure, density, formulation, and test geometry.
sections.applications: Polyurethane is directly represented by open- and closed-cell commercial foam grades as well as polyurethane networks prepared from polyols and isocyanates.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A commercial foam-compression result or a catalyst formulation does not represent all PU: foam density, orientation, grade, formulation, cure, and compression geometry must remain stated.

sections.overview: Polysiloxanes are a family of silicone polymers with siloxane backbones, commonly produced by hydrolysis and condensation of organohalosilanes or by rearrangement of cyclic organosiloxanes. The organosilicon substituents define particular members of the family.
sections.nomenclature: Polysiloxane and silicone-polymer family are collective terms, not one fixed polymer composition. PDMS, fluorosilicones, vinyl-functional materials, and cured silicone elastomers are narrower polymers or networks whose substitution pattern and cure state should be named.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polysiloxanes contain Si–O–Si backbones bearing organic substituents and are commonly built in two stages. Organohalosilanes such as dimethyldichlorosilane are first hydrolyzed to silanols and cyclic or short linear siloxanes, with acid byproduct separated and the hydrolysate washed or neutralized. Those intermediates are then condensed or equilibrated to higher-molar-mass linear, branched, cyclic, or resinous products. Difunctional silanes favor chains, whereas tri- and tetrafunctional silanes introduce branching or networks; monofunctional silanes can cap chains. Ring-opening or redistribution polymerization of cyclic siloxanes is another defining route. One cited patent details controlled organohalosilane hydrolysis and separation of aqueous acid from a polyorganosiloxane hydrolysate. A distinct historical patent polymerizes fully condensed organosiloxanes with sodium- or potassium-alkoxide and alcohol–hydroxide catalysts. Acid or base catalysts, silanolate initiators, water balance, feed functionality, end blockers, and cyclic-monomer/initiator ratio provide architecture and molar-mass control. Subsequent crosslinking of functional polysiloxanes is described in the corresponding silicone-rubber or silicone-resin records.
sections.mechanicalProperties: Polysiloxanes include low-molar-mass fluids, crosslinked silicone elastomers, filled rubbers, resins, and functional copolymers, so a PDMS value cannot represent the whole family. Organosilicon substituents, chain length, network/cure chemistry and crosslink density, filler loading and dispersion, temperature, rate, aging, and test geometry govern response. A bounded commercial-elastomer example is Sylgard 184 PDMS tested at room temperature and 500 mm min−1: Young's modulus 3.9 ± 0.2 MPa, tensile strength 10 ± 1 MPa, and break elongation 119 ± 9%. These are one cured PDMS formulation's tensile values; other siloxane fluids, resins, and silicone-rubber grades can differ substantially.
sections.processing:
Polysiloxane processing depends strongly on whether the material is a low-viscosity silicone fluid, a liquid silicone rubber (LSR), a filled high-consistency elastomer, or a silicone-resin/encapsulant formulation; these forms should not be assigned one family-wide processing window. Liquid and resinous formulations are commonly metered, mixed with fillers or the second component, and degassed before casting, coating, encapsulation, or molding. Vacuum degassing reduces bubbles introduced by high-viscosity mixing, but excessive vacuum or residence time can remove volatile solvent and change the formulation; short pot life also limits hold-up in mixers, feed lines, and molds.

For article conversion, pour or inject low-viscosity silicone into an open, closed, or vacuum mold, then cure in the mold and cool before demolding; LSR injection molding uses cooled feed/mixing hardware to delay cure and a heated cavity for rapid crosslinking. Silicone coatings and encapsulants can be spread or cast onto a substrate and then thermally or otherwise cured, while selected polysiloxane precursor systems can be liquid-cast into thin films or patterned parts. Filled high-consistency silicone compounds require more intensive distributive mixing and may be compression-, transfer-, or extrusion-formed before cure. These operations are formulation- and equipment-specific: shear history changes dispersion and viscosity, trapped air causes voids, and premature cure can block a die, gate, or mold before filling. Cooling, post-cure, and controlled demolding are used when needed to complete conversion, reduce residual volatiles or stress, and preserve dimensions; cure shrinkage and exotherm matter particularly in thick castings and optical encapsulants.

A bounded open experiment by Ishikawa et al. used three liquid silicone rubbers with viscosities of 3–20 Pa·s in an in-vacuum molding system. The silicone was mixed and vacuum-defoamed, allowed about 1 min for air escape after transfer to the tank, poured into molds under vacuum, rested for 2 min after filling, and then cured; the method molded cylindrical structures of 1.2–5 mm diameter without bubbles. This is a soft-robotics molding demonstration for those liquid formulations and mold dimensions, not a general polysiloxane cure schedule. A separate silicone-encapsulant study used cast cylindrical specimens and showed why cure temperature, staged heating, room-temperature cooling, exotherm, and approximately 3% complete-cure shrinkage must be considered for a particular resin geometry.

The broad family therefore supports solution or liquid casting, coating, encapsulation, compression/transfer molding, LSR injection molding, and extrusion of suitable uncured compounds where the named formulation and equipment support them. It does not justify transferring silicone-rubber settings to uncured polysiloxane fluids, silicone resins, filled compounds, or already-cured articles; each grade requires its own viscosity, pot-life, shear, mold temperature, cure, cooling, and post-cure controls.
sections.structureAndMorphology: Polysiloxanes have Si–O backbones with organosilicon substituents; hydrolysis, condensation, and cyclic-siloxane rearrangement determine the chain structure of a specific silicone polymer.
sections.properties: PDMS elastomer behavior is strongly cure- and modification-dependent, as shown by systematic mechanical-property review.
sections.applications: Polysiloxane materials are directly represented by cured PDMS elastomer forms.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: A PDMS result does not describe all polysiloxanes: substitution pattern, molecular weight, crosslinker, cure, filler, and specimen geometry define a particular silicone material.

sections.overview: Styrenic block copolymers are block-copolymer families containing polystyrene blocks paired with diene or hydrogenated-diene blocks. Microphase separation makes many members useful as thermoplastic elastomers, adhesives, and modifiers.
sections.nomenclature: SBC abbreviates styrenic block copolymer. The family includes SBS, SIS, SEBS, SEPS, and related architectures; those members are narrower records rather than interchangeable aliases.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Styrenic block copolymers (SBCs) are sequence-defined polymers containing one or more glassy styrenic blocks and one or more lower-glass-transition blocks. Established thermoplastic-elastomer members include SBS and SIS, made from styrene with 1,3-butadiene or isoprene, and the selectively hydrogenated derivatives SEBS, SEPS, and SEEPS. The principal manufacturing route is living anionic polymerization in a rigorously dry hydrocarbon medium with an organolithium initiator. Sequential monomer charges can build linear A–B–A or multiblock chains; alternatively, living styrene–diene arms are reacted with a di- or multifunctional coupling agent to obtain linear, star, or radial architectures. Initiator amount and block-feed quantities set molar mass and block fraction, while polar modifiers and temperature control diene microstructure. Coupling efficiency sets arm number and residual diblock content. For hydrogenated SBCs, an unsaturated SBS, SIS, or mixed-butadiene/isoprene precursor is contacted with hydrogen and a transition-metal catalyst so that midblock carbon–carbon double bonds are reduced while aromatic styrene rings are largely retained. A cited patent family illustrates sequential and coupling strategies, and a distinct open review places living anionic, controlled radical, and coupling approaches in the broader block-copolymer synthesis landscape. Polymerization is terminated, stabilized, and followed by solvent/catalyst recovery. Polystyrene-rich domains form reversible physical junctions in the finished thermoplastic elastomer; that microphase association is not a covalent cure reaction.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
Styrenic block copolymers (SBCs) include SBS, SIS, and hydrogenated derivatives such as SEBS, SEPS, and SEEPS, as well as linear, star, and multiblock architectures; their mechanical properties therefore should not be represented by one family-wide numerical range. In a conventional ABA thermoplastic elastomer, glassy polystyrene-rich end-block domains sit within a continuous low-glass-transition midblock and act as reversible physical cross-links. Between the midblock and polystyrene glass-transition regions, this structure gives a soft rubbery plateau, large extensibility, and recoverable deformation without permanent chemical cross-linking. Loading can also produce hysteresis, stress softening, and residual set as chains and domains rearrange. Failure may involve end-block pullout from the hard domains, hard-domain rupture, or midblock scission. As temperature approaches the polystyrene-domain softening or order–disorder region, the physical network weakens, creep and permanent set increase, and the material ultimately flows; unsaturated SBS and SIS also lose performance through oxidation more readily than hydrogenated analogues.

Styrene fraction, block molecular weights and dispersity, total molecular weight, linear versus radial architecture, coupling efficiency and diblock content, the fraction of bridging versus loop or dangling chains, and sphere/cylinder/lamella morphology control stiffness, strength, toughness, elongation, hysteresis, and set. Midblock chemistry and microstructure, hydrogenation and any crystallinity, domain size and orientation, oils, tackifiers, fillers, reinforcement, polar functionalization, and blending create additional formulation dependence. Melt shear, cooling rate, annealing, molding orientation, service temperature, strain rate, cyclic history, and thermal or oxidative aging can all change the observed response. Neat hydrocarbon SBCs usually have little direct moisture sensitivity, but absorbed water can matter when polar modifications, hygroscopic additives, fillers, or weak interfaces are present.

One bounded family-member example comes from a 2025 review's data for neat commercial SIS (Quintac 3440): 19 wt% polystyrene, number-average molecular mass about 150 kg/mol, and dispersity 1.15. At a nominal tensile strain rate of 0.10 s−1, that material had Young's modulus 2.7 ± 0.03 MPa, maximum tensile stress 9.1 ± 0.2 MPa, reported break strain 29 ± 0.2 as a strain ratio (about 2900 ± 20% elongation), and tensile toughness 110 ± 1 MJ/m3. Dynamic shear on the same named SIS showed a storage-modulus plateau of about 0.8 MPa from −40 to 80 °C before flow associated with the polystyrene end blocks. These are SIS-grade results, not generic SBC values; the review does not provide the full specimen geometry, conditioning history, replicate count, or modern test-standard designation needed to transfer them to another subtype, compound, or process.
sections.processing:
Styrenic block copolymers are thermoplastic elastomers whose polystyrene-rich domains provide reversible physical junctions: heating permits flow and cooling rebuilds the network without a required chemical cure. Commercial SBC compounds can be injection molded, extruded or coextruded into profiles, sheet, film, and wire coatings, and—when melt strength is sufficient—blown as film or hollow articles. Compounding with oils, tackifiers, polyolefins, fillers, pigments, and stabilizers is common; adhesive formulations are also applied by hot-melt or solution coating and lamination. Grade architecture, unsaturated versus hydrogenated midblock, styrene and diblock content, oil and filler loading, feed consistency, melt temperature, screw shear and residence time, gate or die geometry, solvent removal, cooling, and orientation govern flow, recovery, surface quality, and dimensional stability. Excess shear can separate a formulation or create gate splay, soft molded parts need sufficient cooling for clean ejection, high temperature can volatilize oil, and unsaturated SBS/SIS generally tolerate less thermal and oxidative exposure than hydrogenated SEBS/SEPS. Polymerization and selective hydrogenation belong in Synthesis; compounding and article shaping belong here.

Avient's supplier bulletin says its SBC TPEs normally do not require drying, but separates its formulation guidance by chemistry: SBS/SIS-based grades at 290–350 °F (about 143–177 °C), with possible gels and discoloration above 400 °F (about 204 °C), versus harder, at-least-40-Shore-A SEBS/SEPS grades at 350–410 °F (about 177–210 °C), with degradation possible above 460 °F (about 238 °C). These are GLS compound observations, not universal family windows. As a distinct operating example, Ilyin and co-workers compounded a named 44 wt% styrene SIS (Vector 4411A) with specified oil and asphaltene/resin contents in a twin-rotor mixer at 120 °C for 20 min and 60 rpm, then laminated 160 ± 20 µm films between siliconized PET at 120 °C without curing. That demonstration applies to those SIS adhesive formulations and illustrates one conversion path within the wider SBC family.

sections.overview: Polycarbonate/ABS is a polymer blend combining polycarbonate with acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene. It is a multiphase material system whose behavior depends on blend composition, compatibilization, and formulation.
sections.nomenclature: PC/ABS and PC-ABS are common names for the polycarbonate/ABS blend. They denote a blend, not a chain copolymer or a single repeat-unit polymer, and should not be collapsed into either parent polymer record.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Polycarbonate/ABS (PC/ABS) is a physical thermoplastic blend of preformed polycarbonate and acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene graft polymer; it is not a single copolymerization product. Manufacture normally dry-blends or melt-compounds the two resins in a mixer or single- or twin-screw extruder, with composition, ABS rubber morphology, compatibilizer, impact modifier, stabilizer, and mixing history used to control the dispersed phase and final balance of properties. One cited patent combines a bisphenol-A PC continuous phase with ABS/MBS dispersed phases by blending and extrusion. A distinct patent describes dry- or melt-blending PC/ABS with an ethylene-ester modifier package. Those modifier recipes are bounded examples, not required ingredients of every PC/ABS grade. The synthesis of the PC and ABS components belongs to their respective entries; this tab addresses formation of the named blend.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PC/ABS is a multiphase blend rather than a statistical copolymer: polycarbonate and styrene–acrylonitrile-rich glassy regions carry most of the elastic load, while polybutadiene-containing ABS domains can cavitate and initiate distributed plastic deformation that dissipates fracture energy. Properly formulated material can therefore combine yield strength and stiffness with less notch-sensitive, lower-temperature ductility than a comparable neat PC, but its response is not a simple average of PC and ABS. PC:ABS ratio, ABS manufacturing route, rubber fraction and particle-size distribution, SAN acrylonitrile content and molar mass, PC molar mass, grafting and interphase adhesion, dispersed versus co-continuous morphology, compatibilizers, flame retardants and fillers, recycled-chain degradation, compounding history, injection-flow orientation and weld lines, residual stress, specimen thickness and notch radius, temperature, rate, and environmental stress cracking all alter yield and fracture. A formulation can gain energy absorption in a low-temperature brittle regime yet lose strength or high-temperature ductile fracture energy as its rubber-rich fraction rises.

A bounded commercial example is SABIC CYCOLOY CX7211, an injection-moldable, medium-flow, non-halogenated flame-retardant PC/ABS grade. SABIC reports ASTM D638 Type I tensile yield stress of 66 MPa, break stress of 60 MPa, yield strain of 4%, and break strain of 98% at 50 mm/min, with a 2950 MPa tensile modulus measured at 5 mm/min. ASTM D256 notched Izod impact is listed as 625 J/m at 23 °C and 125 J/m at −30 °C. These are typical laboratory values for a proprietary flame-retardant grade, not a PC/ABS family envelope; PC:ABS ratio, rubber morphology, specimen conditioning and molding record, color package, and statistical scatter are not disclosed, and the accompanying molding window is only general guidance. Independent work on dispersed and co-continuous research blends confirms the scope problem: ABS structure and content, rubber content, temperature, rate, thickness, and notch geometry changed brittle-to-ductile behavior, and the rubber phase reduced constraint ahead of sharp notches. Those mechanisms explain variability but do not make the CX7211 numbers transferable to another formulation.
sections.processing: PC/ABS blends are compounded and converted as two-phase engineering thermoplastics by dry blending followed by twin-screw or other melt mixing, pelletizing, drying, and injection molding; extrusion and sheet/profile routes are also possible for grades designed for them. The dispersed ABS rubber/styrene phase, PC:ABS ratio, flame retardant or glass-fiber package, moisture, and residence time determine flow, weld-line behavior, impact response, and thermal stability. A bounded LyondellBasell PC/ABS-1003 injection/general-purpose grade example calls for drying at 90–100 °C for 2–4 h, barrel/melt temperatures in approximately the 230–272 °C range, and 40–100 °C mold temperature; those settings apply to that grade and machine/product context. An independent patent describes dry pre-blending of preformed PC and ABS with modifiers, melt mixing in extruders, blenders, kneaders, or roll mixers, and pelletizing before article molding. Polymerization of either constituent belongs in Synthesis; this section covers blend compounding, pellet drying, melt shaping, and molding.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PC/ABS is a polymer blend with a polycarbonate-rich continuous phase and dispersed or compatibilized acrylonitrile–butadiene–styrene domains. The rubbery butadiene-containing phase toughens the glassy thermoplastic matrix, while styrenic and acrylonitrile components influence flow and chemical response.
sections.properties: PC/ABS combines impact toughness, dimensional stability, processing ease, and surface quality with better flow than many neat polycarbonates. Heat resistance, flame response, gloss, chemical resistance, and toughness depend on blend ratio, morphology, additives, and processing orientation.
sections.applications: The cited evidence supports PC/ABS as an injection-molded blend and as an automotive-oriented alloy formulation. Appliance, electronic, flame-retarded, and reinforced uses remain grade-specific extensions of that blend scope.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Phase morphology and interfacial adhesion are sensitive to blend ratio, compatibilizer, moisture, shear, cooling, and thermal history. PC/ABS can suffer solvent stress cracking, heat or UV aging, and weld-line weakness; a flame-retarded or filled grade is not equivalent to the base blend.

sections.overview: Poly(phenylene ether)/polystyrene is a polymer blend combining preformed PPE with polystyrene. Its mechanical response changes with blend composition and with use of ordinary versus rubber-modified polystyrene, so it is a material family of blends rather than a single polymer molecule.
sections.nomenclature: PPE/PS and PPO/PS denote the physical blend of poly(phenylene ether) and polystyrene. This record excludes neat PPE and neat polystyrene, as well as blends with additional impact modifiers or polyolefin components unless those components are explicitly named.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Poly(phenylene ether)/polystyrene (PPE/PS, often called PPO/PS) is a physical thermoplastic blend, not a covalent copolymer. The usual composition combines preformed poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene ether) or a related PPE with polystyrene or a specified styrenic resin; changing the PS to high-impact PS or adding a separate modifier produces a compositionally different material. A foundational patent reports dry blending granular PPE and PS followed by single-screw extrusion, with composition as an explicit control. A separate process patent describes high-shear twin-screw melt blending of a PPE/PS blend with hydrogenated block-copolymer/polyolefin modifiers. Those modifier levels and extrusion conditions define the disclosed modified formulation, not the identity of every PPE/PS blend. The blend manufacture must remain distinct from oxidative coupling used to make PPE and radical polymerization used to make PS.
sections.mechanicalProperties:
PPE/PS materials are amorphous engineering-thermoplastic blends whose response spans brittle, relatively low-heat polystyrene-rich compositions through stiffer, higher-temperature PPE-rich compositions. PPE and ordinary styrenic resin can form a compatible glassy phase, but commercial families also use rubber-modified high-impact polystyrene or separate impact modifiers; their dispersed elastomer particles can promote cavitation, crazing, and shear yielding, greatly changing notched impact and elongation. The PPE-to-PS ratio is therefore a primary control on modulus, yield strength, ductility, heat-dependent stiffness, and creep. Other consequential variables include the type, amount, particle size, and dispersion of the rubber phase; PPE and PS molar mass; flame-retardant or plasticizing additives; glass or mineral reinforcement; compounding and molding history; weld lines and flow orientation; physical aging; specimen thickness and notch geometry; loading rate; and test temperature. The family absorbs relatively little moisture, but drying and thermal history can still affect molding quality and defects.

A bounded commercial example is SABIC NORYL HNA055, an unreinforced, injection-moldable PPE/PS grade. Its 2024 product sheet reports typical ASTM D638 values from Type I laboratory coupons tested at 50 mm/min: 2480 MPa tensile modulus, 67 MPa yield stress, 55 MPa break stress, 4.8% yield strain, and 16.3% break strain. ASTM D256 notched Izod impact is reported as 293 J/m at 23 °C and 144 J/m at −30 °C, directly illustrating temperature-sensitive impact response for this formulation. The sheet does not disclose the PPE/PS ratio, impact-modifier chemistry, coupon molding details, or conditioning, and states that its data are indicative rather than design or specification values. These numbers therefore belong only to HNA055 laboratory coupons under the named methods, not to PPE/PS blends generally.
sections.processing:
Poly(phenylene ether)/polystyrene (PPE/PS) blends are amorphous thermoplastics commonly converted by injection molding; suitable extrusion grades can also be made into sheet, profile, or filament, and commercial filament demonstrates fused-filament fabrication (FFF). Moisture uptake is modest, but suppliers still prescribe predrying for demanding high-temperature conversion. Melt temperature, screw speed, back pressure, shot size, mold or build-platform temperature, and cooling determine fill, residual stress, warpage, surface quality, and dimensional stability. Values should be taken from the selected blend grade because PPE/PS ratio, impact modification, flame retardants, fillers, and molecular weight change viscosity and thermal requirements.

For injection molding, SABIC's non-reinforced NORYL HNA055 PPE/PS grade is one bounded example: the October 2024 sheet gives 105–110 °C drying for 3–4 h, a maximum moisture content of 0.02%, melt and nozzle temperatures of 295–315 °C, mold temperature of 75–105 °C, back pressure of 0.3–0.7 MPa, screw speed of 20–100 rpm, and a shot occupying 30–70% of cylinder capacity. The sheet says these are guidelines, not specifications, and may need adjustment for thin walls, large parts, low shot size, or gas-assist molding. As a distinct FFF example, 3DXTECH reports test specimens from THERMAX PPE/PS filament printed on an open-source machine through a 0.4 mm nozzle with 0.25 mm layers, 100% ±45° infill, 310 °C extrusion, a 120 °C bed, and XY-flat orientation. Neither schedule should be transferred to another PPE/PS composition without grade-specific trials.

sections.overview: Unplasticized poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC-U) is the rigid PVC material made from vinyl chloride polymer and formulated without flexibilizing plasticizer. The PVC base is commonly produced by free-radical suspension polymerization, while stabilizers, lubricants, and processing aids may still be present in a rigid formulation.
sections.nomenclature: PVC-U and UPVC are abbreviations for unplasticized poly(vinyl chloride). The record is the rigid, non-plasticized PVC formulation boundary; flexible plasticized PVC, chlorinated PVC, and a particular stabilized article are not alternate names for the base material.
sections.feedstocksAndSynthesis: Unplasticized poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC-U or uPVC) is a rigid PVC formulation, not a different repeat-unit polymer. Its base resin is made by free-radical addition polymerization of vinyl chloride monomer, most often by aqueous suspension polymerization for general-purpose rigid compounds. In a cited historical suspension route, droplets of vinyl chloride are dispersed in water with poly(vinyl alcohol) or another protective colloid and an oil-soluble peroxide or azo initiator; a nonionic dispersant and controlled aqueous pH are route-specific options used to manage particle size and reactor scale. The resulting PVC grains are separated from water, stripped of residual monomer, washed as needed, and dried. Polymerization temperature and initiator system govern chain length, while suspending-agent package, agitation, conversion, and droplet stability govern grain morphology, porosity, and later fusion behavior. The resin becomes PVC-U through compounding without an intentionally added flexibilizing plasticizer. Heat stabilizer is required because PVC can eliminate hydrogen chloride during hot conversion; internal and external lubricants manage fusion and wall friction, while processing aids, impact modifiers, fillers, pigments, and ultraviolet stabilizers are optional according to the application. A cited rigid composition starts from mass- or suspension-polymerized PVC and adds an organotin stabilizer, acrylic processing aids, toner, and both internal and external lubricants but no plasticizer, illustrating the boundary between rigid compounding and plasticized PVC. Additive identity and level, resin K-value, particle morphology, and fusion history control the final compound. Article-shaping temperatures and equipment settings belong in Processing.
sections.mechanicalProperties: PVC-U is the rigid, unplasticized PVC grade family: it is stiff and hard at ordinary temperatures, with a comparatively low glass-transition region (about 80–90 °C in the cited thermal analysis) that makes temperature important to stiffness and deformation. Formulation (especially impact modifier, filler, stabilizer, and pigment package), molecular mass, degree of fusion/gelation, residual stress, processing route, section thickness, weldlines, orientation in pipe or profile extrusion, temperature, and impact-test geometry all affect strength and toughness. An open materials overview identifies degree of gelation as a PVC-U quality variable directly linked to impact strength, and its reference modulus is 2.7–3.0 GPa; it also reports low water absorption as a characteristic. As a tightly bounded product example, Noltewerk’s unmodified PVC-U sheet/rod stock lists 58 MPa tensile strength and 3.30 GPa tensile modulus by DIN EN ISO 527, plus 4 kJ/m² notch toughness by ISO 179. These are supplier reference values for that stock form with no specimen conditioning, test temperature, compound recipe, or impact-specimen geometry provided, not design values or a universal PVC-U range.
sections.processing:
Unplasticized PVC is normally converted as a formulated rigid compound rather than neat resin. Resin powder is dry-blended or melt-compounded with heat stabilizers, lubricants, pigments and, where required, fillers, impact modifiers, and processing aids; the absence of a plasticizer does not mean the absence of other additives. Profile, pipe, and sheet extrusion are central routes, with injection molding used for fittings and other rigid parts. The wider PVC fabrication record also documents calendering, blow molding, compression molding, and solvent casting, but their relevance depends on the rigid formulation and article. Extrusion must develop adequate fusion or gelation without imposing excessive temperature, shear, or residence time: streamlined corrosion-resistant tooling, controlled screw load, venting, prompt sizing and cooling, and avoidance of dead spots help limit discoloration and hydrogen-chloride evolution. Start-up, shutdown, purging, and die cleaning are consequently part of the processing window, not just maintenance details.

Teknor Apex's guide is guidance for its class of rigid-PVC dryblend extrusion compounds, not a family-wide prescription. It says drying is not required, calls for a conical or parallel twin-screw extruder with vacuum venting, and gives barrel, die, and measured-melt ranges of 325–365 °F (163–185 °C), 345–365 °F (174–185 °C), and 370–390 °F (188–199 °C), respectively. It also permits up to 20% regrind blended with virgin compound, recommends slowly increasing screw speed while monitoring load, lists vacuum sizing, spray-tank sizing, or air-rack sizing downstream, and directs processors to purge residual PVC and neutralize hydrochloric-acid residue before rust protection. Those settings belong to the guide's dryblend compounds and equipment assumptions.
sections.structureAndMorphology: PVC-U is rigid PVC compounded without plasticizer; stabilizers, processing aids, lubricants, and gelation state define a particular formulation.
sections.properties: Modulus, notch toughness, and glass-transition behavior are production- and gelation-dependent.
sections.applications: PVC-U is directly supplied as sheet and rod stock and as rigid compound.
sections.limitationsAndVariability: Standard-property tables do not apply to plasticized PVC or every rigid compound; resin, additives, gelation, and production history matter.
